title: Proposition 13.24.8
text: Proposition 13.24.8 . 20027E32C14E Let $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. The conditions \[  \nu (v\circ \pi ,E)=b(E)\text{ for every }\pi ,E, \qquad v\sim _{\mathcal I}u  \] are equivalent. Under either condition, \[  q=P_\theta [v]_{\mathcal I}=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}\sim u,  \] and every $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $w\sim q$ satisfies 027648EDCB33 13.24.9 \begin{equation}  \int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (w) =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q) =\int _ XR^2>0. \end{equation} The background is big and $X$ has the bounded mass property. Proof. Ideal profile and envelope. Choose an integer $C>A$ with $C\kappa \geq \theta $. Both $u$ and $v$ are $C\kappa $-plurisubharmonic. The projective valuative characterization of all-weight ideal types applies in this closed background: generic orders on all smooth projective modifications recover point Lelong numbers by further point blowups, and equality of those numbers is equivalent to ideal equivalence. The stated profile therefore implies $v\sim _{\mathcal I}u$. Conversely, ideal equivalence pulls back under every compact modification by lemma 5.43.23 ; the local valuative criterion theorem 5.37.3 then gives equality of generic coefficients on every such modification. The common factor between growth against $\log |z|$ and the book's $\log |z|^2$ convention does not affect these equalities. The potential $u$ has complex Hessian $S-A\kappa $. By corollary 18.4.9 , its ordinary and ideal envelopes agree and are ordinarily equivalent to $u$. Ideal equivalence identifies the defining families for the two ideal envelopes in the statement, proving the assertion about $q$. The inequality $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq R>0$ proves bigness. For any Hermitian form $h$ on $X$, choose $D$ with $D\kappa \geq h$. Bounded $h$-plurisubharmonic potentials are $D\kappa $-plurisubharmonic, and positivity of bounded mixed products bounds their masses by $\int _ X(D\kappa )^2=D^2$. This proves the bounded mass property. The bounded residual. Fix $w\sim u$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and put $T=C\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$. Its base divisorial coefficients are $a_ j$, so divisorial removal and passage through increasing finite sums give \[  K=T-S=(C-A)\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\geq 0,\qquad h=w-u.  \] The distributional difference has a canonical quasi-plurisubharmonic representative, which is bounded by ordinary equivalence and almost-everywhere order. Thus $K$ has bounded local potentials, and its trace charges no pluripolar set. The current $S$ is carried by the actual pole union $\bigcup _ jH_ j\subset \{ w=-\infty \} $. Thus $\langle T\rangle =K$. For every smooth real $(1,1)$-form $L$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}L=0$, distributional Stokes gives \[  \int _ X L\wedge \langle T\rangle =(C-A)\int _ XL\wedge \kappa .  \] Closed top mass and smooth correction. Put $T_ u=C\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=S+(C-A)\kappa $. For the finite partial sums $u_ N=\sum _{j\leq N}a_ j\ell _ j$, the closed non-pluripolar mass is $(C-\sum _{j\leq N}a_ j)^2$: outside the finite divisor union the current is the smooth residual, and the measure gives that union zero mass. Since $u_0\leq u_ N$, closed-background mass monotonicity, the closed case of theorem 13.17.1 , gives \[  \int _ X\langle T_ u^2\rangle \leq \left(C-\sum _{j\leq N}a_ j\right)^2.  \] For the reverse inequality, locally write $S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b$ with $b$ plurisubharmonic. The currents $(C-A)\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max (b,-k)$ have bounded local potentials and dominate $(C-A)\kappa $. Their squared products, restricted to $\{ b>-k\} $, therefore dominate $(C-A)^2\kappa ^2$ on that set. Letting $k$ increase and using the local truncation definition gives $\langle T_ u^2\rangle \geq (C-A)^2\kappa ^2$. The two bounds prove equality of total masses. Closed mass invariance under bounded changes then gives \[  \int _ X\langle T^2\rangle =(C-A)^2.  \] Set $L=C\kappa -\theta \geq 0$, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}L=0$. Expanding the bounded products of $\max (w,-k)$ in the two backgrounds and restricting to $\{ w>-k\} $ gives, in the limit, \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (w) =\langle T^2\rangle -2L\wedge \langle T\rangle +L^2.  \] All correction measures are finite: the closed top measure has the mass just computed, the degree-one limit is $K$, and the smooth measure $L^2$ gives the pole set zero mass. The same truncations are used in both backgrounds, so this identity is an equality of Borel measures. Integrating yields \[  \int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (w) =(C-A)^2-2(C-A)\int _ XL\wedge \kappa +\int _ XL^2 =\int _ X(\theta -A\kappa )^2.  \] This holds throughout the ordinary type, proving both singularity-volume identities and their strict positivity. $\square$

title: Equation 13.24.9
text: 027648EDCB33 13.24.9 \begin{equation}  \int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (w) =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (q) =\int _ XR^2>0. \end{equation}

title: Example 13.24.10
text: Example 13.24.10 . E76D9C1B44B6 There is a nonclosed pluriclosed background on $\mathbb P^2$ with a nonanalytic ideal type satisfying 13.24.8 . Its prescribed divisors are not contained in a single pencil, and both singularity volumes of its ideal model are at least $1/16$. Proof. In a coordinate ball choose a smooth real cutoff $\chi $ equal to one near the origin, and extend $\alpha =\chi |z_2|^2\mathrm dz_1$ by zero. Put \[  \tau =\partial \overline\alpha +\bar\partial \alpha .  \] It is real and smooth, with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\tau =0$. Where $\chi =1$, \[  \mathrm d\tau =\mathrm dz_2\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_2 \wedge (\mathrm dz_1-\mathrm d\bar z_1)\ne 0.  \] Choose $\epsilon >0$ small enough that $\theta =\kappa +\epsilon \tau \geq \kappa /2$. Set $A=1/4$, $a_ j=A2^{-j}$, $t_ j=2^{-j}$ and \[  H_ j=\{ Z_0+t_ jZ_1+t_ j^2Z_2=0\} .  \] The Vandermonde determinant shows that any three defining linear forms are independent; hence the hyperplanes are not in one pencil. Here $R=\theta -A\kappa \geq \kappa /4$, so $\int _ XR^2\geq 1/16$. The preceding proposition gives the mass throughout the ordinary type and both singularity volumes. There are infinitely many positive base divisor coefficients. An analytic singularity on a compact manifold has only finitely many prime divisorial components, so no analytic potential has this ideal type. $\square$

title: Problem 13.24.11
text: Problem 13.24.11 . D0837305A3CF For a big nonclosed background $\theta $ on a manifold with the bounded mass property, find criteria for $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I})>0$ in terms of restricted multiplier ideals or divisorial orders. When this lower volume vanishes, which implications between envelope equality and upper-volume equality, conditions (i) and (ii) of proposition 13.24.2 , remain valid?

title: 13.25 Model comparison under background changes
text: A smooth change of decomposition $(\theta ,u)\mapsto (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f,u-f)$ preserves the curvature current but changes the zero obstacle used to normalize models. Taking the ordinary envelope again gives an exact correspondence that preserves the volume comparison. An increase of the background changes the volumes; a common positive lower-volume bound controls this change uniformly, and this allows analytic approximants whose curvature error tends to zero. Proposition 13.25.1 . 61209D2B61BD Let $f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$ and $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$. For every $\delta >0$, the map \[  G_ f:\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )\longrightarrow \mathcal M_\delta (\theta '), \qquad G_ f(p)=P_{\theta '}[p-f],  \] is a bijection with inverse $q\mapsto P_\theta [q+f]$. It preserves both singularity volumes, and \[  d_{\theta '}(G_ f(p),G_ f(q))=d_\theta (p,q).  \] It takes analytic models to analytic models and ideal models to ideal models. Proof. The map $u\mapsto u-f$ is a bijection from $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ')$ that preserves curvature currents, singularity types and hence both singularity volumes. Also $\max (u-f,v-f)=\max (u,v)-f$, so \[  d_{\theta '}(u-f,v-f)=d_\theta (u,v).  \] By proposition 18.5.1 , $G_ f(p)+f\sim p$, that is, $G_ f(p)\sim p-f$. Thus $G_ f(p)$ has the same volumes as $p$, and it is an ordinary model by theorem 13.19.5 ; in particular $G_ f(p)\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta ')$. Since the volume comparison depends only on ordinary types, the displayed identity follows. Taking the ordinary envelope of $G_ f(p)+f\sim p$ gives $P_\theta [G_ f(p)+f]=P_\theta [p]=p$. The same argument with the two backgrounds interchanged proves that the map is bijective with the stated inverse. Subtraction of a smooth function and bounded changes preserve analytic singularities. If $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$, proposition 18.5.1 also gives \[  P_{\theta '}[p-f]_{\mathcal I}\sim p-f\sim G_ f(p).  \] The ideal envelope is an ordinary model by corollary 18.4.4 , and ordinary models of the same ordinary type coincide; hence $P_{\theta '}[G_ f(p)]_{\mathcal I}=P_{\theta '}[p-f]_{\mathcal I}=G_ f(p)$. The inverse map gives the converse. $\square$ For the rest of this section and the next, fix a Hermitian form $h$ on $X$, a Hermitian form $\Omega \geq \theta +2h$, a rational number $\kappa >0$ and an analytic $\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\rho \leq 0$ and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \kappa h$; such $\kappa $ and $\rho $ exist by bigness and theorem 5.36.1 . Put $K=v_+(\Omega )$. For $\delta >0$, set \[  b_\delta =1+\frac{\delta }{2^{n+1}nK},\qquad \kappa _\delta =(1-b_\delta ^{-1})\kappa .  \] These constants stay fixed while the potentials and backgrounds vary. Proposition 13.25.2 . F274299A5A71 Let $\beta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form with $\theta \leq \beta \leq \theta +h$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\beta )$ satisfy $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\beta (u)\geq \delta >0$. For every $\varepsilon \in [0,1]$ and every smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\gamma $ with $\beta \leq \gamma \leq \beta +\varepsilon h$, both singularity volumes satisfy \[  \operatorname {vol}_\beta (u) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\gamma (u) \leq (1+\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n\operatorname {vol}_\beta (u).  \] Proof. Normalize $u\leq 0$, so that $u\leq V_\beta $, and note that $\rho \leq V_\beta $. Since $\Omega \geq \beta $ and $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\beta (u)\geq \delta $, lemma 13.20.1 , applied in the big background $\beta $, shows that $H=Q_{b_\delta }(u,V_\beta )$ is defined. The potential \[  w=b_\delta ^{-1}H+(1-b_\delta ^{-1})\rho  \] satisfies $w\leq u$ and $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq (1-b_\delta ^{-1})(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )\geq \kappa _\delta h$. The addition argument in the proof of proposition 13.20.6 , with $h$, $\kappa _\delta $ and $t=\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta $ in place of $\omega $, $\delta $ and $t$, therefore gives the upper bound, with constants independent of $\beta $ and $u$. The lower bound is volume monotonicity. $\square$ Corollary 13.25.3 . 1ED63BC3072B Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ have lower volume at least $\delta >0$, and let $\eta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form with $\theta \leq \eta \leq \theta +\varepsilon h$, where $0\leq \varepsilon \leq 1$. Then 9EE86F88EB92 13.25.4 \begin{equation}  \left|d_\eta (P_\eta [u],P_\eta [v])-d_\theta (u,v)\right| \leq 2K\left((1+\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n-1\right). \end{equation} Proof. The preceding proposition, with $\beta =\theta $ and $\gamma =\eta $, applies to $u$, $v$ and $m=\max (u,v)$, and their upper volumes in background $\theta $ are at most $v_+(\Omega )=K$. Thus, for $x=u,v,m$, the errors \[  e_ x=\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\eta (x) -\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (x)  \] lie between zero and $K((1+\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n-1)$. The difference $d_\eta (u,v)-d_\theta (u,v)$ equals $2e_ m-e_ u-e_ v$, whose absolute value is at most twice this bound. Finally, the projection invariance in proposition 13.22.4 , applied in background $\eta $, gives $d_\eta (u,v)=d_\eta (P_\eta [u],P_\eta [v])$, which is the comparison appearing in ( 13.25.4 ). $\square$ In particular, for $p_ j,p\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ and $\theta \leq \eta _ j\leq \theta +\varepsilon _ jh$ with $\varepsilon _ j\to 0$, \[  d_\theta (p_ j,p)\longrightarrow 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad d_{\eta _ j}(P_{\eta _ j}[p_ j],P_{\eta _ j}[p])\longrightarrow 0.  \] Here the backgrounds $\eta _ j$ need not be monotone in $j$. The next result allows the analytic approximants themselves to belong only to the larger backgrounds $\eta _ j$. Theorem 13.25.5 . CBA354870D02 Let $p$ be an ordinary model of positive lower volume, and let $\eta _ j$ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms with $\theta \leq \eta _ j\leq \theta +\varepsilon _ jh$, where $\varepsilon _ j\geq 0$ tends to zero. Then $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$ if and only if there are analytic $a_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta _ j)$ with \[  d_{\eta _ j}(a_ j,p)\longrightarrow 0.  \] The $a_ j$ may be required to be ordinary models in their respective backgrounds. Given any such analytic approximants, convex combinations with the fixed potential $\rho $, with rational coefficients, produce analytic $b_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ whose ordinary envelopes satisfy \[  d_\theta (P_\theta [b_ j],p)\longrightarrow 0, \qquad P_\theta [b_ j]\longrightarrow p \quad \text{in }L^1\text{ and capacity}.  \] Proof. Suppose first that $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$. By theorem 13.24.3 , there are analytic ordinary models $r_ j$ in background $\theta $ with $d_\theta (r_ j,p)\to 0$ and a common positive lower-volume bound. Corollary 13.25.3 and projection invariance in background $\eta _ j$ give $d_{\eta _ j}(r_ j,p)\to 0$, so $a_ j=r_ j$ works. One can also use the ordinary models $a_ j=P_{\eta _ j}[r_ j]$, since $P_{\eta _ j}[r_ j]\sim r_ j$ by proposition 18.4.8 . Conversely, suppose that such $a_ j$ exist. Normalize them below zero, and put $m_ j=\max (a_ j,p)$ and $\delta =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)>0$. Inequality ( 13.22.2 ) and proposition 13.25.2 give \[  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(a_ j),\quad \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(m_ j) \longrightarrow \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p).  \] Indeed, the upper volume of $p$ in background $\eta _ j$ tends to its upper volume in background $\theta $, and the differences of $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(a_ j)$ and $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(m_ j)$ from $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(p)$ are bounded in absolute value by $d_{\eta _ j}(a_ j,p)$. Enlarge the errors $\varepsilon _ j$ to positive rational numbers tending to zero, and put \[  c_ j=\frac{\kappa }{\kappa +\varepsilon _ j},\qquad b_ j=c_ ja_ j+(1-c_ j)\rho ,\qquad r_ j=P_\theta [b_ j].  \] As in the proof of theorem 13.24.3 , $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ j\geq 0$ and $b_ j$ has analytic singularities. Choose $A>0$ with $\theta \leq Ah$, and set \[  \widehat\theta _ j=\theta +(1+A/\kappa )\varepsilon _ jh, \qquad \widehat m_ j=P_{\widehat\theta _ j}[m_ j].  \] Then $\widehat\theta _ j\geq \eta _ j$ and $c_ j\widehat\theta _ j\geq \theta $. Since $r_ j\sim b_ j$ and $\rho \leq 0$, the potential $r_ j/c_ j$ is a nonpositive $\widehat\theta _ j$-plurisubharmonic function more singular than $a_ j$, hence more singular than $m_ j$. Therefore $r_ j\leq c_ j\widehat m_ j$. Also $p\leq \widehat m_ j\leq c_ j\widehat m_ j$. The lower volume of $m_ j$ in background $\eta _ j$ is at least $\delta $. For large $j$, proposition 13.25.2 applies with $\beta =\eta _ j$, $\gamma =\widehat\theta _ j$ and $\varepsilon =(1+A/\kappa )\varepsilon _ j$. Consequently \[  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\widehat\theta _ j}(m_ j) \longrightarrow \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p).  \] By theorem 13.19.5 , $\widehat m_ j$ has the same upper volume in background $\widehat\theta _ j$ as $m_ j$. On the other hand, \[  c_ j\eta _ j+(1-c_ j)(\theta -\kappa h)\leq \theta .  \] Addition, applied to $c_ ja_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,c_ j\eta _ j)$ and $(1-c_ j)\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,(1-c_ j)(\theta -\kappa h))$, and background monotonicity therefore bound the upper volume of $b_ j$ below by $c_ j^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(a_ j)$. Since $r_ j\sim b_ j$, the two comparisons yield \[  \begin{split}  c_ j^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(a_ j) & \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (r_ j) \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\max (r_ j,p))\\ & \leq c_ j^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\widehat\theta _ j}(m_ j). \end{split}  \] Here the last inequality uses $\theta \leq c_ j\widehat\theta _ j$ and $\max (r_ j,p)\leq c_ j\widehat m_ j$. Both outer terms tend to $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$, which proves $d_\theta (r_ j,p)\to 0$. By proposition 18.4.8 , $r_ j=P_\theta [b_ j]_{\mathcal I}$ is an ideal model, so theorem 13.24.5 gives $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$. For large $j$, the upper-volume deficit from $r_ j$ to $\max (r_ j,p)$ is small, and lemma 13.18.1 with $b=2$ gives a convex lower bound for $r_ j$ whose first term is $\frac12\max (r_ j,p)$. Volume addition gives $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (r_ j)\geq 2^{-n}\delta $. Thus proposition 13.22.4 , theorem 13.23.3 give the asserted $L^1$ and capacity convergence of the models $r_ j$. $\square$ Since the volume comparison depends only on singularity types, the theorem asserts convergence of the ordinary models $P_\theta [b_ j]$, not of the analytic potentials $b_ j$ themselves. When the background errors may have either sign, $p$ need not be admissible in the perturbed backgrounds; the next section constructs reference models there.

title: Proposition 13.25.1
text: Proposition 13.25.1 . 61209D2B61BD Let $f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$ and $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$. For every $\delta >0$, the map \[  G_ f:\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )\longrightarrow \mathcal M_\delta (\theta '), \qquad G_ f(p)=P_{\theta '}[p-f],  \] is a bijection with inverse $q\mapsto P_\theta [q+f]$. It preserves both singularity volumes, and \[  d_{\theta '}(G_ f(p),G_ f(q))=d_\theta (p,q).  \] It takes analytic models to analytic models and ideal models to ideal models. Proof. The map $u\mapsto u-f$ is a bijection from $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ')$ that preserves curvature currents, singularity types and hence both singularity volumes. Also $\max (u-f,v-f)=\max (u,v)-f$, so \[  d_{\theta '}(u-f,v-f)=d_\theta (u,v).  \] By proposition 18.5.1 , $G_ f(p)+f\sim p$, that is, $G_ f(p)\sim p-f$. Thus $G_ f(p)$ has the same volumes as $p$, and it is an ordinary model by theorem 13.19.5 ; in particular $G_ f(p)\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta ')$. Since the volume comparison depends only on ordinary types, the displayed identity follows. Taking the ordinary envelope of $G_ f(p)+f\sim p$ gives $P_\theta [G_ f(p)+f]=P_\theta [p]=p$. The same argument with the two backgrounds interchanged proves that the map is bijective with the stated inverse. Subtraction of a smooth function and bounded changes preserve analytic singularities. If $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$, proposition 18.5.1 also gives \[  P_{\theta '}[p-f]_{\mathcal I}\sim p-f\sim G_ f(p).  \] The ideal envelope is an ordinary model by corollary 18.4.4 , and ordinary models of the same ordinary type coincide; hence $P_{\theta '}[G_ f(p)]_{\mathcal I}=P_{\theta '}[p-f]_{\mathcal I}=G_ f(p)$. The inverse map gives the converse. $\square$

title: Proposition 13.25.2
text: Proposition 13.25.2 . F274299A5A71 Let $\beta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form with $\theta \leq \beta \leq \theta +h$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\beta )$ satisfy $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\beta (u)\geq \delta >0$. For every $\varepsilon \in [0,1]$ and every smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\gamma $ with $\beta \leq \gamma \leq \beta +\varepsilon h$, both singularity volumes satisfy \[  \operatorname {vol}_\beta (u) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\gamma (u) \leq (1+\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n\operatorname {vol}_\beta (u).  \] Proof. Normalize $u\leq 0$, so that $u\leq V_\beta $, and note that $\rho \leq V_\beta $. Since $\Omega \geq \beta $ and $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\beta (u)\geq \delta $, lemma 13.20.1 , applied in the big background $\beta $, shows that $H=Q_{b_\delta }(u,V_\beta )$ is defined. The potential \[  w=b_\delta ^{-1}H+(1-b_\delta ^{-1})\rho  \] satisfies $w\leq u$ and $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq (1-b_\delta ^{-1})(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )\geq \kappa _\delta h$. The addition argument in the proof of proposition 13.20.6 , with $h$, $\kappa _\delta $ and $t=\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta $ in place of $\omega $, $\delta $ and $t$, therefore gives the upper bound, with constants independent of $\beta $ and $u$. The lower bound is volume monotonicity. $\square$

title: Corollary 13.25.3
text: Corollary 13.25.3 . 1ED63BC3072B Let $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ have lower volume at least $\delta >0$, and let $\eta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form with $\theta \leq \eta \leq \theta +\varepsilon h$, where $0\leq \varepsilon \leq 1$. Then 9EE86F88EB92 13.25.4 \begin{equation}  \left|d_\eta (P_\eta [u],P_\eta [v])-d_\theta (u,v)\right| \leq 2K\left((1+\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n-1\right). \end{equation} Proof. The preceding proposition, with $\beta =\theta $ and $\gamma =\eta $, applies to $u$, $v$ and $m=\max (u,v)$, and their upper volumes in background $\theta $ are at most $v_+(\Omega )=K$. Thus, for $x=u,v,m$, the errors \[  e_ x=\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\eta (x) -\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (x)  \] lie between zero and $K((1+\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n-1)$. The difference $d_\eta (u,v)-d_\theta (u,v)$ equals $2e_ m-e_ u-e_ v$, whose absolute value is at most twice this bound. Finally, the projection invariance in proposition 13.22.4 , applied in background $\eta $, gives $d_\eta (u,v)=d_\eta (P_\eta [u],P_\eta [v])$, which is the comparison appearing in ( 13.25.4 ). $\square$

title: Equation 13.25.4
text: 9EE86F88EB92 13.25.4 \begin{equation}  \left|d_\eta (P_\eta [u],P_\eta [v])-d_\theta (u,v)\right| \leq 2K\left((1+\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n-1\right). \end{equation}

title: Theorem 13.25.5
text: Theorem 13.25.5 . CBA354870D02 Let $p$ be an ordinary model of positive lower volume, and let $\eta _ j$ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms with $\theta \leq \eta _ j\leq \theta +\varepsilon _ jh$, where $\varepsilon _ j\geq 0$ tends to zero. Then $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$ if and only if there are analytic $a_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta _ j)$ with \[  d_{\eta _ j}(a_ j,p)\longrightarrow 0.  \] The $a_ j$ may be required to be ordinary models in their respective backgrounds. Given any such analytic approximants, convex combinations with the fixed potential $\rho $, with rational coefficients, produce analytic $b_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ whose ordinary envelopes satisfy \[  d_\theta (P_\theta [b_ j],p)\longrightarrow 0, \qquad P_\theta [b_ j]\longrightarrow p \quad \text{in }L^1\text{ and capacity}.  \] Proof. Suppose first that $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$. By theorem 13.24.3 , there are analytic ordinary models $r_ j$ in background $\theta $ with $d_\theta (r_ j,p)\to 0$ and a common positive lower-volume bound. Corollary 13.25.3 and projection invariance in background $\eta _ j$ give $d_{\eta _ j}(r_ j,p)\to 0$, so $a_ j=r_ j$ works. One can also use the ordinary models $a_ j=P_{\eta _ j}[r_ j]$, since $P_{\eta _ j}[r_ j]\sim r_ j$ by proposition 18.4.8 . Conversely, suppose that such $a_ j$ exist. Normalize them below zero, and put $m_ j=\max (a_ j,p)$ and $\delta =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)>0$. Inequality ( 13.22.2 ) and proposition 13.25.2 give \[  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(a_ j),\quad \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(m_ j) \longrightarrow \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p).  \] Indeed, the upper volume of $p$ in background $\eta _ j$ tends to its upper volume in background $\theta $, and the differences of $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(a_ j)$ and $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(m_ j)$ from $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(p)$ are bounded in absolute value by $d_{\eta _ j}(a_ j,p)$. Enlarge the errors $\varepsilon _ j$ to positive rational numbers tending to zero, and put \[  c_ j=\frac{\kappa }{\kappa +\varepsilon _ j},\qquad b_ j=c_ ja_ j+(1-c_ j)\rho ,\qquad r_ j=P_\theta [b_ j].  \] As in the proof of theorem 13.24.3 , $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ j\geq 0$ and $b_ j$ has analytic singularities. Choose $A>0$ with $\theta \leq Ah$, and set \[  \widehat\theta _ j=\theta +(1+A/\kappa )\varepsilon _ jh, \qquad \widehat m_ j=P_{\widehat\theta _ j}[m_ j].  \] Then $\widehat\theta _ j\geq \eta _ j$ and $c_ j\widehat\theta _ j\geq \theta $. Since $r_ j\sim b_ j$ and $\rho \leq 0$, the potential $r_ j/c_ j$ is a nonpositive $\widehat\theta _ j$-plurisubharmonic function more singular than $a_ j$, hence more singular than $m_ j$. Therefore $r_ j\leq c_ j\widehat m_ j$. Also $p\leq \widehat m_ j\leq c_ j\widehat m_ j$. The lower volume of $m_ j$ in background $\eta _ j$ is at least $\delta $. For large $j$, proposition 13.25.2 applies with $\beta =\eta _ j$, $\gamma =\widehat\theta _ j$ and $\varepsilon =(1+A/\kappa )\varepsilon _ j$. Consequently \[  \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\widehat\theta _ j}(m_ j) \longrightarrow \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p).  \] By theorem 13.19.5 , $\widehat m_ j$ has the same upper volume in background $\widehat\theta _ j$ as $m_ j$. On the other hand, \[  c_ j\eta _ j+(1-c_ j)(\theta -\kappa h)\leq \theta .  \] Addition, applied to $c_ ja_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,c_ j\eta _ j)$ and $(1-c_ j)\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,(1-c_ j)(\theta -\kappa h))$, and background monotonicity therefore bound the upper volume of $b_ j$ below by $c_ j^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(a_ j)$. Since $r_ j\sim b_ j$, the two comparisons yield \[  \begin{split}  c_ j^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(a_ j) & \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (r_ j) \leq \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (\max (r_ j,p))\\ & \leq c_ j^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\widehat\theta _ j}(m_ j). \end{split}  \] Here the last inequality uses $\theta \leq c_ j\widehat\theta _ j$ and $\max (r_ j,p)\leq c_ j\widehat m_ j$. Both outer terms tend to $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$, which proves $d_\theta (r_ j,p)\to 0$. By proposition 18.4.8 , $r_ j=P_\theta [b_ j]_{\mathcal I}$ is an ideal model, so theorem 13.24.5 gives $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$. For large $j$, the upper-volume deficit from $r_ j$ to $\max (r_ j,p)$ is small, and lemma 13.18.1 with $b=2$ gives a convex lower bound for $r_ j$ whose first term is $\frac12\max (r_ j,p)$. title: 13.26 Two-sided background perturbations
text: A potential in the original background may cease to be admissible when the background decreases. Mixing it with the strict potential $\rho $ restores positivity, and ordinary projection then gives a model in the new background. The volume comparison controls the error of this transport uniformly on models with a common positive lower-volume bound, and it shows that the resulting notion of analytic approximation does not depend on the strict potential used in the correction. We first make the estimate of the preceding section uniform for pairs of forms near $\theta $. Lemma 13.26.1 . D5C96B9222A4 For every $\delta >0$ there are $C_\delta >0$ and $\varepsilon _0>0$ with the following property. Let $\beta ,\gamma $ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms with \[  \theta -\varepsilon h\leq \beta \leq \gamma \leq \theta +\varepsilon h, \qquad 0\leq \varepsilon \leq \varepsilon _0,  \] and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\beta )$ satisfy $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\beta (u)\geq \delta $. Then both singularity volumes satisfy \[  0\leq \operatorname {vol}_\gamma (u)-\operatorname {vol}_\beta (u) \leq C_\delta \varepsilon .  \] For two such potentials $u,v$, one also has \[  \left|d_\gamma (P_\gamma [u],P_\gamma [v])-d_\beta (u,v)\right| \leq 2C_\delta \varepsilon .  \] Proof. Put $\theta _0=\theta -\kappa h/2$ and $h_0=(1+\kappa /2)h$. Since $\theta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \kappa h/2$, the form $\theta _0$ is big, and $\rho $ is a strict analytic potential for it with the rational margin $\kappa /(2+\kappa )$ relative to $h_0$. Let $\varepsilon \leq \min (\kappa /2,1/2)$. Then $\theta _0\leq \beta \leq \theta _0+h_0$ and $\beta \leq \gamma \leq \beta +2\varepsilon h_0$, so proposition 13.25.2 applies with $\theta _0$, $h_0$, $\rho $ and a fixed Hermitian form $\Omega _0\geq \theta _0+2h_0$ in place of $\theta $, $h$, $\rho $ and $\Omega $. These choices do not depend on $\beta $ and $\gamma $. Since the volumes in background $\beta $ are at most $v_+(\Omega _0)$, the multiplicative estimate of the proposition implies the additive estimate, with a constant $C_\delta $ independent of $\beta $, $\gamma $ and $u$. Applying it to $u$, $v$ and $\max (u,v)$, the three-error calculation in the proof of corollary 13.25.3 and projection invariance in background $\gamma $ give the second assertion. $\square$ We now define the transport. Choose $A>0$ with $\theta \leq Ah$ and put $B=2(1+A/\kappa )$. For $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $p\leq 0$, a number $\varepsilon $ with $0<\varepsilon <\min (\kappa /2,1/B)$, and a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\eta $ with $\theta -\varepsilon h\leq \eta \leq \theta +\varepsilon h$, set 2826105ED7B3 13.26.2 \begin{equation}  c_\varepsilon =1-\varepsilon /\kappa ,\qquad T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(p) =P_\eta [c_\varepsilon p+(1-c_\varepsilon )\rho ],\qquad \widehat\theta _\varepsilon =\theta +B\varepsilon h. \end{equation} The mixed potential $c_\varepsilon p+(1-c_\varepsilon )\rho $ is $\eta $-plurisubharmonic, since $1-c_\varepsilon =\varepsilon /\kappa $ and therefore $\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(c_\varepsilon p+(1-c_\varepsilon )\rho )\geq \eta -\theta +\varepsilon h\geq 0$. Theorem 13.26.3 . 218C2CE831D1 Let $p\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, and let $\varepsilon $ and $\eta $ be as above. The transport $T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(p)$ of ( 13.26.2 ) is an ordinary model in background $\eta $, of lower volume at least $c_\varepsilon ^ n\delta $, and its volumes satisfy D190CC4FAB40 13.26.4 \begin{equation}  c_\varepsilon ^ n\operatorname {vol}_\theta (p) \leq \operatorname {vol}_\eta (T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(p)) \leq c_\varepsilon ^ n\operatorname {vol}_{\widehat\theta _\varepsilon }(p). \end{equation} For $p,q\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, 5E725A41F096 13.26.5 \begin{equation}  \begin{split} & \left|d_\eta (T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(p),T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(q)) -c_\varepsilon ^ n d_\theta (p,q)\right|\\ & \qquad \leq 2c_\varepsilon ^ nK \left((1+B\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n-1\right). \end{split} \end{equation} For fixed $p$, these models tend to $p$ in $L^1$ and in capacity as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Finally, suppose that two choices of the strict analytic potential $\rho $, of its rational margin $\kappa $ and of error bounds $\varepsilon _ j\to 0$ are admissible for the same backgrounds $\eta _ j$. Then the volume comparison in background $\eta _ j$ between the two transports of $p$ tends to zero. Proof. Write $c=c_\varepsilon $, $s=1-c$, $v=cp+s\rho $ and $T(p)=T^\rho _{\eta ,\varepsilon }(p)$. Since $s\rho \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,s(\theta -\kappa h))$, addition gives $\operatorname {vol}_{\theta -s\kappa h}(v)\geq c^ n\operatorname {vol}_\theta (p)$, and since $\theta -s\kappa h=\theta -\varepsilon h\leq \eta $, monotonicity gives the lower bound in ( 13.26.4 ) for $v$. In particular $v$ has positive lower volume in background $\eta $, so theorem 13.19.5 shows that $T(p)=P_\eta [v]$ is an ordinary model with the same two volumes as $v$. Since $\varepsilon <\kappa /2$, we have $c\geq 1/2$, and the choice of $B$ gives \[  c\widehat\theta _\varepsilon -(\theta +\varepsilon h) \geq \varepsilon (cB-1-A/\kappa )h\geq 0.  \] Since $\eta \leq \theta +\varepsilon h\leq c\widehat\theta _\varepsilon $, every competitor $w$ for $T(p)$, that is, every nonpositive $\eta $-plurisubharmonic $w\preceq v$, satisfies $w/c\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\widehat\theta _\varepsilon )$ and $w/c\preceq p$, because $\rho \leq 0$. Taking envelopes, and using that $v\leq 0$ is itself a competitor, yields 14679059DAF2 13.26.6 \begin{equation}  cp+s\rho \leq T(p)\leq cP_{\widehat\theta _\varepsilon }[p]. \end{equation} Volume monotonicity, together with theorem 13.19.5 in the larger background $\widehat\theta _\varepsilon $, proves the upper bound in ( 13.26.4 ). Now let $q\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ and $m=\max (p,q)$. The same pointwise bounds give \[  cm+s\rho \leq \max (T(p),T(q)) \leq cP_{\widehat\theta _\varepsilon }[m].  \] Consequently the upper volumes of $T(p)$, $T(q)$ and of their maximum lie between $c^ n$ times the respective upper volumes of $p$, $q$, $m$ in the backgrounds $\theta $ and $\widehat\theta _\varepsilon $. The lower volumes of $p$, $q$ and $m$ are at least $\delta $, and their upper volumes are at most $K$. By proposition 13.25.2 with $\beta =\theta $ and $\gamma =\widehat\theta _\varepsilon $, each of the three errors $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\eta (T(x))-c^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (x)$, $x=p,q,m$ (with $T(m)$ read as $\max (T(p),T(q))$), is nonnegative and at most $c^ nK((1+B\varepsilon /\kappa _\delta )^ n-1)$. As in the proof of corollary 13.25.3 , this proves ( 13.26.5 ). For fixed $p$, corollary 13.21.4 , lemma 5.29.19 give $P_{\widehat\theta _\varepsilon }[p]\to p$ in $L^1$ and in capacity along every decreasing sequence $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. An arbitrary sequence $\varepsilon _ j\to 0$ is handled by comparing with the decreasing sequence $\sup _{k\geq j}\varepsilon _ k$, since the envelopes increase with the background and lie above $p$. Quasi-continuity and integrability give $cp+s\rho \to p$ in both senses. The bounds ( 13.26.6 ) prove the asserted limits. To compare two choices along a sequence $\eta _ j$, denote their coefficients by $c_ j^{(i)}$ and their upper backgrounds by $\theta +B_ i\varepsilon _ j^{(i)}h$, $i=0,1$. Put $c_ j=\min _ i c_ j^{(i)}$ and $a_ j=\max _ i B_ i\varepsilon _ j^{(i)}$. Since the envelopes are nonpositive, both transported models lie below $c_ jP_{\theta +a_ jh}[p]$. Moreover $\eta _ j\leq c_ j(\theta +a_ jh)$, by the form inequality above for an index attaining the smaller coefficient. The upper volume of the maximum of the two transported models is therefore at most $c_ j^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\theta +a_ jh}(p)$, which tends to $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$. Each of their individual upper volumes is at least $(c_ j^{(i)})^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$ and at most the upper volume of the maximum, so it has the same limit. Hence their $d_{\eta _ j}$-comparison tends to zero. $\square$ For $p_ j,p\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, ( 13.26.5 ) shows that $d_\theta (p_ j,p)\to 0$ if and only if the comparisons of the transported models tend to zero along backgrounds whose errors tend to zero. The next criterion allows approximants chosen directly in those backgrounds. Theorem 13.26.7 . 279D427FE3F2 Let $p$ be an ordinary model of positive lower volume. Let $\varepsilon _ j$ be rational numbers with $0<\varepsilon _ j<\min (\kappa /2,1/B)$ tending to zero, let $\eta _ j$ be smooth real $(1,1)$-forms with $\theta -\varepsilon _ jh\leq \eta _ j\leq \theta +\varepsilon _ jh$, and put $p_ j=T^\rho _{\eta _ j,\varepsilon _ j}(p)$. Then $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$ if and only if there are analytic $a_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\eta _ j)$ with \[  d_{\eta _ j}(a_ j,p_ j)\longrightarrow 0.  \] The approximants may be required to be ordinary models. This condition does not depend on the choice of the strict analytic potential and of the admissible error bounds used to transport $p$. For every such analytic approximation, the convex combinations with $\rho $ of theorem 13.25.5 give analytic potentials in the original background whose ordinary envelopes converge to $p$ for $d_\theta $, in $L^1$ and in capacity. Proof. Suppose that $p=P_\theta [p]_{\mathcal I}$. By theorem 13.24.3 , there are analytic ordinary models $r_ j$ in background $\theta $ with $d_\theta (r_ j,p)\to 0$ and a common positive lower-volume bound. The transports $a_ j=T^\rho _{\eta _ j,\varepsilon _ j}(r_ j)$ have analytic singularities: the convex coefficients are rational, and ordinary projection preserves the singularity type of an analytic potential by proposition 18.4.8 . The estimate ( 13.26.5 ) gives $d_{\eta _ j}(a_ j,p_ j)\to 0$. Conversely, assume that such analytic approximants exist, and put $\delta =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$. By theorem 13.26.3 , the lower volume of $p_ j$ is at least $c_{\varepsilon _ j}^ n\delta \geq 2^{-n}\delta $. The upper-volume deficit from $a_ j$ to $\max (a_ j,p_ j)$ is at most $d_{\eta _ j}(a_ j,p_ j)$, which tends to zero. Applying lemma 13.18.1 with $b=2$ in background $\eta _ j$, and then addition, gives \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\eta _ j}(a_ j)\geq 2^{-2n}\delta  \] for all sufficiently large $j$. Put $\beta _ j=\theta +\varepsilon _ jh$. Lemma 13.26.1 , with $\beta =\eta _ j$ and $\gamma =\beta _ j$, and projection invariance in background $\beta _ j$ imply $d_{\beta _ j}(a_ j,p_ j)\to 0$. Also $d_{\beta _ j}(p_ j,p)\to 0$. Indeed, ( 13.26.6 ) bounds $\max (p_ j,p)$ above by $c_{\varepsilon _ j}P_{\widehat\theta _{\varepsilon _ j}}[p]$, and $c_{\varepsilon _ j}\widehat\theta _{\varepsilon _ j}\geq \beta _ j$ by the form inequality in the proof of theorem 13.26.3 . Hence the upper volume of this maximum in background $\beta _ j$ is at most $c_{\varepsilon _ j}^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\widehat\theta _{\varepsilon _ j}}(p)$, which tends to $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$. The upper volumes of $p_ j$ and $p$ in background $\beta _ j$ lie between $c_{\varepsilon _ j}^ n\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$ and this bound, so they have the same limit. Project $a_ j$, $p_ j$ and $p$ to ordinary models in background $\beta _ j$. Their lower volumes have a common positive bound, and their upper volumes are bounded by $v_+(\Omega )$, since $\beta _ j\leq \Omega $. The three-point estimate ( 13.22.6 ) in background $\beta _ j$ therefore gives $d_{\beta _ j}(a_ j,p)\to 0$, with constants independent of $j$. Now theorem 13.25.5 , applied with the backgrounds $\beta _ j$, shows that $p$ is an ideal model and gives the stated approximation in the original background. For another choice of transport, theorem 13.26.3 shows that the two reference models in background $\eta _ j$ have volume comparison tending to zero. The lower-volume bound just proved and the same uniform three-point estimate transfer the convergence condition in both directions. This proves independence of the choice. $\square$

section: 13.27 A complete metric on positive-volume models
text: The three-point modulus controls convergence even though $d_\theta $ need not satisfy the triangle inequality; two lines in the projective plane already show the failure. A complete metric can nevertheless be constructed from finite chains, as in the metrization of uniform structures. Continuity of the lower volume controls the chain estimates locally, and the reciprocal of the lower volume prevents Cauchy sequences from escaping to the zero-volume boundary. Example 13.27.1 . A1CA1768E392 Let $\theta $ be the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^2$, normalized by $\int _{\mathbb P^2}\theta ^2=1$. There are analytic ordinary models $p,q,r$ of positive lower volume such that \[  d_\theta (p,q)>d_\theta (p,r)+d_\theta (r,q).  \] Proof. Write $|Z|^2=|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2+|Z_2|^2$ in homogeneous coordinates. Fix a rational $a\in (0,1/2)$ and put \[  u=a\log \frac{|Z_0|^2}{|Z|^2},\qquad v=a\log \frac{|Z_1|^2}{|Z|^2},\qquad w=u+v.  \] With $H_ i=\{ Z_ i=0\} $, the corresponding currents are $a[H_0]+(1-a)\theta $, $a[H_1]+(1-a)\theta $ and $a[H_0]+a[H_1]+(1-2a)\theta $. The background is closed, so each singularity volume equals the non-pluripolar mass, which is the mass of the smooth part: \[  U(u)=U(v)=(1-a)^2,\qquad U(w)=(1-2a)^2.  \] The maximum $\max (u,v)$ has the ordinary type of \[  z=a\log \frac{|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2}{|Z|^2}.  \] To compute its volume, blow up the common point $[0:0:1]$ of $H_0$ and $H_1$. Denote the blowup by $\pi :Y\to \mathbb P^2$, its exceptional divisor by $E$, and the pencil map $[Z_0:Z_1]$ by $f:Y\to \mathbb P^1$. For the Fubini–Study form $\omega _1$ of mass one on $\mathbb P^1$, the Poincaré–Lelong formula gives \[  \pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(z\circ \pi )=a[E]+\beta , \qquad \beta =(1-a)\pi ^*\theta +af^*\omega _1.  \] Here $\beta $ is smooth and semipositive. Also \[  \int _ Y(\pi ^*\theta )^2=1,\qquad \int _ Y\pi ^*\theta \wedge f^*\omega _1=1,\qquad (f^*\omega _1)^2=0.  \] The mixed integral is one because every fiber of the pencil maps onto a line. By lemma 10.17.3 and change of variables off $E$, \[  U(\max (u,v))=\int _ Y\beta ^2=1-a^2.  \] Since $w\leq u$ and $w\leq v$, ( 13.22.2 ) and the definition of $d_\theta $ give \[  \begin{split}  d_\theta (u,v)& =4a-4a^2,\\  d_\theta (u,w)+d_\theta (w,v)& =4a-6a^2. \end{split}  \] Set $p=P_\theta [u]$, $q=P_\theta [v]$ and $r=P_\theta [w]$. By proposition 18.4.8 , these models have the same analytic singularity types as $u$, $v$ and $w$, and their lower volumes are at least $(1-2a)^2$. By projection invariance (proposition 13.22.4 ), they have the same comparisons, and the difference between the two sides is $2a^2>0$. $\square$ We return to the big background $\theta $ on the $n$-dimensional manifold $X$. Write $L(p)=\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (p)$, and let \[  \mathcal M_+(\theta )=\bigcup _{\delta >0}\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )  \] be the space of ordinary models of positive lower volume. We keep the notation $U$ and $M$ of section 13.22 . Proposition 13.27.2 . 44E1935166EC For $p,q\in \mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, 160186BB8FD9 13.27.3 \begin{equation}  |L(p)-L(q)|\leq nM\min \left\{ 1, \left(\frac{2d_\theta (p,q)}\delta \right)^{1/n}\right\} . \end{equation} If $p_ j,p\in \mathcal M_+(\theta )$ and $d_\theta (p_ j,p)\to 0$, then $L(p_ j)\to L(p)>0$. Proof. Put $s=d_\theta (p,q)$ and $m=\max (p,q)$. If $s\geq \delta /2$, the bound follows from $|L(p)-L(q)|\leq M$, and if $s=0$, then $p=q$ by proposition 13.22.4 . Suppose $0<s<\delta /2$ and take $t=(2s/\delta )^{1/n}$. The upper-volume deficit from either $p$ or $q$ to $m$ is at most $s$, while $L(m)\geq \delta $. Thus lemma 13.18.1 gives a potential $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with \[  (1-t)m+th\leq p.  \] Volume addition and monotonicity imply $L(p)\geq (1-t)^ nL(m)\geq (1-t)^ nL(q)$, so $L(q)-L(p)\leq (1-(1-t)^ n)M\leq nMt$. Interchanging $p$ and $q$ proves the bound. For the last assertion, put $s_ j=d_\theta (p_ j,p)$. Whenever $0<s_ j<L(p)/2$, the same stretching argument applied to $\max (p_ j,p)$ gives \[  L(p_ j)\geq (1-t_ j)^ nL(p),\qquad t_ j=\left(\frac{2s_ j}{L(p)}\right)^{1/n}.  \] If $s_ j=0$, then $p_ j=p$. Hence $L(p_ j)\geq L(p)/2$ for all sufficiently large $j$, and ( 13.27.3 ) with $\delta =L(p)/2$ gives $L(p_ j)\to L(p)$. $\square$ Theorem 13.27.4 . 126E2D85CA62 There is a complete metric $\mathfrak d_\theta $ on $\mathcal M_+(\theta )$ such that C3F22D1C1644 13.27.5 \begin{equation}  \mathfrak d_\theta (p_ j,p)\longrightarrow 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad d_\theta (p_ j,p)\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} A sequence $p_ j$ is $\mathfrak d_\theta $-Cauchy if and only if it is $d_\theta $-Cauchy and the sequence $1/L(p_ j)$ is Cauchy in $\mathbb R$. On each $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, the metric $\mathfrak d_\theta $ and the comparison $d_\theta $ define the same uniform structure, and the restriction of $\mathfrak d_\theta $ is complete. Proof. Step 1: a decreasing family of symmetric relations. Set $C=1+M$ and $m(p)=L(p)/C$, so that $0<m(p)<1$. Put $a_1=1$, $a_{k+1}=na_ k+1$, and choose $0<\varepsilon _1<1$. Recursively choose $\varepsilon _{k+1}>0$ so small that, with $r_ k=4^{a_{k+1}}\varepsilon _{k+1}$, \[  3\varepsilon _{k+1}<\varepsilon _ k,\qquad 3r_ k+4nM\left(\frac{2r_ k}{C}\right)^{1/n}<\varepsilon _ k.  \] Let $\mathcal U_0=\mathcal M_+(\theta )^2$ and, for $k\geq 1$, set \[  \mathcal U_ k=\left\{ (p,q): \left|\frac1{m(p)}-\frac1{m(q)}\right|<\varepsilon _ k, \quad d_\theta (p,q)<\varepsilon _ k\min \{ m(p),m(q)\} ^{a_ k}\right\} .  \] These symmetric sets contain the diagonal and decrease with $k$, and their intersection is the diagonal by proposition 13.22.4 . The reciprocal differences along this chain have total less than $3\varepsilon _{k+1}<1$, so $1/m(p_ i)>1/m_*-1$. Hence $m(p_ i)\leq 4m_*$ for every $i$: if $m_*\leq 3/4$, this follows from $1/m_*-1\geq 1/(4m_*)$, and otherwise from $m(p_ i)<1$. Each successive comparison is therefore less than \[  e=r_ k m_*^{a_{k+1}}.  \] All four models have lower volume at least $Cm_*$. Define 3DFF4A358B9C 13.27.7 \begin{equation}  \mathfrak d_\theta (p,q)=\inf \sum _{i=1}^ N2^{-k_ i}, \end{equation} where the infimum runs over finite chains $p=p_0,p_1,\ldots ,p_ N=q$ and integers $k_ i\geq 0$ with $(p_{i-1},p_ i)\in \mathcal U_{k_ i}$; we call $\sum _ i2^{-k_ i}$ the cost of the chain. A single edge in $\mathcal U_0$ gives $\mathfrak d_\theta \leq 1$. Reversing and concatenating chains gives symmetry and the triangle inequality, while diagonal edges with arbitrarily large indices give $\mathfrak d_\theta (p,p)=0$. We next prove the inclusions D335BA8A7131 13.27.8 \begin{equation}  \{ \mathfrak d_\theta <2^{-(k+1)}\}  \subset \mathcal U_ k\subset \{ \mathfrak d_\theta \leq 2^{-k}\}  \qquad (k\geq 1). \end{equation} The second inclusion follows by using a single edge. For the first, we prove by induction on the number of edges that every chain of cost less than $2^{-k}$ has its endpoints in $\mathcal U_{k-1}$, simultaneously for all $k\geq 1$. For one edge this follows because the $\mathcal U_ k$ decrease. For a chain of cost $A<2^{-k}$, choose $l\geq k$ with \[  2^{-(l+1)}\leq A<2^{-l}.  \] Split the chain at the first edge at which the cumulative cost reaches $2^{-(l+1)}$. The subchains before and after this edge both have cost less than $2^{-(l+1)}$, so by induction their endpoint pairs lie in $\mathcal U_ l$; an empty subchain is interpreted as a diagonal pair. Every edge cost is a power of two smaller than $2^{-l}$, so the middle edge lies in $\mathcal U_{l+1}\subset \mathcal U_ l$. By ( 13.27.6 ), the endpoints of the whole chain form a pair in $\mathcal U_{l-1}\subset \mathcal U_{k-1}$. This completes the induction and proves ( 13.27.8 ). Since the $\mathcal U_ k$ intersect in the diagonal, $\mathfrak d_\theta $ separates points, so it is a metric. Step 3: convergence and completeness. By ( 13.27.8 ), $\mathfrak d_\theta (p_ j,p)\to 0$ if and only if $(p_ j,p)$ eventually lies in every $\mathcal U_ k$. This implies $d_\theta (p_ j,p)\to 0$. Conversely, if $d_\theta (p_ j,p)\to 0$, then proposition 13.27.2 gives $L(p_ j)\to L(p)>0$, so for each fixed $k$ both inequalities defining $\mathcal U_ k$ hold eventually. This proves ( 13.27.5 ). The same inclusions show that a $\mathfrak d_\theta $-Cauchy sequence is $d_\theta $-Cauchy and has Cauchy reciprocal lower volumes. These reciprocals are bounded, so a tail of the sequence lies in some $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$. By theorem 13.22.7 , the sequence converges there for $d_\theta $, and hence for $\mathfrak d_\theta $. This proves completeness. Conversely, a $d_\theta $-Cauchy sequence with Cauchy reciprocal lower volumes has a common positive lower-volume bound on a tail, and then both inequalities defining each $\mathcal U_ k$ hold for all pairs of sufficiently late terms. This proves the Cauchy criterion. On $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$, ( 13.27.3 ) controls the reciprocal differences uniformly in terms of $d_\theta $, while $m(p)\geq \delta /C$ controls the second threshold in $\mathcal U_ k$. Thus $\mathfrak d_\theta $ and $d_\theta $ define the same uniform structure there. Continuity of the lower volume makes $\mathcal M_\delta (\theta )$ closed for $\mathfrak d_\theta $, so the restriction of $\mathfrak d_\theta $ to it is complete. $\square$ Corollary 13.27.9 . 5AF48DFCEE5A The ideal models in $\mathcal M_+(\theta )$ form a closed, hence complete, subspace of $(\mathcal M_+(\theta ),\mathfrak d_\theta )$, and the analytic ordinary models of positive lower volume are dense in it. Equivalently, this subspace is the metric completion of the analytic ordinary models of positive lower volume with the restricted metric. Proof. By theorem 13.24.5 , an ordinary model of positive lower volume that is a $d_\theta $-limit of ideal models is again an ideal model. The same theorem, which relies on theorem 13.24.3 , gives the density of analytic models. Now apply ( 13.27.5 ) and the completeness of $\mathfrak d_\theta $. $\square$

title: 13.28 Model potentials on curves
text:
On a curve the preceding theory becomes explicit. The part of the curvature current carried by the pole set determines the ordinary envelope, and its atomic part determines the ideal envelope. Comparing these two measures describes both the zero-volume boundary and the failure of analytic approximation for diffuse polar singularities. Total variation of the polar measures keeps this singularity data and at the same time controls convergence of the model potentials in capacity. In this section, $Y$ is a compact connected Riemann surface, $	heta $ is a smooth positive $(1,1)$-form on $Y$, and $A=\int _ Y	heta $. By Stokes' theorem every bounded $	heta $-plurisubharmonic function has mass $A$; thus $Y$ has the bounded mass property, $	heta $ is big, and the preceding results apply with $Y$ in place of $X$. For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,	heta )$ write $T_ u=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, and let $\mu _ u=\mathbf1_{\{ u=-\infty \} }T_ u=T_ u^{\mathrm{pol}}$ be the polar curvature of $u$ (subsection 5.27.13 ); in this and the following sections, $\mu _ u$ no longer denotes $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (u)$. A positive measure carried by a polar set will be called a polar measure. On the chosen compact coordinate disk, $G(x,y)\leq \log |x-y|^2+C$ for a fixed constant $C$. For $x\in K$, integrating over the interval of level $k$ containing $x$, and using $G\leq 0$ elsewhere, gives \[  u(x)\leq A2^{-k}(2\log r_ k+C)\longrightarrow -\infty .  \] Thus $u=-\infty $ on $K$, while $u$ is smooth off $K$, since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=-\theta $ there. Hence $K$ is polar, $\mu _ u=A\sigma $ and $U(u)=0$. By lemma 13.28.1 , $p=P_\theta [u]$ has the same polar curvature. Since this measure already has mass $A$, we get $T_ p=T_ u$, and therefore $p=u-\sup _ Yu$. The Lelong numbers of $p$ vanish because $\sigma $ has no atoms, so all its multiplier ideals are trivial and its ideal envelope is zero. Finally $\tau (p)=A$, which gives the distance by ( 13.28.12 ). $\square$

title: 13.28.15 The ordinary-type topology on a curve
search_title: The ordinary-type topology on a curve
text: We now compare the polar metric with the topology on ordinary singularity types introduced in section 18.8 . That topology also uses the ordinary envelope, but it measures the total variation only of the atomic part of the curvature. On ideal models the atomic part is the whole polar measure, so the two topologies agree there. On arbitrary ordinary models, diffuse polar mass can concentrate without being detected by the atomic total variation. We keep $Y$, $\theta $, $A$ and the decomposition $\mu _ u=D_ u+\sigma _ u$, and we use $\eta =\theta /A$ for $L^1$ norms. Let $\mathfrak S(Y,\theta )=\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )/{\sim }$ be the space of ordinary singularity types, and write $[u]$ for the class of $u$. Recall from proposition 18.8.4 that $\tau _{\theta ,0}$ is the uniform topology on $\mathfrak S(Y,\theta )$ generated by the $L^1$ distances between ordinary envelopes and between ideal envelopes, by the total variation of divisorial Lelong numbers on each fixed modification, and by the controlled ideal relations $\mathcal U(t,a)$ of ( 18.8.3 ). For ordinary classes put D1D81F67E5DB 13.28.16 \begin{equation}  d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta ([u],[v]) =\| P_\theta [u]-P_\theta [v]\| _{L^1(\eta )} +\| D_ u-D_ v\| _{\mathrm{TV}}. \end{equation} Theorem 13.28.17 . 1BAAC809D02C The finite pseudometric $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $ induces $\tau _{\theta ,0}$ on $\mathfrak S(Y,\theta )$. For $0\leq s\leq A$, the classes of ideal models \[  \mathcal C_ s=\{ [q_ D]:D\text{ positive atomic},\  D(Y)\leq s\}   \] form a complete metric space both for $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $ and for the distance $\| D-E\| _{\mathrm{TV}}$ between $[q_ D]$ and $[q_ E]$, and these two metrics induce the same topology. The space $\mathcal C_ s$ is not totally bounded if $s>0$, and $\mathcal C_0=\{ [0]\} $. Proof. A smooth compact modification of a smooth curve is an isomorphism, and the divisor weight of a point is one. Hence the divisorial distance in proposition 18.8.4 is exactly the atomic total variation, and the two summands of ( 13.28.16 ) are among the coordinates defining $\tau _{\theta ,0}$. Conversely, suppose that a net $[u_ j]$ converges to $[u]$ for $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $. The ideal envelope of $u$ is $q_{D_ u}$, by lemma 20.3.20 . Convergence of the atomic parts in total variation implies $L^1$ convergence of these envelopes, by theorem 13.28.4 , theorem 13.28.8 . These results also apply to nets: the map $D\mapsto q_ D$ goes between metric spaces, so sequential continuity is equivalent to continuity. It remains to check the controlled ideal relations. At a point $x$ with local coordinate $z$, the multiplier ideals on the curve are \[  \mathcal I(tu)_ x=(z^{\lfloor tD_ u(\{ x\} )\rfloor }).  \] This follows from theorem 5.37.3 , lemma 5.37.1 : on a smooth curve the Lelong number at $x$ determines the ideal, and the logarithmic germ with that Lelong number has the displayed ideal. Write $D_ j=D_{u_ j}$ and $D=D_ u$, and fix $t>0$ and $a>1$. The set $F=\{ x:D(\{ x\} )\geq 1/(2t)\} $ is finite. At its points, $aD_ j(\{ x\} )\geq D(\{ x\} )$ and $aD(\{ x\} )\geq D_ j(\{ x\} )$ eventually. Outside $F$, the bound \[  \sup _ x|D_ j(\{ x\} )-D(\{ x\} )|\leq \| D_ j-D\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\longrightarrow 0  \] makes both $\mathcal I(tu)_ x$ and $\mathcal I(tu_ j)_ x$ unit ideals for large $j$. Hence both inclusions in ( 18.8.3 ) hold eventually at every point. This proves that $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $ induces $\tau _{\theta ,0}$. The map $D\mapsto q_ D$ is injective, so $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $ is a metric on $\mathcal C_ s$. The positive atomic measures of mass at most $s$ are closed in total variation: a limit is positive, satisfies the mass bound, and is carried by the countable union of the sets of atoms of the sequence. Completeness of the space of finite signed measures therefore gives completeness for total variation. A $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal C_ s$ is Cauchy in total variation; its limit is again atomic, and theorem 13.28.8 gives convergence of the envelope coordinate. This proves completeness for $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $ as well as the equality of the two topologies. If $s>0$, fix $0<b\leq s$ and infinitely many distinct points $x_ j$. The measures $b\delta _{x_ j}$ have pairwise total-variation distance $2b$, so $\mathcal C_ s$ is not totally bounded for either metric. For $s=0$ only the zero measure remains. $\square$ By lemma 20.3.20 , for $0\leq \delta \leq A$ the set $\mathcal C_{A-\delta }$ consists exactly of the classes of ideal models of mass at least $\delta $. The whole set $\mathcal C_ A$, including the models of zero mass, is complete. Its subset of positive mass is incomplete: for a point $x$, the measures $D_ j=A(1-1/j)\delta _ x$ form a Cauchy sequence whose limit $A\delta _ x$ has zero mass. For general ordinary classes, the corresponding statement concerns a pseudometric. Put \[  \mathcal G_{\theta ,\delta } =\left\{ [u]:P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I},\quad \int _ Y\mathrm{MA}_\theta (P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I})\geq \delta \right\} .  \] For $0\leq \delta \leq A$ this set is complete for $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $, since every class $[u]$ in it is at distance zero from $[q_{D_ u}]\in \mathcal C_{A-\delta }$; limits need not be unique as ordinary classes. The set is not totally bounded when $\delta <A$. At $\delta =A$ the pseudometric vanishes identically on it, although it contains distinct classes by proposition 18.10.1 . The union of these sets over all $\delta >0$ is incomplete, by the same one-atom sequence.

title: 13.28.18 Concentration of diffuse polar curvature
text: The atomic total variation cannot be omitted from theorem 13.28.17 . On $\mathbb P^1$ with its Fubini–Study form $\theta $ of area one, fix a rational $0<\tau <1$ and take the atomic probability measures $\nu _ j$ and the ideal models $r_ j=P_\theta [(1-\tau )q_ j]_{\mathcal I}$ of proposition 18.6.6 , choosing the rational approximations so that the largest atom of $\nu _ j$ tends to zero. The ordinary and ideal envelopes of $r_ j$ both tend to zero in $L^1$, and for each $t>0$ and $a>1$, the pair $([r_ j],[0])$ eventually lies in $\mathcal U(t,a)$. The currents $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r_ j$ converge weakly to $\theta $. Nevertheless, \[  d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta ([r_ j],[0]) \geq \| D_{r_ j}\| _{\mathrm{TV}}=1-\tau >0.  \] Thus these weaker conditions do not imply convergence for $\tau _{\theta ,0}$, even at a fixed positive mass. The opposite difficulty concerns diffuse polar mass: the pseudometric controls the ordinary envelope in $L^1$, but not the total variation of the diffuse measure itself. Proposition 13.28.19 . 4651CC70BDA5 For the Fubini–Study form $\theta $ of area one on $\mathbb P^1$, the space $(\mathfrak S(\mathbb P^1,\theta ),d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta )$ is incomplete. In fact, there is a $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $-Cauchy sequence without limit consisting of ordinary models of one fixed positive non-pluripolar mass, all with trivial multiplier ideals. Proof. Choose a nonatomic polar probability measure $\sigma $ with compact support in an affine chart, using the Cantor construction in example 13.28.14 . Fix $0<c<1$ and a point $x$ in that chart. Translating and shrinking the support towards $x$ gives nonatomic polar probability measures $\sigma _ j$ supported in disks about $x$ with radii tending to zero. Let $p_ j=p_{c\sigma _ j}$ be the ordinary models of lemma 13.28.1 . Their polar measures are $c\sigma _ j$, their masses are $1-c$, and $D_{p_ j}=0$. Hence their Lelong numbers vanish, their multiplier ideals are trivial, and their ideal envelopes are zero. We claim that $p_ j\to q_{c\delta _ x}$ in $L^1$. Write $q_ y=q_{c\delta _ y}$. Rotations of $\mathbb P^1$ preserving $\theta $ and sending $x$ to $y$ can be chosen to depend continuously on $y$ near $x$. They transport $q_ x$ to $q_ y$, so continuity of translations in $L^1$ gives $q_ y\to q_ x$ in $L^1$ as $y\to x$. Set \[  w_ j=\int _{\mathbb P^1}q_ y\, \mathrm d\sigma _ j(y).  \] The common $L^1$ bound for normalized potentials makes this integral well defined. The function $w_ j$ is nonpositive, its curvature current dominates $c\sigma _ j$, and $w_ j\to q_ x$ in $L^1$. By ( 13.28.3 ), $p_ j$ is the upper envelope of all $v\leq 0$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq c\sigma _ j$, so $w_ j\leq p_ j$. By normalized compactness, every subsequence of $p_ j$ has a further subsequence converging in $L^1$ to some $v\leq 0$. The inequalities $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p_ j\geq c\sigma _ j$ pass to the limit and give $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq c\delta _ x$. Since $q_ x=p_{c\delta _ x}$, the same envelope description gives $v\leq q_ x$. The lower bound $w_ j\leq p_ j$ gives $v\geq q_ x$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere. This identifies every cluster point and proves the claim. Since $P_\theta [p_ j]=p_ j$ and $D_{p_ j}=0$, the classes $[p_ j]$ form a $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta $-Cauchy sequence. A limit $[v]$ would satisfy $D_ v=0$ and $P_\theta [v]=q_ x$. This is impossible: the ordinary envelope preserves all multiplier ideals and hence all atoms, whereas $q_ x$ has an atom of mass $c$ at $x$. The sequence therefore has no limit in $\mathfrak S(\mathbb P^1,\theta )$. $\square$ On ordinary models, $\tau _{\theta ,0}$ and the topology of the polar metric $d_\theta $ are also different. Choose the Cantor support of $\sigma $ inside a positive real interval in the affine coordinate $z$, away from zero. The rotations $R_ j(z)=\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\varepsilon _ j}z$, with $0<\varepsilon _ j\to 0$, move this support off itself. Put $p=p_{c\sigma }$ and $\widetilde p_ j=p\circ R_ j^{-1}$. By rotation invariance of the envelope, the $\widetilde p_ j$ are ordinary models with polar measures $c(R_ j)_*\sigma $, which have no atoms. Continuity of rotations in $L^1$ yields $d^{\mathrm{ot}}_\theta ([\widetilde p_ j],[p])\to 0$, whereas the polar measures have disjoint supports, so $d_\theta (\widetilde p_ j,p)=2c$ by theorem 13.28.4 . Conversely, polar total variation controls both terms of ( 13.28.16 ), by theorem 13.28.8 . Thus $\tau _{\theta ,0}$ is strictly weaker than the polar metric topology on ordinary models, although the two agree on ideal models. The failure of continuity under smooth gauge changes with a fixed zero obstacle (proposition 18.11.2 ) gives a further difference: the polar metric is invariant under such changes, by section 13.29 .
