title: 24.11 Equations on singular spaces
text: On a resolution of a singular space, a pulled-back Hermitian form degenerates, and the pulled-back density can vanish or become singular. Existence on the resolution must therefore be combined with an estimate that allows the solution to descend. 9.11 develops potentials, envelopes, ideal equivalence and extended Monge–Ampère measures on reduced irreducible compact unibranch spaces, keeping the original nonclosed background. On projective cones, theorem 9.11.34 , theorem 9.11.43 solve explicit equations, for prescribed angular and radial data, in full ordinary logarithmic classes and in the bounded class of the closed background. The logarithmic construction includes nonclosed deformations that preserve the determinant, and its full solution descends even when the smooth residual is nonconstant on the exceptional fiber. The continuity results discussed in section 25.21 use additional geometric and integrability hypotheses, notably log terminal singularities. On the regular locus of a compact reduced irreducible Hermitian space of dimension at least two there is a conformal Gauduchon metric uniformly comparable to the original metric; see section 25.21 . This existence theorem does not by itself give the nonlinear equations asked for below. In dimension one, theorem 9.11.54 gives a different sufficient condition: the normalization is a torus, the prescribed ordinary type has finitely many logarithmic poles of total weight smaller than the mass of the background, and the measure has a nonnegative $L^ p$ density, $p>1$, with respect to the flat area on the normalization. Convolution with a Green function compensates for the degeneracy of the pulled-back background. The atoms at the poles determine the mass of every potential in the prescribed type and give uniqueness even among solutions that are a priori rough, and the residual descends continuously. The projective cusp of example 9.11.57 has an unbounded density on the curve itself although the data on the normalization are smooth. Every background on a curve is closed, so this construction gives no equation with a nonclosed background in higher dimension. The family of logarithmic densities in theorem 9.11.60 makes the integrability issue precise. Densities on the normalization with local form $C_0|z|^{-2}(\log (1/|z|))^{-\gamma }$ are integrable for $\gamma >1$, but they give a solution in the prescribed ordinary type exactly when $\gamma >2$. For $1<\gamma \leq 2$, the constructed solution keeps all multiplier ideals and the same non-pluripolar mass, but loses the lower bound defining the type. Multiplier-ideal equivalence alone therefore does not give a bounded residual. A criterion for general integrable data remains to be found. Problem 24.11.1 . A63319B4B931 Consider reduced irreducible compact unibranch complex spaces with a Hermitian form, as in 9.11 . Beyond the projective cones of subsection 9.11.27 , determine geometric conditions on such spaces and conditions on the measure that give existence and uniqueness of solutions in specified singularity classes. Identify estimates ensuring finite mass, descent from resolutions and continuity, and describe their behavior under common refinements of resolutions. In the cone examples, the pulled-back density vanishes on the exceptional divisor, and the logarithmic remainder solves an equation in a strictly positive background; the bounded equation for the closed background uses instead an energy that is coercive off that divisor. More general spaces of higher dimension require a replacement for these two controls. The curve construction uses a Green operator on the normalization; a linear construction by traces on a singular space needs further estimates across the singular locus.

title: 25.2 Historical notes
text: Local regularization and products provide a common starting point for the results of this book. A smooth local correction makes these methods available for nonclosed backgrounds, including on Kähler manifolds. Global arguments must distinguish a closed class on a non-Kähler manifold from a nonclosed background: the former may lack the Kähler positivity used in classical existence theorems, while the latter loses the cohomological control of Monge–Ampère masses. Gauduchon duality, relative envelopes and the available mass bounds connect the sources discussed below. Their hypotheses also decide whether a solution keeps the ordinary singularity type of its reference or belongs only to its relative envelope class. These notes identify the sources of the results of the book, with precise locators, and explain how the arguments given in the book relate to the original ones. Indications such as v1 or arXiv version in a locator refer to the version of the source that was used. Where needed, the conversion from the normalization of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ or of the Chern–Ricci form used in a source to the conventions fixed at the beginning of the book is indicated next to the citation.

title: 25.3 Plurisubharmonic functions and regularization
text: Compactness, integrability and regularization are local properties, and they survive the passage to a nonclosed background because a quasi-plurisubharmonic function becomes plurisubharmonic after a smooth local correction. The $L^1$ compactness of normalized potentials in theorem 5.25.2 , also stated by Dinew [ Proposition 6.2 , Dinew16 ] , follows by propagating local compactness over a connected coordinate cover. Local exponential integrability, as recalled by Zeriahi [ Section 1 , Zeriahi01 ] , becomes uniform over normalized potentials in lemma 5.26.2 , through a contradiction argument with a weighted sum of potentials. The comparison of convolutions in different coordinate charts in lemma 5.30.1 , corollary 5.30.3 is the bounded part of the argument of Błocki and Kołodziej [ §2, Lemmas 4–5 , BK07 ] . Their full regularization theorem [ Theorem 1 , BK07 ] allows unbounded potentials and a positive continuous background. The proof of theorem 5.32.1 treats only the bounded case, which is all that the construction of products requires; it includes the extraction of a decreasing diagonal sequence and the rescaling that keeps the regularized forms strictly positive. Demailly's regularization by the flow of the Chern connection [ Theorem 4.1 , Dem94 ] applies to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, where $\theta $ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form: the theorem concerns a closed current with an arbitrary smooth lower bound, here $-\theta $, and this lower bound need not be closed. The monotonicity and logarithmic convexity of the regularization enter the estimate ( 5.42.11 ), whose linear error rate follows from the curvature inequality [ Lemma 4.4 , Dem94 ] and the expansion in [ Proposition 3.8, equations (3.11), (4.3), and (4.5) , Dem94 ] . In the present situation the curvature inequality needs neither a small $\epsilon $ term nor an $M_\epsilon $ correction, and local trace bounds make the constants uniform in the center and the radius. The same expansion underlies the truncated Kiselman transform of lemma 5.42.1 ; see [ Theorem 4.1 and Remark 4.7 , Dem94 ] and Kołodziej–Nguyen [ Lemma 4.1 , KN19 ] . In lemma 5.42.4 the full base–fiber error is kept as a modulus tending to zero, and, as in [ Remark 4.7 , Dem94 ] , a term linear in the radius absorbs the mixed and vertical errors. This formulation accommodates the unbounded potentials with finite $L^1$ norm that occur in theorem 15.8.1 , where localizing the averaging radius makes the minimum-principle argument available away from the singular barrier. For a continuous potential, the logarithmic derivative of the Chern averages tends to zero. Together with Dini's theorem and uniform continuity, this gives the uniform smooth approximation with vanishing curvature loss in lemma 5.42.5 . For a Hölder reference, lemma 5.42.7 retains a common Hölder norm and rescales to genuine potentials. Dinh, Ma and Nguyên [ Theorem 2.1, pp. 551–555 , DMNFekete17 ] prove quantitative smooth regularization in a Kähler background using its local potentials. The proof here uses Chern averages and the continuous-potential curvature-loss estimate on the Hermitian background. Their quantitative Kähler estimate is not used. Demailly's regularization in the form of theorem 5.36.5 , whose approximants become divisorial with a smooth remainder after finitely many blowups, is the statement of Demailly and Păun [ Theorem 3.2 , DP04 ] . It allows an arbitrary smooth lower bound on a Hermitian manifold, and the smooth remainder after resolution is essential for its applications here. This sequence is in general different from the multiplier-ideal sequence of theorem 5.36.1 , and we do not assume that a single sequence has the additional properties of both. The analyticity of the sets where the Lelong number is at least $c>0$, recalled in 5.34.2 and used in lemma 12.19.4 , theorem 11.8.1 , is Siu's theorem [ Main Theorem, p. 53 , Siu74 ] ; a smooth local correction makes it applicable to quasi-plurisubharmonic functions. The dimension bound for the Lelong level set and the existence of global irreducible components are stated in Demailly's book [ Chapter III, Corollary 8.5, p. 174; Chapter II, Theorem 5.3, pp. 102–103 , DemCADG ] . The non-strict inequality is essential. In example 5.34.4 , a summable series of line currents on the projective plane has the property that the set where the Lelong number exceeds one is a sequence of points accumulating at a point outside that set. The closedness of polar curvature currents, proposition 5.46.7 , is proved by the complete pluripolar restriction argument of Boucksom, Eyssidieux, Guedj and Zeriahi [ author preprint v2, Theorem 1.8, Lemma 1.9 and Remark 1.10 , BEGZ10 ] . The chain rule for bounded functions allows cutoffs that converge only pointwise, so the complete pluripolar set need not be closed, and a smooth local correction extends the argument to quasi-plurisubharmonic potentials with an arbitrary smooth background. Combined with the recovery of closed currents carried by a Lebesgue-null set from their traces, this removes the hypothesis that the pole set be closed from corollary 18.26.11 , proposition 18.26.12 . The simultaneous realization of the limiting currents is a separate question. The Hausdorff estimate of corollary 5.34.3 follows from the Lelong mass formulas in Demailly's book [ Chapter III, formulas (5.5)–(5.8), pp. 158–159 , DemCADG ] and holds in every positive bidimension. When a closed polar current vanishes outside an exceptional locus, the support theorem for currents carried by analytic sets [ Chapter III, Corollaries 2.11 and 2.14, pp. 141–143 , DemCADG ] identifies the remaining divisorial part. Full local Monge–Ampère products at an unbounded locus of Hausdorff dimension zero rely instead on [ Chapter III, Theorem 4.5 and Proposition 4.9, pp. 152–156 , DemCADG ] , as stated in theorem 5.27.18 . These products keep their top-degree mass on the pole set, whereas every lower-degree coefficient measure vanishes there. The local maximum argument of lemma 5.27.19 compares the residual measures and shows that they are invariant under bounded perturbations. Their global consequences for masses and models are discussed in section 25.4 , section 25.11 . The local reference-integral estimate lemma 5.29.7 is related to the Hölder estimates for measure functionals of Dinh and Nguyên [ arXiv v1, Lemma 3.5 and Proposition 3.6, pp. 9–10 , DNHolder14 ] . Here the tests are bounded plurisubharmonic functions on nested balls. Keeping the cutoff-gradient terms gives a bound uniform in the Hölder norm of the reference; a finite cover yields corollary 5.29.9 for bounded tests with a common curvature lower bound. The local moderation theorem of Dinh, Nguyên and Sibony [ Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2, pp. 466–467; proof pp. 468–471 , DNSModerate10 ] gives exponential integrability with respect to locally moderate currents. The top-degree estimate lemma 5.29.10 follows here by applying the reference-integral estimate to consecutive truncations and absorbing their polynomial growth into the exponential tail. Guedj and Zeriahi's extremal-capacity comparison [ Theorem 5.2, pp. 622–623, and Proposition 7.1, p. 632 , GZIntrinsic05 ] motivates lemma 5.29.12 . Its proof uses conservation of mass only for the closed Fubini–Study form on an auxiliary projective space. Local capacity comparison gives the Hermitian estimate proposition 5.29.13 with constants uniform for a common Hölder norm. The convergence against a fixed non-pluripolar measure in lemma 5.44.2 rests on Cegrell's classical fixed-measure argument, which Kołodziej and Nguyen also state in a form allowing extraction of subsequences [ Lemma 2.1 and Corollary 2.2 , KN22 ] . Applying that statement to every subsequence gives convergence of the whole bounded sequence. Let $f$ be a holomorphic function and $\chi $ a convex nondecreasing function. The sharp Sobolev criteria for the potentials $\chi (\log |f|)$ in 5.27.20 are due to Chen, Shao and Wang [ v1, Theorems 1.1–1.2, pp. 2–3 and 19–22 , CSW26 ] ; their estimate in terms of the smallest multiplicity and their energy bound on small sublevel sets are [ v1, Lemma 4.1 and Proposition 3.8, pp. 16–20 , CSW26 ] . The proofs given here use the regularizations $\chi (\frac12\log (|f|^2+\varepsilon ^2))$, $\varepsilon >0$, to identify the weak gradient and to keep track of the residual divisor term in the distributional Laplacian, a term that the classical Laplacian omits. The power examples and their endpoint obstruction in example 5.27.24 are the calculation in normal coordinates and the table of [ v1, Lemma 2.1 and Section 6.1, pp. 6–7 and 24–25 , CSW26 ] . These local criteria for derivatives should not be confused with the theorem on products at a small unbounded locus discussed above. The concentration example of proposition 5.27.31 is the point-mass case of Qin's [ v1, Corollary 3.6, p. 14 , QinLimits26 ] . Here the mass is computed directly from the transverse identity ( 5.27.30 ), which gives a smooth variant of the logarithmic truncation in [ Lemma 2.4, pp. 9–10 , QinLimits26 ] . The conclusion of lemma 5.27.28 for sequences with a common local bound agrees with [ Proposition 7.2, p. 26 , QinLimits26 ] ; in the book it follows from the local range estimate proved earlier. Theorem 5.27.36 , which adds an arbitrary positive Radon measure to the Monge–Ampère measure of a fixed bounded potential in the limit, is Qin's [ v1, Theorem B, p. 3 , QinLimits26 ] . The addition along finitely many test functions and the passage to a determining family correspond to [ Proposition 3.2 and Theorem 3.4, pp. 11–14 , QinLimits26 ] . In the proof given here, the smooth ridge gives the limits of the lower-degree currents directly, finite iteration over atoms controls every mixed term, and the one-sided logarithmic bound also gives convergence in local capacity. The smoothness of the approximants is asserted for a smooth background, whereas Qin also treats continuous backgrounds. The classification of vague cluster sets in theorem 5.27.39 , according to which every vaguely closed set of positive measures is the full cluster set of a sequence of potentials tending to zero, is the case of the zero potential in [ v1, Theorem A, pp. 2–3 , QinLimits26 ] . The metric for the vague topology and the concatenation of dense sequences are [ Lemma 3.3, p. 12 and Lemma 4.1, p. 14 , QinLimits26 ] , and the comparison example with moving measures is [ Example B.1, p. 28 , QinLimits26 ] . In the book, finite addition of atoms gives smooth approximants that converge in local capacity directly. The construction with moving measures over a fixed bounded background in theorem 5.27.42 also corresponds to [ Theorem 3.4, pp. 13–14 , QinLimits26 ] . The cutoff argument of lemma 5.27.41 shows that, under convergence in local capacity, every limit measure dominates the Monge–Ampère measure of the background; this gives a complete classification of the cluster sets for bounded backgrounds approximated from below. Convergence in local capacity is a stronger requirement than the $L^1$ convergence in Qin's general classification of reachable sets, whose argument for reaching the zero measure needs additional hypotheses on maximal approximation and on the domain; that argument is not used here. Let $\phi _1,\ldots ,\phi _ r$ be plurisubharmonic weights with exponents $p_1,\ldots ,p_ r>1$, as in theorem 5.37.15 . The division estimate with two summands, lemma 5.37.10 , is the case of two weights in Takakura's [ v1, Theorem 1.3, pp. 2 and 5–6 , TakDivision26 ] . Since the relevant kernel is a line, the proof can use the Hessian formula for a scalar function instead of the general curvature theorem for subbundles. The constant in the a priori inequality ( 5.37.13 ) follows from the twisted Bochner identity in Demailly's notes [ Section 13.A, pp. 123–124 , DemAM11 ] by a weighted Cauchy inequality. Proposition 13.4 there states the weaker constant $2$; keeping the full factor $\eta +\lambda $ gives the constant $1$ used here. For a single weight, proposition 5.37.14 is the case $r=1$ of [ Theorem 1.2, pp. 1–2 and 6–7 , TakDivision26 ] . Applying it successively gives the product constant of theorem 5.37.15 , with no condition on $\sum _ i1/p_ i$. The coordinate example in its proof extends [ Example 3.2, p. 7 , TakDivision26 ] and shows that this constant is optimal when $r\leq n$. For $2\leq r\leq n$ the product is strictly smaller than $1-r^{-1}\sum _ i1/p_ i$, the constant stated in Takakura's theorem. For $r>n$ the product need not improve Takakura's dimension-dependent estimate, and by itself it does not determine the optimal constant. In dimension one, theorem 5.37.22 gives the optimal constant for every number $r$ of weights, including the range $\sum _ i1/p_ i\geq 1$ in which it vanishes. When $\sum _ i1/p_ i<1$, it equals the dimension-one constant of [ Theorem 1.2, pp. 1–2 , TakDivision26 ] , and a common logarithmic pole shows that it is sharp. The local argument in lemma 5.37.18 uses the logarithmic fundamental solution and the characterization of positive distributions in [ Chapter I, Sections 4.A–4.C, pp. 30–36 , DemCADG ] ; in our normalization, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |z|^2=\delta _0$. The global lifting in lemma 5.37.20 is the locally free planar case of vanishing for coherent sheaves. It is proved here with the vector-valued $L^2$ estimate for complete metrics in [ Theorem 5.1 and its proof, pp. 33–34 , DemAM11 ] , whose Bochner identity is [ Section 4.C, p. 30 , DemAM11 ] . We do not determine the optimal constant when $n\geq 2$ and $r>n$.

title: 25.4 Mass and energy
text: On a nonclosed background, the variation of the Monge–Ampère mass and the failure of the usual energy to have a primitive are related manifestations of torsion. Chiose's polarization argument [ Theorems 1–2 , Chiose16 ] gives the characterization of mass invariance in theorem 11.1.7 . Yi Li constructed energies corrected by torsion terms [ Equation (1.18) and Theorem 1.2 , YiLi10 ] . The correction changes the one-form being integrated, in agreement with theorem 11.2.4 , which shows, for $n\geq 2$, that the uncorrected one-form has no primitive unless $\omega $ is closed; proposition 11.2.10 computes the difference by a first variation. Cutoffs of diffuse poles separate this variation of the background from a fixed loss of mass at the singularity. Let $n\geq 2$, and let $H$, $C$ and $M$ be the cutoff, the curvature constant and the residual mass of proposition 18.26.19 ; fix $0<t<1/C$ and put $A=\int _ X\omega ^ n$. The mass of $tH$ is a polynomial in $t$ whose finite torsion coefficients come from Stokes calculations for compactly supported bounded products. By proposition 18.26.21 , every representative that is ordinarily bounded-equivalent to $tH$ loses the same top residual mass $Mt^ n$, although its lower-degree coefficients can vary. If $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^ q)=0$ for $1\leq q<n$, invariance of the mass under bounded changes and invariance of the residual give the mass $A-Mt^ n$ throughout the class (corollary 18.26.20 ); this applies to every compact complex surface with a Gauduchon form. On a surface, corollary 18.26.22 shows that the mass is constant on the class if and only if $\omega $ is Gauduchon, since admissible smooth bounded perturbations detect any failure of the Gauduchon condition. The failure of the bounded mass property on a Hopf threefold is the counterexample of Xia and Zhang [ Theorem 1.1 , XZ26 ] . There a Gauduchon background converts vertical Dirichlet energy into Monge–Ampère mass, a mechanism developed in section 23.1 . Combined with theorem 13.14.18 , it produces infinite extended mass with trivial multiplier ideals at every positive weight, and the results on integrability and convergence of coefficients in subsection 13.14.20 describe the linear current carried by this construction. Xia and Zhang use the operator $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial $ [ Section 1 , XZ26 ] ; dividing their background forms by $2\pi $ and leaving their potentials unchanged preserves positivity and changes the coefficient of the mass identity. The local matrix, heat potential, Gaussian gradient estimate and completed square used in subsection 23.1.41 are those of Xia and Zhang [ v1, Lemma 2.2, pp. 4–5; Lemmas 3.1–3.3, pp. 6–9; equation (4.2), p. 10 , XZ26 ] . The faster initial time in theorem 23.1.52 changes the radial length and the integrated defect, so its positive correction is proved at that scale. The positive fiber flux and depth estimate give the square-root upper bound for all potentials in the declared unitary invariant class. The lower-density regions then give a single infinite weighted measure and concentration on a pole divisor at the critical weight; they also impose necessary conditions without the symmetry assumption. The unrestricted optimal sufficient rate remains open. The passage from smooth to bounded and unbounded invariant potentials uses the classical bounded product and capacity theory developed in section 5.27 , section 5.29 . The local product construction and decreasing continuity are Bedford and Taylor's [ Theorem 2.1, pp. 4–7; Theorem 2.4, pp. 7–9; Corollary 2.8, p. 10 , BT82 ] ; their quasi-continuity and zero-capacity results are [ Theorem 3.5, p. 14; Theorems 6.9–6.10, pp. 25–26 , BT82 ] . They use $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=2\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial $, which is $4\pi $ times our operator and changes capacities only by a fixed factor. The local $L^1$ compactness underlying theorem 5.25.2 is also described in [ Chapter I, Proposition 4.21, pp. 36–37; Proposition 5.9, p. 40 , DemCADG ] . In the present argument, group convolution and canonical truncation give the original Hermitian capacity convergence, including the boundary mass at a truncation level. The extension in theorem 23.1.35 keeps the same threefold heat family. Its proof first bounds the actual mass on the negative radial half-line by exact integration over the elliptic fiber, then uses lemma 23.1.33 to compare the angularly integrated densities in different dimensions. The additional angular factor has a fixed positive lower bound on the half-line carrying the divergent mass. Corollary 23.1.36 transfers this failure to every Hermitian metric on the same scalar Hopf manifold. The failure of positive lower mass is a different phenomenon; it occurs on the elliptic threefold of section 12.19 . Sufficient conditions for a positive lower bound come instead from the sign of the torsion: ( 12.16.4 ) is the three-dimensional case of a formula of Angella, Guedj and Lu [ Theorem 3.2 , AGL23 ] , who call the condition $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \leq 0$ plurinegativity. The principal elliptic bundles of subsection 24.4.7 are special cases of the torus bundles of Goldstein and Prokushkin [ Section 2 , GP04 ] . The metric calculation on these bundles gives an upper bound for the mass, but it does not decide whether the lower mass vanishes. The radial calculation of proposition 24.4.13 bounds the root volume of the specified affine test family at fixed degree; the lower mass over all potentials remains open. The completion energy of subsection 11.2.14 is the Dinew–Popovici functional. Hanwen Liu defines it and computes its variations in [ v1, Section 2.1, pp. 3–5 , LiuCritical26 ] , and proves the identity relating energy and volume along potential variations, together with the indefiniteness of the Hessian, in [ Theorems 5.1–5.2, pp. 16–19 , LiuCritical26 ] . Liu assumes that the ambient manifold is Kähler. The proofs in the book use only the finite-dimensional space of closed holomorphic completions and Stokes' theorem, so these statements about potential variations hold on every compact Hermitian symplectic fourfold. Liu's calculation of criticality for products [ Lemma 2.3 and Theorem 2.4, pp. 7–9 , LiuCritical26 ] gives the mechanism of example 11.2.23 , where an explicit Fourier form on the square torus replaces the general existence argument on surfaces. Neither the general existence criterion of that paper in terms of the canonical bundle nor its convergence theorem for the global torsion flow is used here. Liu's convention is $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}=\mathrm i(\bar\partial -\partial )$; rewritten with the book's $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$, the formulas of that paper for potential variations give ( 11.2.20 ) with the coefficients shown there. Combined with Chiose's criterion, the energy identity gives the equivalence between flatness of the energy and invariance of the mass in corollary 11.2.21 . The calculation with one nonclosed factor in example 11.2.24 shows that this flatness along potentials implies neither criticality in the full Aeppli class nor the existence of a primitive for the Monge–Ampère one-form.

title: 25.5 Gauduchon metrics and positivity
text: Gauduchon metrics replace the cohomological conservation of mass by a linear trace identity. In the form recalled by Tosatti and Weinkove immediately before [ Lemma 2.3 , TW10 ] , Gauduchon's conformal theorem starts, in dimension $n\geq 2$, from a Hermitian form $\eta $ and constructs a smooth real function $f$ such that $\gamma =\mathrm e^ f\eta $ is Gauduchon; the multiplier in theorem 11.4.2 is then $\rho =\mathrm e^{(n-1)f}$. The resulting trace comparison, corollary 11.5.3 , also underlies the first mixed-volume bounds of Guedj and Lu [ Proposition 3.3 , GL22 ] . For lemma 11.24.1 , the constant-coefficient estimate is the order-zero multiplier theorem in Taylor [ Chapter 13, Theorem 5.1 and its proof, pp. 16–21 , Taylor13 ] ; compactness is [ Chapter 13, (6.9), p. 24 , Taylor13 ] . Freezing the continuous coefficients gives the Sobolev estimate, and the proof writes out the classical Alexandrov–Bakelman–Pucci contact-set bound and tangent-ball maximum principle before applying the method of continuity and compact-perturbation index theory. It does not differentiate the coefficients. The trace identity has a dual form: positivity can be tested against Gauduchon metrics. For an arbitrary smooth background, the generalized Lamari criterion theorem 11.6.1 is stated by Boucksom, Guedj and Lu [ Lemma 1.15 , BGL25 ] ; its proof combines a separation argument with a right inverse of a scalar elliptic operator. In theorem 11.8.1 , Lamari duality combines with normalized compactness and Siu analyticity to turn bounded transverse test pairings into a global hypersurface. The regularized logarithmic potentials in proposition 11.8.2 give the converse bound when a Cartier divisor agrees with the cutoff hypersurface throughout its chart. The same linear control gives the bound ( 11.5.6 ) for the normalization constant, which is used in the weak existence arguments of [ Section 4 , BGL25 ] . The deformation obstruction for convex norms in theorem 11.9.4 is due to Liu and Wan [ v1, Theorem 3.2 and Sections 3.1–3.3, pp. 9–13 , LiuWanKobayashi26 ] , and the normalization of line metrics in lemma 11.9.1 is their Lemma 3.1, p. 8. The proof combines derivative estimates along the line axes with an average of the horizontal curvature and the formal adjoint on a fixed sphere bundle. The resulting $C^4$ neighborhood is uniform over all smooth complex norms, and the positive Gauduchon test forms may differ from one line summand to another. The regularization of homogeneous functions in theorem 11.10.4 is the case of a compact base of a lemma of Kuang-Ru Wu [ v1, Section 2.3, Lemma 13, pp. 10–13 , WuFinslerIII23 ] . Its gluing step uses the closure under maxima, the stability under smooth perturbations and the semilocal approximation of Greene and Wu [ Definitions 1.1, 1.3–1.4, pp. 48–49; Lemma 4.1 and Theorem 4.1, pp. 80–81 , GreeneWu79 ] , while the local positivity properties are proved directly from a holomorphic shear formula. The replacement in proposition 11.10.5 assumes that a strictly plurisubharmonic homogeneous function is given, and corollary 11.10.6 keeps the hypothesis of local strong convexity in the fibers. The local example example 11.10.1 adapts the quadratic maximum of Fukuoka and Setti [ v1, Example 3.18, p. 20 , FukuokaSettiStrongConvex26 ] to a complex rank-two bundle over a disk. A geometric series of squared holomorphic moduli gives its total-space plurisubharmonicity. Its fiberwise quadratic margin tends to zero at nearby base points, showing why local strong convexity in theorem 11.10.4 requires a common margin on a total-space neighborhood. The example concerns this distinction between hypotheses; the general real-Finsler smoothing and connection-convergence theorems of that paper are not used. The existence result of Liu and Wan [ v1, Theorem 2.1, p. 7 , LiuWanKobayashi26 ] that is needed here is proved directly by the tautological construction of lemma 11.11.1 , proposition 11.11.2 : a metric with positive curvature on the dual of the tautological line bundle gives a homogeneous squared norm that is strictly plurisubharmonic off the zero section. When the dual vector bundle is ample, such a line metric is a root of the Fubini–Study metric pulled back by a very ample embedding. The result is the strictly plurisubharmonic homogeneous function used in their regularization [ v1, Lemma 3.4, pp. 13–14 , LiuWanKobayashi26 ] , and it gives corollary 11.11.3 . The construction of polar norms in 11.12 gives a proof of Liu and Wan's [ v1, Proposition 3.5, pp. 14–16 , LiuWanKobayashi26 ] . A Schur complement and a holomorphic correction of the second jet give local pluriharmonic supporting functions for the logarithm of the polar square. A uniform upper bound for the real Hessian of the primal squared metric gives strong convexity of the dual through its exact Legendre expression; neither real convexity of the primal metric nor uniqueness of a maximizer is assumed. The tautological construction for an ample dual and the homogeneous regularization then give the smooth replacement and the curvature obstruction of corollary 11.12.7 , under the hypotheses stated there. On Hirzebruch surfaces, the ample comparison quotient and the two prioritary points of proposition 11.13.2 , lemma 11.13.3 are Liu and Wan's [ v1, Proposition 4.2 and Lemma 4.3, pp. 17–20 , LiuWanKobayashi26 ] . The facts about Hirzebruch surfaces that they need are proved directly in lemma 11.13.1 , from sections along the ruling and a very ample embedding. The positive Gauduchon tests for the individual dual line bundles in proposition 11.13.4 are the divisor calculation in their proof of Theorem 1.1, p. 23. These constructions give the ample point and the test forms used in theorem 11.15.5 , corollary 11.15.6 . The stability of extensions in proposition 11.14.1 is Liu and Wan's [ v1, Proposition 4.4, pp. 20–21 , LiuWanKobayashi26 ] , including the equality case on $\mathbb F_0$. The proof of proposition 11.14.2 uses the exact sequences of $\operatorname {Hom}$ groups and applies to every extension, while restriction to a fiber of the ruling shows that none of them is ample. The explicit family of Dolbeault operators in proposition 11.14.3 converges to the split operator in every finite $C^ m$ norm. These stable, nonample approximations give the stable point used in the deformation argument of theorem 11.15.5 . The approximation theorem theorem 11.15.5 is Liu and Wan's [ v1, Theorem 4.1, p. 17; proof, p. 22 , LiuWanKobayashi26 ] . Its input on the stack of prioritary sheaves is Walter's [ v1, Proposition 2, p. 2 , WalterPrioritary93 ] , which applies to all prioritary torsion-free sheaves of fixed rank at least two with fixed numerical Chern classes, without any semistability assumption. The required openness statements are proved directly by the family arguments in lemma 11.15.1 , lemma 11.15.2 , lemma 11.15.3 ; on a Hirzebruch surface, slope stability reduces to finitely many classes of line bundles. Parallel transport and compactness, in lemma 11.15.4 , give convergence on the fixed smooth bundle and on its dual in every finite $C^ m$ norm. Combining this approximation with the Gauduchon-degree obstruction and the polar construction above gives corollary 11.15.6 , which is Liu and Wan's [ v1, Theorem 1.1, p. 2; proof, p. 23 , LiuWanKobayashi26 ] . The fixed Stein hypersurface of theorem 11.16.3 , corollary 11.16.4 corresponds to Liu and Wan's [ v1, Proposition 5.1, pp. 24–27 , LiuWanKobayashi26 ] for explicit algebraic bundles. A positive horizontal direction and the vertical critical hyperplane give the test on the Levi index, and a holomorphic quadratic jet makes the real Hessian nondegenerate without changing the Levi form. Separability of the relevant metric space gives countably many robust local tests, which lemma 11.16.1 , lemma 11.16.2 place on a single global graph by Runge and Oka–Weil approximation. The graph is chosen before the metric, whereas the critical point that detects the failure may depend on the metric. The dual norm of a concave neighborhood, theorem 11.17.2 , is Liu and Wan's [ v1, Lemma 5.2, pp. 27–32 , LiuWanKobayashi26 ] . After a correction by a pure jet, a negative tangent plane of the boundary gives a supporting holomorphic section. Balls of uniform size tangent to the boundary from inside then express the squared dual norm as a supremum of functions with a common margin of strong real convexity, and ampleness together with homogeneous regularization gives a smooth replacement. Let $E$ be an ample bundle of rank $r$, and write $U_ E=\mathbb P(\mathcal O_ X\oplus E)\setminus \mathbb P(\mathcal O_ X)$ for the complement of the zero section in its projective completion. The argument at high levels of an exhaustion in corollary 11.17.4 , which shows that $U_ E$ is not $r$-convex when $E^*$ admits no smooth complex norm with plurisubharmonic square, is their [ v1, Corollary 5.3, p. 32 , LiuWanKobayashi26 ] . Combined with the norm obstruction and the stable ample approximation, it gives corollary 11.17.5 . The case of positive mean curvature in theorem 11.18.2 , corollary 11.18.4 is Liu and Wan's [ v1, Proposition 5.4, pp. 32–33 , LiuWanKobayashi26 ] . The calculation with the reciprocal of the norm gives the more general count, in which $s$ positive horizontal directions of the curvature give $(n+r-s)$-convexity of $U_ E$ for a bundle $E$ of rank $r$. For stable bundles of positive degree, the application uses the existence of Hermitian–Einstein metrics, proved by Uhlenbeck and Yau [ UhlenbeckYau86 ] in the Kähler case and extended to Gauduchon metrics by Li and Yau [ LiYau87 ] . The degree of definition 11.18.3 pairs the Bott–Chern first Chern class with the Gauduchon form; with the unscaled curvature $F_ h$ of a Hermitian metric $h$, the integrated trace carries the factor $2\pi n$. The resulting least convexity index three in corollary 11.18.5 is [ v1, Corollary 5.5, p. 33 , LiuWanKobayashi26 ] ; the lower bound uses the dual-norm obstruction above. The negative-bundle weight in proposition 11.19.1 is the construction of Kusakabe and Matsumura [ v1, Lemma 3.2(a,b,d), pp. 20–21 , KusakabeMatsumuraOka26 ] . The complete metric of corollary 11.19.3 uses the two exhaustion barriers in the first paragraph of their proof of [ v1, Lemma 3.3, p. 21 , KusakabeMatsumuraOka26 ] . Their jet-vanishing condition [ v1, Lemma 3.4, p. 21 , KusakabeMatsumuraOka26 ] follows here from the smooth-center multiplier-ideal formula, which gives the exact ideal and the sharp threshold for every real weight in corollary 11.19.2 . In their argument the logarithmic weight supports weighted $\bar\partial $ estimates and the gluing of local sprays; here its direct Levi calculation relates negative bundle curvature to the singularity along the zero section. Suppose that, for a holomorphic bundle $F$ of rank $r$, the complement $F^\times $ of the zero section carries a smooth positive plurisubharmonic function that is homogeneous of degree two. Taking maxima over the level spheres, proposition 11.21.1 then shows that the least convexity index of $U_ F$ is $n+r$: a negative radial derivative makes the Levi form restricted to the level set nonpositive on a complex hyperplane. Unitary-flat metrics give corollary 11.21.3 . For the line bundles $E_ a$ on a Hopf manifold in example 11.21.4 , restriction to an elliptic fiber and positive curvature give the least index two when $|a|<1$, whereas a homogeneous plurisubharmonic metric gives the least index $n+1$ when $|a|\geq 1$; the Gauduchon degree distinguishes the three signs, although the de Rham first Chern class vanishes. A metric with Griffiths-nonpositive curvature gives the same homogeneous function in corollary 11.21.2 . For split bundles on Hopf manifolds, proposition 11.21.5 combines the weighted curvature with the exact loss of dimension under restriction to closed submanifolds in lemma 11.17.3 . It gives the least indices $r+1$ and $n+r$ in the two pure regimes; in the mixed regime, only separate upper and lower bounds are obtained. For external tensor products, theorem 11.20.2 applies the same exhaustion with one positive curvature direction from each factor. The positive mean curvatures lifted from the factors control every vector of the tensor product, including the indecomposable ones, and give corollary 11.20.3 . For the tangent bundle of a surface with a nonflat Ricci-flat Kähler metric, corollary 11.27.5 combines the exhaustion instead with the directional positivity of theorem 11.27.4 : this tangent bundle admits no metric whose mean curvature is positive definite, but its RC-positive metric still gives the required exhaustion. For the logarithmic parabolic Monge–Ampère flow on Kähler manifolds, the calculation of $L^ p$ norms of the volume ratio is Jiyuan Han's [ v1, Lemma 3.2, pp. 13–14 , HanParabolic26 ] . The chain rule and Stokes computation in proposition 11.23.8 keep the additional term coming from the derivative of the Hermitian background. When the forms along the flow remain Gauduchon, convex entropies decrease (corollary 11.23.11 ), and varying the target probability measure gives the exact criterion at the initial time in proposition 11.23.12 . These statements apply on any interval on which a smooth solution exists. Han's uniform estimates for degenerating families of Calabi–Yau manifolds, and the Green-function estimates on which they depend, are not part of this calculation. The calculation of the total variation in proposition 11.23.16 is a direct variation of determinants on a flat torus, whose coefficient is given by the two Haar averages of lemma 11.23.14 . Corollary 11.23.17 compares this growth of the distance between two solutions with the initial derivatives of the individual entropies. The support lemma for currents carried by a smooth hypersurface, lemma 11.22.1 , is the local statement used by Dinh and Sibony in [ proof of Theorem 4.1, pp. 965–966 , DinhSibonyRegularization04 ] , where it is attributed to Bassanelli. The proof given here tests against a quadratic function of the normal coordinate and polarizes horizontal forms; it applies whenever $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R$ has order zero, $R$ being the positive current supported on the hypersurface. The estimate for pullbacks in lemma 11.22.2 follows directly from the classical $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-lemma for currents on compact Kähler manifolds, applied to a fixed closed pushforward; the current that is paired with the distributional primitive is smooth. The smoothing of positive pluriharmonic forms with continuous coefficients in lemma 11.22.3 uses the heat equation of the Hodge Laplacian, the Kähler identities and a positive correction tending to zero. For continuous potentials and closed backgrounds on a compact Kähler manifold, Dinh and Sibony construct the product of the curvature current with a positive pluriharmonic current through an energy [ Theorem 5.1, Proposition 5.2 and identity (12), pp. 967–969 , DinhSibonyRegularization04 ] . The proofs of lemma 11.31.10 , theorem 11.31.11 integrate by parts against the current of bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$ itself, so that no auxiliary power of a Kähler form is needed. They give a positive measure as product, depending jointly continuously on the factors, on any compact Hermitian manifold, for every smooth real background and continuous potential. The descent of horizontal currents in lemma 11.22.4 follows directly from the positivity of the coefficient matrix together with the Liouville theorem for harmonic functions on the complex line, or the maximum principle on a compact connected curve. It therefore applies both to bundles with fiber $\mathbb C$ and to bundles of compact curves. On the elliptic threefold, the exact vertical trace form gives lemma 10.19.1 for positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed currents, and its closed case gives the calculation of the Bott–Chern cone. The mean-curvature criterion for RC-positivity and the conformal construction in lemma 11.26.2 , theorem 11.26.3 correspond to Chou and Wu's [ v1, Definition 5 and Lemmas 7–8, pp. 5–6 , ChouWuRC26 ] . The scalar equation in the construction is the Gauduchon compatibility condition of proposition 11.23.2 , and taking the curvature margin over a closed ball makes it uniform in both the base point and the unit fiber vector. Example 11.26.6 shows directly that the order of these two quantifiers matters, and proposition 11.26.7 gives a global obstruction to interchanging them when the determinant bundle admits a flat Hermitian metric. The RC-positive tangent metrics on Ricci-flat surfaces in theorem 11.27.4 are Chou and Wu's [ v1, Theorem 1 and Lemmas 9–15, pp. 7–12 , ChouWuRC26 ] . The pointwise criterion is the invertibility of the anti-self-dual curvature operator. The identities behind ( 11.27.3 ) are Derdziński's [ equations (33)–(35), p. 414 , Derdzinski83 ] , with the nonnegative Laplacian on functions used there replaced by $\operatorname {div}\nabla $ and with the same norm on endomorphisms; summing the three equations for the eigenvalues gives the coefficient $36$. The commuting curvature factors in [ Lemma 2, p. 412 , Derdzinski83 ] also show directly that a nonzero parallel operator with three distinct eigenvalues cannot occur here. This gives the required nonempty open set and a conformal tangent metric whose associated form is not closed. The symmetrized sectional-curvature average and the integrated trace identity in lemma 11.28.2 , proposition 11.28.3 are Xueyuan Wan's [ v1, Lemma 2.1 and Proposition 3.3 with Lemmas 3.1–3.2, pp. 5–8 , WanHermitianSectional26 ] . The average is proved here by complex Gaussian moments, and the connection calculation retains the exact term until Stokes' theorem removes it. The auxiliary metric $g$ is Kähler, while the tangent metric $h$ can be nonclosed. Their identity gives corollary 11.28.5 directly from the signs of its three terms. This use of the identity does not require the auxiliary Hessian equation or the canonical-bundle positivity argument of that paper. The torus and finite torus-cover statements of proposition 11.28.7 , corollary 11.28.8 follow from this identity and periodic integration by parts: the symmetric connection difference vanishes, forcing the Hermitian coefficients to be constant. In dimension one, the same conclusion is the maximum principle for the logarithm of the metric coefficient. The first-jet characterization of Griffiths positivity on projective manifolds, theorem 11.29.9 , is due to Du and Xie [ v1, Theorem 1.1 and Proposition 2.1, pp. 1–4 , DuXieFirstJet26 ] ; the identity in normal frames is written in the curvature convention used above. The density with two derivatives that the argument requires is proved directly in lemma 11.29.6 , lemma 11.29.7 , through normalized projective coordinates and Bernstein polynomials. The immersion test without twist, corollary 11.29.10 , is the calculation in [ v1, Section 3.1, pp. 4–5 , DuXieFirstJet26 ] . The positive measure in the dual alternative lives on the sphere bundle of the dual bundle, so the condition that it annihilates all metrics is different from Gauduchon duality on the base. The double cover in section 11.30 , branched over $2q$ points, gives an explicit model with a computable space of sections in which a strictly positive line bundle fails the test without twist. The decomposition of sections into even and odd parts and the projective embedding are proved explicitly. A root of a very ample Fubini–Study metric gives a separately defined weighted family of tests, and proposition 11.30.3 identifies its first successful level $j=q-1$, together with obstructions by one or two atoms at the lower levels. The original criterion with a fixed very ample twist $m$ follows the subsequence $j=qm$, so this calculation does not determine its first successful twist. The obstructions at a single level should also be distinguished from an adjoint measure annihilating every smooth metric.

title: 25.6 Bounded products and extended measures
text: The Bedford–Taylor product of bounded potentials is local even when the background is not closed: expanding against smooth local corrections, as Kołodziej and Nguyen [ Section 1 , KN15 ] and Boucksom, Guedj and Lu [ Section 2.1 , BGL25 ] do, gives proposition 5.28.2 . Restricting the products of the truncations to the sets where the potential exceeds the truncation level then defines the extended measure of theorem 13.14.3 , by the mechanism of [ Proposition 2.1 , BGL25 ] . Finiteness becomes decisive when these restrictions are removed in the category of currents, and [ Theorem 2.2 , BGL25 ] uses a uniform bound on the variation for this purpose. An infinite extended positive measure is still given by the local construction, but it is not a global current of order zero. The independence of the bounded mass property from the metric, and the reduction to smooth potentials, in proposition 13.14.15 recover the comparison made after [ Definition 1.16 , BGL25 ] ; decreasing regularization with exact curvature bounds gives the passage from smooth to bounded potentials. The Gauduchon trace bound and the cancellation of the exact top-degree wedge product used in proposition 13.15.2 also appear in Guedj and Lu's [ Proposition 3.3(i), (vi) , GL22 ] , and the estimate in terms of the range of the potential keeps their polynomial dependence on the oscillation. The local mixed Monge–Ampère inequality, theorem 5.27.5 , is Dinew's [ Theorem 1.2 , Dinew09 ] , for locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions whose Monge–Ampère measures dominate nonnegative measurable densities with respect to Lebesgue measure. Its extension to smooth backgrounds is proved in section 5.28 and used in subsection 15.18.2 . Freezing the coefficients of the two smooth backgrounds gives lemma 5.28.7 and the trace inequalities ( 15.14.3 ) and lemma 13.14.12 , the latter keeping the mass of the linear trace on the pole set. The same argument also recovers the inequality for smooth volume forms used by Nguyen [ Lemma 1.9 , Nguyen16 ] .

title: 25.7 Envelopes and comparison
text: Narzillaev studies weighted extremal functions of a compact set $K\subset \mathbb C^ n$ with a bounded weight $\psi $ on $K$ and logarithmic growth $\delta \log ^+\lVert z\rVert $, $\delta >0$. The concavity in the growth parameter and the alternatives for regular contact in theorem 16.28.14 are stated in [ v1, Lemma 3.1 and Theorem 1.1, p. 6 , NarzillaevWeighted26 ] ; the proof given here also shows directly, by scaling, that the set of parameters at which the unregularized envelope attains the obstacle on $K$ is empty or a ray. Lemma 16.28.9 , Proposition 16.28.10 derive the correspondence with compact envelopes on projective space, the finiteness of the envelope and its almost-everywhere order from the compactness and extension results proved earlier in the book. In the book's convention, the growth $\delta \log ^+\lVert z\rVert $ corresponds to the projective background $(\delta /2)\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ and to the obstacle $\psi -\delta \log (1+\lVert z\rVert ^2)/2$; Narzillaev's operator $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial /2$ is $\pi $ times the book's. None of the theorems of that preprint on products, plurithinness or weighted counterexamples is used in these proofs. For the zero obstacle, corollary 16.28.13 gives the case of compact sets of the classical fact, recalled in [ v1, Section 2, equation (4), p. 4 , NarzillaevWeighted26 ] , that removing a pluripolar set does not change the extremal function. For bounded weights, the proof uses the logarithmic pole barrier of lemma 16.28.12 . Proposition 5.40.6 carries out the corresponding argument for compact sets in an arbitrary smooth big background, using the correction of pointwise competitors in lemma 5.40.5 . The estimates for increments in the growth parameter in lemma 16.28.18 are [ v1, Lemma 3.1, p. 6 , NarzillaevWeighted26 ] , and at a point of regular contact proposition 16.28.20 , corollary 16.28.24 recover [ v1, Proposition 3.2, p. 7 , NarzillaevWeighted26 ] . The proof given here keeps the estimates for the initial and the later slopes at every point of $\mathbb C^ n$ and every positive growth parameter, including the uniform error for large increments. The representation by probability measures and the attained derivative in theorem 16.28.27 , theorem 16.28.29 come from [ v1, Theorems 3.3–3.4, pp. 8–9 , NarzillaevWeighted26 ] ; the same argument with the finite envelope extends them to every point and every positive parameter. The passage to weak limits of these probability measures uses the continuity of the weight. The joint response to changes of the weight and of the growth, and the criteria for differentiability, in lemma 16.28.33 , proposition 16.28.35 , corollary 16.28.37 , corollary 16.28.39 , follow directly from the attained representation and the compactness of its set of active pairs. Example 16.28.40 gives an explicit corner in the dependence on the weight, on the closed unit disk. The relative extremal function of definition 5.27.4 follows the convention for compact sets in [ v1, Section 2, equation (8), p. 5 , NarzillaevWeighted26 ] . Lemma 16.28.43 , which shows that the relative extremal function equals $-1$ at a point exactly when the global extremal function vanishes there, is proved by an explicit logarithmic gluing and the pole barrier above. Lemma 16.28.45 , Theorem 16.28.46 give [ v1, Lemma 4.1 and Theorem 4.2, p. 10 , NarzillaevWeighted26 ] , including the local strictness hypothesis $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi \geq c\omega _0$ near the point, with $\omega _0=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\lVert z\rVert ^2$, a global weight $\Psi $ in the given growth class extending the weight on $K$, and the closed compact pieces inside the ball. Narzillaev's operator and Euclidean form are both $\pi $ times those of the book, so the coefficient $c$ and the bound for the defect are unchanged. The pointwise consequence for the Hessian in corollary 16.28.48 is the observation following that theorem on p. 10. The planar disks and the quantitative barrier of lemma 16.28.50 come from [ v1, Lemma 6.1, pp. 12–13 , NarzillaevWeighted26 ] . Proposition 16.28.51 proves part of the product construction in [ v1, Lemma 6.2, pp. 13–14 , NarzillaevWeighted26 ] , namely the contact defect along the exceptional fiber and the failure of plurithinness at the interior point specified there. The logarithmic series is constructed by convergence of canonical representatives on compact sets, and an explicit pole barrier produces competitors that satisfy the obstacle everywhere. The proof needs neither a general product formula nor a classification at all boundary points. The formula on normal fibers for the pluricomplex Green function with a divisorial pole, proposition 5.40.10 , is the case of the unit ball of Dao, Nguyen and Tran's [ v1, Proposition 4.2, p. 25 , DNTGreen26 ] , with logarithms normalized as $\log |\zeta |^2$ in the normal coordinate $\zeta $; the proof uses the maximum principle in one variable. The bounded minorants of proposition 5.40.12 converge at every interior point, including the points of the divisor, with an explicit error bound. This is a special model for the approximation by bounded envelopes in [ Theorem 1.7, pp. 5–6 , DNTGreen26 ] , whose general result assumes an inward deformation in a sector and uses B-regularity for continuity. The calculation of boundary cluster values in example 5.40.15 concerns the trace of the divisor on the boundary, whereas that theorem asserts continuity inside the domain. Contact sets connect the order of potentials with the order of their Monge–Ampère measures. For semipositive big backgrounds, theorem 16.28.5 is due to Alehyane, Lu and Salouf [ Theorem 2.2 , ALS26 ] ; the passage from bounded to unbounded potentials in the book removes the bigness assumption and a uniform mass assumption. For a general big background, Boucksom, Guedj and Lu [ Theorem 2.9 and Proposition 2.11 , BGL25 ] prove that the measure of the envelope is concentrated on the contact set under bounded mass, and local replacement together with a strict singular barrier gives theorem 15.8.6 without that assumption. The measure estimate for envelope fixed points, proposition 16.28.7 , is [ Proposition 2.12 , ALS26 ] . Let $\theta $ be smooth and semipositive, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ satisfy $P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi $ for the ordinary envelope of definition 5.40.4 . The proof given here uses the identity $P_\theta (\varphi +1,0)=\varphi $, where $P_\theta (\varphi +1,0)$ is the largest $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function lying below $\min (\varphi +1,0)$ (section 5.40 ); contact with the first obstacle occurs only on the pluripolar set $\{ \varphi =-\infty \} $, so only contact with zero contributes to the measure. For bounded potentials, the proof of the domination principle by envelopes, theorem 16.28.56 , is due to Guedj and Lu [ Proposition 2.8 , GL22 ] . Difference envelopes give a relative class in which singular potentials can still be compared. The construction appears for semipositive big backgrounds in [ Proposition 2.4 and Lemma 2.5 , ALS26 ] and for arbitrary big backgrounds in Xuan Li's [ Section 2.1 , XL26 ] ; the estimate for sublevel sets shows that the envelope is not identically $-\infty $ as soon as its family of competitors is nonempty. The relative envelope class of definition 16.28.61 follows [ Definition 3.2 , ALS26 ] , and the proof of its closure under convex stretching, lemma 16.28.63 , is the argument of [ Proposition 3.5 , ALS26 ] . The condition ( 16.28.67 ) on the reference and its consequence, positivity of the mass of each individual potential in the class, appear in [ Proposition 2.10 and the discussion after Definition 2.13 , ALS26 ] ; that paper does not assume bounded mass for its equations with $L^ p$ data in a fixed ordinary type. This positivity for individual potentials must be distinguished from a positive infimum of the mass over the whole ordinary singularity type. The mechanism giving the lower bound for the mass in theorem 16.28.70 is that of [ Proposition 3.8 , ALS26 ] . For lower semicontinuous obstacles the contact argument requires an approximation. The proof of proposition 16.28.3 follows Guedj and Lu [ Theorem 2.3 , GL22 ] and uses the Bedford–Taylor convergence theorem for increasing bounded sequences [ Theorem 7.4 , BT82 ] ; smooth local corrections and an expansion against the remaining background extend it to nonclosed backgrounds. The modified comparison principle, theorem 14.19.6 , is due to Kołodziej and Nguyen [ Theorem 0.2 , KN15 ] . The proof given here follows the finite induction of Guedj and Lu [ Theorem 1.5 , GL22 ] , with larger dimensional constants.

title: 25.8 Smooth and continuous equations
text: On a Hermitian manifold, the smooth Monge–Ampère equation determines a normalization constant together with the potential. For $n\geq 2$, the existence theorem theorem 14.2.1 is Tosatti and Weinkove's [ Corollary 1 , TW10 ] . Their equation, for a smooth function $F$ prescribing the logarithm of the density, is written with $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial \varphi $; the substitution $u=2\pi \varphi $ gives the convention of this book, and a prescribed smooth volume form $\mathrm dV$ is absorbed by replacing $F$ with $F+\log (\mathrm dV/\omega ^ n)$. The concavity argument with Gauduchon metrics for the normalization constant in theorem 14.8.1 also appears in Collins's [ Theorem 2.13 , Collins21 ] . The proof of the uniform estimate for the potential in section 14.1 by weighted integration follows Cherrier and Tosatti–Weinkove [ Cherrier87 , TW10 ] : a finite recurrence absorbs the torsion terms before the Sobolev iteration. The calculation of the torsion terms in the second-order estimate of section 14.1 goes back to Cherrier; its form with completed squares and the maximum-principle argument follow [ Sections 3 and 9 , TW15 ] . The interpolation in lemma 14.5.7 is the mechanism of Jiaogen Zhang and Xi Zhang's [ v1, Proposition 4.1 and its proof, p. 16 , ZhangHessianInterpolation26 ] . The fixed scalar operator is uniformly elliptic for a Hermitian metric as well, so the linear implication here does not require closedness. Their nonlinear Hessian application assumes a Kähler metric and a small product of its negative bisectional-curvature bound with the solution's oscillation. Its argument for data close to one in $L^1$ uses a stability estimate with $q>n/k$ and a uniform $L^ q$ bound; the smallness threshold depends on that bound. The interpolation lemma supplies neither this nonlinear trace estimate nor an arbitrary-$L^1$ stability criterion. Prescribing the volume form of a Gauduchon metric leads to a different equation, which contains first-order torsion terms. The existence theorem theorem 14.10.1 is due to Székelyhidi, Tosatti and Weinkove [ Theorem 1.4 , STW17 ] , again with the potential multiplied by $2\pi $. The bound for the potential in section 14.11 follows Székelyhidi's [ Propositions 10–11 and Remark 12 , Sze18 ] , specialized to the determinant of the Gauduchon equation, and the second-order argument in section 14.14 follows [ Section 3 , STW17 ] . The identities ( 14.13.4 ), taken from [ Section 4 , STW17 ] , explain the structure of the first-order perturbation. The gradient estimate combines a blow-up argument with a Liouville theorem. In ( 14.16.3 ), where $A_ j$ are the rescaling factors of the blow-up, the first-order term is kept before rescaling and tends to zero at the rate $A_ j^{-1}$, as in [ Section 6 , Sze18 ] . The Euclidean argument in section 14.15 specializes [ Theorem 20 , Sze18 ] to the Gauduchon cone. Once the equation is uniformly elliptic, lemma 14.17.1 uses the Evans–Krylov theorem for variable coefficients of Tosatti, Wang, Weinkove and Yang [ Definition 3.2 and Theorem 3.4 , TWWY15 ] . For densities in $L^ p$, the existence of continuous solutions of the equation with a normalization constant (theorem 14.19.2 ) and of the exponential equation ( 14.19.4 ) is due respectively to Kołodziej and Nguyen [ Theorem 0.1 , KN15 ] and to Nguyen [ Theorem 0.1 , Nguyen16 ] . Their operator is twice the one used here: for the exponent $\lambda >0$ in ( 14.19.4 ), the conversion is $u=2\varphi $, where $\varphi $ is their solution, and the exponent in their equation is $2\lambda $. These results require neither bounded mass nor positive lower volume. Compactness comes from local capacity estimates: the arguments of [ Section 5 , KN15 ] and [ Section 6 , Dinew16 ] lead to theorem 14.19.21 , which is the statement of [ Corollary 5.10 , KN15 ] . A common bound for the densities is essential here; the $L^1$ compactness of normalized potentials alone does not suffice. For measures satisfying a power bound in capacity, Kołodziej and Nguyen [ Proposition 2.4, pp. 2954–2956 , KNHolder18 ] give stability measured against the Monge–Ampère measure of the solution. The thin-sublevel estimate and backwards iteration of lemma 14.19.14 , lemma 14.19.16 follow the capacity argument in [ v2, Theorem 5.3 and Lemma 5.4, pp. 10–12 , KN15 ] , using their modified comparison theorem [ v2, Theorem 2.3, pp. 5–6 , KN15 ] . The geometric iteration in the book covers every power $1+\alpha $, $\alpha >0$, including the total-capacity endpoint. Choosing the sublevel height proportional to the cube of the comparison reserve gives the exponent $\alpha /[3n(1+\alpha )+\alpha ]$ in proposition 14.19.23 ; the square-capacity case has exponent $1/(6n+1)$. The measure can be singular. The preprint [ v2, p. 1 , KN15 ] uses $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial /\pi $, twice our operator; its backgrounds become $2\omega $ with the same potentials, and its top products acquire the factor $2^ n$. The threshold equation in theorem 15.33.1 combines this iteration with bounded-density solvability and the full Gauduchon formula. Local $L^1$ compactness uses Demailly's Propositions 4.21 and 5.9 [ Chapter I, pp. 36–37 and 40 , DemCADG ] . The weighted local product estimate is Nguyen's [ v1, Proposition 1.1, pp. 5–6 , Nguyen16 ] ; uniform continuity of bounded products is Bedford and Taylor's [ Corollary 2.8 and Theorem 2.10, p. 10 , BT82 ] . For a Hermitian background, the local closed product must still be expanded with every smooth correction factor, as in proposition 5.28.2 . The logarithmic construction in theorem 15.33.6 uses the exponential volume–capacity estimate ( 5.29.3 ) and gives a datum outside every higher $L^ p$ class with an exact continuous threshold solution. The added capacity hypothesis leaves the general root-tail and exact-equation questions open. For a continuous solution whose measure is dominated by a Hölder reference, theorem 15.5.4 combines the weighted Chern estimate with the square-capacity stability. The coordinated transform parameter and comparison reserve keep the minimizing radii comparable to the smoothing radius. The resulting exponent is sufficient for the range theorem; no optimal exponent is asserted. The argument assumes continuity of the solution. The smoothness theorem theorem 14.19.32 is the strictly positive, globally smooth-data case of Badiane, Lu and Zeriahi's [ v1, Theorem 1.1, p. 2; Section 4.2, p. 17 , BLZBoundedSmooth26 ] . Their auxiliary second-order estimate is Proposition 4.1, pp. 13–17. The square of the prescribed potential in lemma 14.19.31 absorbs the derivatives of the frozen density, and bounded exponential comparison identifies the uniform limit with the original solution. The argument then uses the concave uniformly elliptic extension of the logarithmic determinant and the Evans–Krylov theorem for variable coefficients [ Definition 3.2, Theorem 3.4, and the paragraph following it , TWWY15 ] . Only the strictly positive Hermitian background and global smooth positive density are treated here; the primary paper also considers degenerate backgrounds and data with a singular regular locus. The exponential term gives a comparison principle even when the densities have no positive lower bound; lemma 14.19.28 recovers [ Lemma 2.3 , Nguyen16 ] . Letting the exponent tend to zero then identifies the normalization constant through ( 14.19.35 ), as in [ Corollary 0.2 , Nguyen16 ] . This proves uniqueness of the constant, but not uniqueness of the limiting potential. The weighted mean ( 14.19.27 ), taken from [ Proposition 2.5 , Nguyen16 ] , controls the normalization; here its lower bound follows directly from the estimate for sublevel sets. Equations with prescribed singularities require relative envelopes and separate assumptions on the reference potential and on the ambient metric. The results of Alehyane–Lu–Salouf and of Xuan Li [ ALS26 , XL26 ] are therefore treated separately in section 15.1 , section 15.37 , section 10.31 ; their sources are discussed in section 25.12 . For fully nonlinear concave equations, the uniform estimate under a quantitative subsolution condition is due to Guo and Phong [ v1, Theorem 3.1 and its proof, pp. 8–11 , GP24 ] . The strict asymptotic gap of an admissible reference, the matrix bound, the linear stability estimate and the uniform compactness in subsection 14.19.42 follow Guo and Song [ v1, Lemma 2.1, Proposition 2.8 and Lemma 2.9, pp. 4–11 , GS26 ] . In the book, the zero-order estimate uses the real contact-set construction of proposition 14.11.1 , and theorem 14.19.19 bounds both the auxiliary potential and its normalization constant; with these inputs the constants do not depend on a positive lower bound for the right-hand sides. Writing the potential of these sources as $u/(2\pi )$ converts their convention for smooth curvature forms into the normalization of this book. The gradient estimate in subsection 14.19.47 is Guo and Song's [ v1, Theorem 1.1 and Proposition 3.1 with Lemmas 3.2–3.6, pp. 11–17 , GS26 ] ; the earlier alternative for convex level sets is Székelyhidi's [ arXiv v3, Propositions 5–6, pp. 5–7 , Sze18 ] . The tangent-hyperplane argument in lemma 14.19.48 uses the common strict gap to keep the constants uniform at every positive level. The differentiation is carried out for $U=u/(2\pi )$, where $u$ is the solution, and the final finite net of smooth comparison functions is provided by corollary 14.19.46 .

title: 25.9 Uniqueness and selection
text: When the exponent is zero, uniqueness of the normalization constant leaves open the separate question of uniqueness of the potential. Degeneration of the density affects comparison, whereas the family of equations with positive exponent can select a particular solution of the critical equation. The argument by concentration of mass for densities restricted to a set, around ( 14.25.6 ), follows Lu, Phung and Tô [ proof of Theorem 3.7 and Remark 3.8 , LPT20 ] . The exterior-ball argument for ( 14.22.11 ) instead propagates the maximum, following Bardi and Goffi [ Proposition 2.4 and Theorem 2.5 in the cited preprint , BG18 ] . The uniqueness theorem for bounded potentials, theorem 14.24.1 , concerns a continuous nonnegative density whose positivity set is connected and dense, and is proved with energy estimates on level sets and auxiliary test potentials. The mixed inequality and the passage to coefficient densities use the local calculus of section 5.21 , and the continuity of bounded solutions is obtained in the book itself, by a comparison argument, in corollary 14.19.29 . The smooth local Dirichlet problem needed for proposition 14.24.13 is solved by Guan's theorem [ Theorem 1.1, pp. 687–688 , Guan98 ] , whose hypothesis is satisfied by a strictly plurisubharmonic quadratic subsolution. The estimate on the real contact set then gives a constant that depends only on the fixed geometry and the $L^2$ bound, and not on the height of the test density. For measurable densities that are bounded above and bounded away from zero, uniqueness is derived in corollary 14.24.17 from the same energy argument on level sets. The classical counterpart is [ Corollary 3.9 and Remark 3.13 , KN19 ] , where the locators refer to the authors' version indicated in the bibliography.

title: 25.10 Complex Hessian equations
text: The cone inequalities and the estimate with a prescribed potential in section 8.1 follow Fang's [ v1, Lemma 2.2, Proposition 2.3 and Theorem 3.1, pp. 5–6 and 8–17 , FangHessianSmooth26 ] . The scalar shift in 8.2.3 is proved through real roots, including its endpoint. Polarized positivity then gives the mixed-trace and linearized coefficient bounds. The largest-eigenvalue argument keeps the Chern torsion terms and evaluates every derivative of the Hessian root at the original matrix, while a separate positive perturbation supplies its smooth lower support. In the quadratic weight used for the potential, the bound $-3A\leq \Psi '\leq -A$ determines the choice of the small eigenvalue parameter. The absolute mixed-form estimate below Hessian degree $m$ and the torsion bounds for products are the mechanisms of Kołodziej and Nguyen [ arXiv v2, Section 2.1, pp. 4–7 , KNHessian16 ] . The Euclidean Liouville theorem 8.3.2 is due to Dinew and Kołodziej [ arXiv v2, Theorem 3.2, pp. 8–11 , DKHessian17 ] . Their rescaling argument is Section 2, pp. 6–7, there; its Hermitian version is also used by Székelyhidi [ arXiv v2, Section 6, pp. 26–27 , Sze18 ] . The proof here uses constant-cone linear tests and lower viscosity tests to pass to the maximal limit, so it does not require a variable-background Hessian-product convergence theorem. The averaging proof obtains the uniform directional energy bound with a fixed dependence on the smaller averaging radius. The subsequent local Laplace estimate controls the real Hessian in finite $L^ p$ spaces. Smooth proper existence and admissible approximation are the mechanisms of Kołodziej and Nguyen [ arXiv v2, Theorem 3.17 and Lemma 3.20, pp. 23–25 , KNHessian16 ] and Guedj and Lu [ arXiv v1, Theorem 1.7, pp. 4–5 , GLHessian25 ] . Here the smooth trace and gradient estimates first close the proper continuity path. Its penalty equations then approximate every continuous admissible potential uniformly. This construction precedes the definition of continuous Hessian products and does not use a domination theorem. For positive exponential coefficient $a$, rescaling both the metric and the potential reduces the equation to coefficient one. The maximum comparison in 8.8.1 gives the coefficient $a^{-1}$ for continuous data. The existence assertion in 8.8.3 then follows from a contraction on the interval between constant barriers, followed by the continuous regularity theorem. The decreasing approximation theorem 8.6.6 extends the construction to bounded potentials and recovers Kołodziej and Nguyen's [ arXiv v2, Lemma 3.20, pp. 25–26 , KNHessian16 ] . The bounded upper-test characterization is the one used by Guedj and Lu [ arXiv v1, Section 1.1.1, pp. 3–4 , GLHessian25 ] , through smooth strictly elliptic linear tests. Here successive smooth obstacles are chosen below the preceding admissible approximant, and the penalty error is then made smaller than their fixed gap. This gives a decreasing sequence before defining any product of the bounded potential. The same squeeze proves 8.7.4 after the continuous obstacle envelope has been constructed. Continuous mixed products and their uniform continuity are [ arXiv v2, Proposition 2.11 and Corollary 2.12, pp. 10–11 , KNHessian16 ] . The contact comparison, nonvanishing and domination arguments of section 8.7 follow Guedj and Lu [ arXiv v1, Lemma 1.10, Theorems 2.1–2.2 and Corollaries 2.3–2.4, pp. 6 and 8–9 , GLHessian25 ] . The continuous obstacle envelope is constructed by the same penalty solutions, giving continuity and contact support directly. Differentiated background factors are interpreted using the signed lower-degree products. In the mass nonvanishing proof, the telescoping form has degree $n-1$ and retains each power of the original potential. The normalized linear Green estimate rules out an open set on which the stretched difference envelopes tend to $-\infty $. The bounded recursion in section 8.9 follows the construction of Kołodziej and Nguyen [ Lemmas 3.1–3.2, Theorem 3.3 and Proposition 3.7, pp. 125–129 , KNHermitianMeasures26 ] . Their local cone is imposed on $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, whereas the book imposes it on $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. The proof here therefore expands each raw factor into a shifted admissible factor minus the smooth background before applying the coefficient estimates. The first limit is in the first potential, and the final limit is in the last potential; the top unwedged current remains distributional. The positive shifted wedge has measure coefficients, while its background derivatives are given explicitly in 8.9.7 . Permutation invariance does not follow from this ordered construction alone, as the source also points out in [ Remark 3.6, p. 128 , KNHermitianMeasures26 ] . Its later capacity and weighted-convergence results concern the source local class. The elementary correction in 8.9.8 places $u+\rho $ in that class while retaining the same Hermitian metric. It preserves the nonclosed background terms and does not itself prove the capacity quasicontinuity needed for higher-degree simultaneous convergence. The two-factor argument in section 8.10 uses instead the global conformal Gauduchon multiplier of theorem 11.4.2 . The energy identity for $u^2$ bounds the Sobolev norm, and first-order integration by parts retains the $\mathrm dT$ term of the nonclosed Gauduchon test. Sobolev truncation and mollification prove the capacity bound for the positive linear trace; the second-cone inequality transfers it to every first-Hessian coefficient. Tail convex combinations from Mazur's lemma identify quasicontinuity with the canonical potential pointwise. A common exceptional set, Dini's theorem and bounded continuous extension then give the weighted convergence used in 8.10.5 . This argument controls two factors without applying the source's local capacity results to a shifted cone. The cutoff absolute-coordinate potentials in 8.10.7 show that a two-Hessian measure can charge a smooth real codimension-two set of zero Sobolev capacity. Thus this capacity estimate cannot supply the higher-degree argument. The local capacity and decreasing-convergence conclusions are studied in [ Corollaries 3.18–3.19, p. 137, and Lemma 5.1, pp. 143–145 , KNHermitianMeasures26 ] . In section 8.11 , smooth competitors suffice to control the coefficients of the book's ordered currents. A fixed regularized maximum localizes decreasing smooth approximations near the boundary. The smooth energy variation retains every derivative of the Hermitian background and gives convergence in these local capacities. Outer-open coefficient estimates and bounded continuous extension then prove the weighted convergence needed for 8.11.12 . This proof uses the global approximation already established in the chapter and avoids an identification of gradients in a singular weighted Sobolev completion. It gives decreasing convergence for the book's shifted class. At degree $m$ the unwedged current converges in distributions, while its positive wedge $Q_ m$ converges as a Radon measure. The coefficient estimate in 8.2.8 uses Newton's inequality on the list with two coordinates deleted. A related bound appears in [ equation (2-8), p. 111 , KNHermitianMeasures26 ] . The torsion estimate at degree $m-1$ corresponds to [ Lemma 2.4 and Corollary 2.5, pp. 113–114 , KNHermitianMeasures26 ] . Its proof sums the diagonal wedge coefficients before taking absolute values and compares them with the positive gradient coefficients. This extends the smooth capacity induction to degree $m$. Positive shifted currents are then dominated by the corrected local Hessian traces, and 8.11.14 gives the weighted decreasing convergence studied in [ Lemma 5.1(b), pp. 144–145 , KNHermitianMeasures26 ] . The unwedged $D_ m$ retains its distributional meaning. The strict locality and maximum inequality in 8.12.1 , 8.12.2 correspond to [ Corollary 5.2, p. 145 , KNHermitianMeasures26 ] , which concerns local unshifted Hessian products. The arguments here apply to the book's global shifted products. Continuous functions of decreasing potentials supply the strict-set cutoffs; a decreasing constant shift includes the contact set in the measure inequality. The torsion-weight identity in 8.12.4 extends the smooth integration-by-parts argument using the coefficient capacity $c_{m-1}$. In 8.12.5 , it allows the truncation argument of 8.7.6 to apply to bounded potentials on arbitrary Hermitian backgrounds. This is positivity of each individual mass; it does not supply a uniform positive lower bound over the admissible class. The bounded mass formula in 8.13.1 extends the integration-by-parts calculation of theorem 11.1.5 using the recursive currents. The necessity argument in 8.13.4 is the polarization mechanism of [ Theorems 1–2 , Chiose16 ] , used above in theorem 11.1.7 . At Hessian degree $m$, only the powers $n-m,\ldots ,n-1$ occur. Sufficiency follows from the mixed maximum inequality, while 8.13.3 keeps the exact total-mass difference on arbitrary backgrounds. The example in 8.13.5 extends the smooth varying-mass torus calculation of example 11.1.12 . The mixed torsion comparison and weak modified comparison in 8.13.7 , 8.13.8 use the mechanism of Gu and Nguyen [ Lemmas 3.8–3.10, pp. 1197–1200 , GuNguyenBoundary18 ] . Their local bounded-product construction uses a locally conformal Kähler reference metric. Here the global decreasing approximation and weighted torsion currents give the integration-by-parts identity for the chapter's shifted products. A finite mixed-degree induction controls the error by diagonal traces; rescaling the upper potential then absorbs the lower traces on a sufficiently small sublevel set. The pointwise order in 8.2.10 uses the canonical linear subharmonic representatives of the admissible class. The positive volume term from 8.12.3 and weak modified comparison prove 8.13.10 , 8.13.11 on arbitrary Hermitian backgrounds. The same strict comparison proves the logarithmic-data estimate in 8.13.12 for a fixed finite Radon right-hand measure. Together with smooth proper existence, it identifies the bounded solution in 8.13.13 without a separate continuity argument. The continuous-potential domination results in 8.7.7 , 8.7.8 use the earlier envelope argument. The conclusion of 8.8.2 is the continuous-solution case of Fang's [ v1, Theorem 4.1, pp. 17–19 , FangHessianSmooth26 ] . The theorem here assumes continuity of the given admissible weak solution; Fang's statement treats bounded solutions and also invokes a continuity result for them. The uniformly elliptic concave extension uses only a bounded complex Hessian. Its regularity input is the continuous-viscosity version of the Evans–Krylov–Caffarelli estimate in Tosatti, Wang, Weinkove and Yang [ arXiv v2, Theorem 3.4 and the paragraph following it, pp. 16–20 , TWWY15 ] . It applies directly to the auxiliary limit. The general bounded-solution continuity theory and results for degenerate backgrounds are separate from this argument.

title: 25.11 Volumes under mass bounds
text: For a nonclosed background, the mass of a single potential does not determine the masses in its singularity type. The lower and upper volumes $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$ and $\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)$ of definition 16.28.58 , the infimum and the supremum of the mass over the ordinary singularity type of $u$, record the information that a single mass loses. Under bounded mass, comparison of these volumes controls envelopes and defines a topology on models of positive lower volume.
