On curves, polar curvature describes the boundary where the lower volume vanishes.

title: 25.11.1 Singularity volumes and relative classes
text: The volumes used in section 13.17 are those of Boucksom, Guedj and Lu [ Definition 3.1 , BGL25 ] , expressed in terms of potentials. For closed backgrounds the two volumes coincide, because the non-pluripolar mass is invariant under bounded changes of the potential, as recalled in [ Example 3.2 , BGL25 ] . In the big case, the monotonicity theorem theorem 13.17.1 is [ Proposition 3.7 , BGL25 ] , and the argument for lower volumes in proposition 13.17.2 is Li's [ Proposition 2.5 , XL26 ] . The order test in 13.24.8 uses the projective valuative characterization of Darvas and Xia [ Theorem 2.13 and Proposition 2.30 , DX22 ] in a common closed Kähler background. Their Lelong convention differs from the divisor coefficient used here by a factor of two, which leaves equality of order profiles unchanged. The countable divisorial domination and envelope arguments are those of lemma 5.38.5 , corollary 18.4.9 ; they identify the whole ordinary type before its mass is computed. The upper bound for the closed top mass uses Witt Nyström's monotonicity theorem [ WN19 ] , while the lower bound follows directly from local bounded truncations. Expansion with smooth corrections, as in [ Section 2.1 , BGL25 ] , then gives the nonclosed mass throughout this type. This computation applies to the prescribed summable hyperplane profile with positive smooth residual; it does not assert mass invariance for arbitrary unbounded types in a pluriclosed background. The relative full-mass class of definition 13.18.4 is [ Definition 3.2 , XL26 ] . The stretching criterion lemma 13.18.1 is [ Lemma 3.1 , XL26 ] ; the proof given here keeps track of the deficit of upper volumes and chooses a representative whose mass is close to its upper volume. The case of zero deficit gives theorem 13.18.5 , and a uniform bound for Lelong numbers turns the convex comparisons into the estimate of proposition 13.18.3 . The domination principle theorem 13.19.1 is [ Proposition 3.2 , XL26 ] ; its proof uses that the reference has positive lower volume, but not that it is an envelope fixed point. The estimate for relative obstacles, lemma 13.19.4 , is [ Proposition 3.3 , XL26 ] . Together they give the identity for upper volumes in [ Lemma 3.2 , XL26 ] and the identity for lower volumes in [ Corollary 3.3 , XL26 ] , both stated in theorem 13.19.5 . For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, the proof first shows that the increasing limit of the obstacle envelopes has the ordinary singularity type of $P_\theta [u]$, so that domination can be applied before the equality of volumes is established. The resulting characterization of full mass gives the volume criterion in proposition 13.24.2 . When the pole set is compact of Hausdorff dimension zero and the lower volume is positive, theorem 13.19.6 shows that ordinary projection preserves the whole residual measure. Bounded mass gives uniform bounds for the traces of all local closed powers of the ordinary rooftop envelopes. Away from the pole set, convergence in capacity of bounded functions identifies the limits, and the Hausdorff estimate removes all mass of the lower-degree coefficients on the pole set; hence the lower-degree global pairings preserve the full total mass. Since the rooftop envelopes all have the same residual measure, positivity together with the local order of residuals forces the model to have this residual as well. The argument also identifies the weak limit of the full Monge–Ampère measures of these rooftop envelopes. The sources of the local inputs are given in section 25.3 . The construction of small stretches, lemma 13.20.1 , is [ Proposition 3.1 , XL26 ] , and its bound for mixed masses gives an explicit uniform scale of stretching. The additive estimate for lower volumes in proposition 13.20.6 is the case of smooth perturbations of [ Proposition 3.3(ii) , BGL25 ] , with the mixed bound of [ Lemma 2.4 , BGL25 ] written in terms of potentials. The strict barrier gives the multiplicative comparison at positive lower volume, as in [ Proposition 3.5(ii), Step 1 , XL26 ] . Consequently, corollary 13.21.4 gives continuity of the lower volume of every fixed potential as the background varies, while continuity of the upper volume and of the ordinary envelope still requires positive lower volume. The continuity along increasing sequences, theorem 13.21.1 , is [ Proposition 3.5(i) , XL26 ] : contact identifies the limit of the envelopes and its upper volume, and the deficit estimate then shows that the approximating lower volumes are positive. The continuity along decreasing sequences of models, theorem 13.21.2 , is [ Proposition 3.5(ii) , XL26 ] , including its conclusion when the lower volume of the limit vanishes. The uniform small stretch shows that a positive lower bound along the models forces their limit to have positive lower volume, and strict corrections and tail envelopes reduce the variation of the background to the argument for a fixed background. Li states the result for perturbations $\theta +\varepsilon _ j\omega $ with $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, whereas the proof here treats arbitrary smooth backgrounds that decrease uniformly in the order of forms. The criterion for positive lower volume, proposition 13.21.3 , is [ Proposition 3.5(iii) , XL26 ] . The deficit bound gives uniform convergence of Lelong numbers on each fixed compact model, and the envelopes of the restricted analytic approximants give the exact traces of corollary 13.21.5 . For semipositive backgrounds, proposition 13.20.4 is the forward direction of [ Proposition 2.11 , ALS26 ] , deduced here from the strict barrier. This direction requires neither the identity for ordinary envelopes nor positivity of the lower mass $v_-(\theta )$ of definition 13.14.14 ; that assumption is used for the converse. Applied to an envelope fixed point, the proposition compares Li's condition ( 13.20.5 ) with the condition ( 16.28.67 ) of Alehyane, Lu and Salouf.

title: 25.11.2 Model topology and analytic approximation
text: The comparison function $d_\theta $ of definition 13.22.1 , defined through the upper volumes of two potentials and of their maximum, is introduced in [ Section 4.2 , XL26 ] . That it separates models follows from the characterization by envelopes. The normalized stretching argument of [ Lemma 4.2 , XL26 ] gives the quantitative $L^1$ bound in proposition 13.22.4 , and the three-point estimate ( 13.22.6 ) passes convergence from a subsequence to the whole Cauchy sequence. The construction by maxima of tails in theorem 13.22.7 follows [ Theorem 4.3 , XL26 ] , with a fixed $\delta >0$ and the non-strict lower bound $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (u)\geq \delta $. The strict bound $>\delta $ used in version 1 of Li's preprint is not preserved under limits of Cauchy sequences, as example 13.22.8 shows. Li explicitly allows $d_\theta $ to violate the triangle inequality, and example 13.27.1 gives an example of such a failure with intersecting divisors. The criterion for finite rooftop envelopes, lemma 13.23.1 , is [ Lemma 4.1 , XL26 ] : after choosing representatives whose masses are close to their upper volumes, a collapse would contradict the lower volume of the common upper bound. Li's argument with softened stretches [ Proposition 4.4 , XL26 ] gives proposition 13.23.2 ; only the limiting potential needs positive lower volume, and the same comparison gives convergence of the lower volumes of the rooftop envelopes. The two stretching scales in [ Theorem 4.4 , XL26 ] produce the monotone bounds of theorem 13.23.3 . Since finite rooftop envelopes are again normalized models, continuity along decreasing models passes their volume bounds to the infinite tails; monotone convergence in capacity then applies, and the subsequence criterion gives convergence of the original sequence. The results on analytic approximation in section 13.24 combine this continuity of volumes with the limit of the dyadic multiplier-ideal envelopes. Mixing with a strict analytic potential, with rational coefficients, removes the curvature error in any smooth big background, and two comparisons of backgrounds then give the exact excess of upper volume in ( 13.24.4 ). Conversely, stretching and concavity of the multiplier-ideal envelope show that its fixed points are closed under the upper-volume comparison at positive lower volume. This proves the analytic criterion theorem 13.24.5 and the Cauchy completeness inherited there. The boundary where the lower volume vanishes in higher dimension, and positivity criteria in terms of ideals, are the separate questions of 13.24.11 . The comparisons of backgrounds in section 13.25 follow from the same arguments with volumes and envelopes. Transport by a smooth gauge preserves the competitor currents, and ordinary projection corrects the zero obstacle; the explicit scale of small stretches makes the strict barrier uniform on sets of models whose lower volumes are bounded below by a positive constant. This yields ( 13.25.4 ) and extends the analytic criterion to positive background errors that tend to zero. These statements concern singularity volumes and canonical models; they neither identify the mass of the unregularized envelope with a gauge invariant nor assert convergence of arbitrary representatives. The two-sided transport in section 13.26 mixes the original model with a strict analytic potential. A common upper background bounds both this transport and the maximum of two transported models, and the resulting volume bounds give uniform comparison, convergence of the transported reference, and equivalence of the limiting comparisons obtained with different strict corrections. The estimate for nearby backgrounds and the three-point modulus then reduce the analytic criterion of that section to theorem 13.25.5 . The complete metric in section 13.27 is obtained by the standard construction with finite dyadic chains, carried out directly from the three-point modulus. Stretching first gives continuity of the lower volume, and the reciprocal of the lower volume controls the boundary where it vanishes; the statement about the analytic completion then follows from the approximation criterion above. This metric induces the topology of the upper-volume comparison; it does not turn the comparison function itself into a metric. In dimension $n\geq 2$, polar curvature on all modifications still does not detect all ordinary models. The Cantor construction of example 13.28.14 gives the curve potentials of lemma 18.26.15 ; their maximum has vanishing first polar currents, but its truncations keep a positive top-degree mass $M$ near the common pole set. A rank bound for smooth maxima gives the construction in every dimension. By proposition 18.26.17 , corollary 18.26.18 , every compact Kähler manifold, with Kähler form $\omega $ and $A=\int _ X\omega ^ n$, carries a complete ordered interval of diffuse models $p_ t$ with volumes $A-Mt^ n$ and distances $M|s^ n-t^ n|$ between $p_ s$ and $p_ t$, and every choice of the first polar comparison collapses this interval. Hence the closure of the analytic models for the polar comparison contains models that are not ideal. The identities for invariant mass extend these formulas to the setting of corollary 18.26.20 . For an arbitrary Hermitian background with bounded mass and positive lower mass, the mass bounds for representatives give proposition 18.26.23 . This applies to every Hermitian metric on a compact complex surface, by the existence of Gauduchon metrics, the independence of the bounded mass property from the metric (proposition 13.14.15 ) and corollary 12.19.15 . Preservation of residuals and additivity of volumes then give corollary 18.26.24 for all parameters in the strict range. The upper volume along this interval is strictly decreasing and Lipschitz, although in general the length of the interval is not given by the power formula valid for closed backgrounds, and all first polar coordinates still vanish. In proposition 18.26.25 , two cutoffs with disjoint supports have equal total residual masses and vanishing first polar data, yet their maximum is zero and their distance is positive; in backgrounds with invariant mass, both singularity volumes coincide as well. These scalar data therefore cannot recover the spatial distribution of the residual mass. A direct calculation with maxima in lemma 18.26.16 identifies the full residual measure as the tensor product of the measures on the curve factors, multiplied by the product of the positive weights; for a smooth maximum the coefficient reduces to the volume of a simplex. In proposition 18.26.26 , a common cutoff and a uniform curvature bound give a compact family of models indexed by a box of positive weights. Invariance under projection identifies the comparison distance in this family, up to a fixed scale, with the Lebesgue measure of the symmetric difference of coordinate rectangles. The subfamilies on which the product of the weights is constant are complete and have real dimension $n-1$, although their members have the same full residual measure on $X$, the same two singularity volumes, the same multiplier ideals and the same first polar currents. The construction takes place in a background with invariant mass and concerns the residual measure on $X$ itself; it does not identify the full residual products on every modification. The problem of describing the complete topology remains open.

title: 25.11.3 Curves and zero-volume limits
text: The inverse maximum principle in the plane, lemma 5.27.14 , is the two-dimensional case of the result stated by Brezis and Ponce [ Theorem 3.1 , BP04 ] , who attribute it to Dupaigne and Ponce; the proof given here uses harmonic barriers on shrinking neighborhoods of a compact polar set. Applied to differences of potentials, it shows that the polar curvature measures are ordered as the potentials are, and subtracting a common Green potential gives the formula ( 5.27.16 ) for the maximum. Since these local facts are general, they are proved in section 5.21 . The classification of models on curves in section 13.28 combines this order of polar measures with the Green representation of subsection 20.3.9 . Every prescribed polar measure gives an ordinary model equivalent to its Green potential, and the characterization of envelopes of positive mass, together with uniqueness of harmonic functions at zero mass, identifies every ordinary envelope with such a model. The formula for the maximum then turns the upper-volume comparison into the total variation of measures, and completeness, geodesics and the nearest ideal model follow from the corresponding operations on measures. The exact defect of analytic approximation is the nonatomic polar mass, which for the Cantor example is the full curvature mass. For a finite map of curves, the fiber maximum in 5.43.15 follows from the local branched coordinates and the removable-singularity theorem for subharmonic functions. The weighted trace in 5.43.16 includes the local degrees at atoms; its agreement with current pullback follows from the Riesz representation on a disk and the Poincaré–Lelong formula. These elementary operations give the envelope identities of 18.24.1 . Applying the curve classification gives the degree-scaled metric embedding and the averaging retraction of 18.24.2 . The component factorization then gives the complete subspace of models descending to the original base in 18.24.3 . The cubic example 18.24.4 distinguishes this averaging from the nearest ideal retraction. The continuity statement for curves, theorem 13.28.8 , uses the theorem on convergence in capacity at positive volume in the interior. At zero mass the polar curvature is the whole current, which gives convergence of the currents in total variation. The local estimate lemma 5.27.11 , which follows from the Green representation on a disk, the mean-value estimate for harmonic functions and the weighted Chern–Levine–Nirenberg inequality, gives convergence in capacity at this boundary. Moving a pole distinguishes this topology from that of total variation, while the approximation by finitely many atoms in theorem 18.6.4 distinguishes weak convergence of the curvature currents from convergence in capacity. The correspondences between backgrounds in section 13.29 follow from the same classification by polar measures, which smooth gauges extend to every smooth background of positive area on a curve. Changes of background with equal area preserve total variation, whereas rescaling the area gives homotheties compatible with extraction of atoms and hence with ideal projection. These correspondences are realized by a smooth gauge, obtained from the scalar Poisson equation, followed by ordinary projection. Comparing the new obstacle with its maximum and minimum gives a uniform bound, which yields continuity in $L^1$ and in capacity up to the boundary of zero mass. Rationality is needed only for the assertion that analytic singularities are preserved under rescaling of the area, because analytic singularities in this book have rational coefficients. At zero area, positivity and Stokes' theorem leave a single normalized potential. The general convergence statement theorem 5.29.23 , proved in section 5.21 , follows from compactness of normalized potentials, uniqueness of harmonic functions and the local estimate relating total variation and capacity. It also gives the collapse of the model representatives as the unscaled metric diameters tend to zero.

title: 25.12 Equations with prescribed singularities
text: Relative envelopes allow the solution of an equation to keep prescribed singularities while the measure on the right-hand side changes. Equations with $L^ p$ data in a prescribed ordinary type, equations with general measures, and equations under mass bounds on the metric use this framework in different ways. They differ both in the estimates available and in the singularity type of the solution obtained.

title: 25.12.1 Equations of prescribed ordinary type
text: The equations of prescribed ordinary type in theorem 15.12.1 are [ Theorems 5.4 and 5.7 , ALS26 ] . Replacing their reference volume $\omega ^ n$ by $\mathrm{d}V$ multiplies the density by a smooth positive function and preserves its $L^ p$ class, and a change of the normalization of the complex Hessian by a positive constant is absorbed by rescaling both the potential and the exponent. The two constructions of [ Lemmas 5.5–5.6 , ALS26 ] are the relative estimate theorem 15.12.3 and the rooftop supersolution lemma 15.12.4 ; together they keep the solution in the ordinary type of the reference. For a big background, the argument with bounded subsolutions of Guedj and Lu [ Lemma 3.3 and Theorem 3.4 , GL23E ] gives lemma 15.3.1 , theorem 15.3.3 . The trace calculation with a barrier in section 15.19 follows Guyett and Mc Gowan [ v1, Proposition 3.2, pp. 7–12 , GM26 ] . Their geometric setting is a small crepant resolution, in Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$, of a normal projective Calabi–Yau variety, and their abstract Theorem 3.1 treats a closed semipositive big background with an upper bound for the mass. In the book, the arguments with bounded subsolutions and exponential comparison of lemma 15.3.1 , theorem 15.3.3 give uniform bounds for the potentials and the scalars when the density is a fixed smooth positive function. The trace argument keeps the torsion of the perturbation and also allows a fixed nonzero Chern–Ricci form. Its conclusion is convergence of the potentials along subsequences, in a semipositive background with an explicit strict analytic barrier. The assertions of that paper about metric completions and conifold contractions are not part of this argument. The bundle and the contraction in 15.19.8 form the standard model of a node used in [ v1, Equation (2.1), p. 4, and Section 4, pp. 15–16 , GM26 ] . The logarithmic curvature identity ( 15.19.11 ) gives a strict barrier for this model directly, and a cutoff in a positive collar makes it global. This proves the convergence of the potentials and the assertion about the area of the exceptional curves for these local resolutions, without using a classification of small resolutions or a theorem on metric completions. Since the canonical bundle is torsion, its local holomorphic trivializations give the Chern–Ricci-flat density. The equation on the singular space, ( 15.19.16 ), is obtained through the general correspondence of theorem 9.11.5 between potentials on a resolution and potentials on the singular space defined by disk inequalities. For closed backgrounds, the identification in [ v1, Lemma 3.1 and the proof of Corollary 1.1, pp. 13–14 , GM26 ] uses the equation on normal spaces and the estimate for adapted measures of Eyssidieux, Guedj and Zeriahi [ arXiv v2, Theorem 6.3 and Lemma 6.4, pp. 28–29 , EGZ09 ] . In the standard model of a node, ( 15.19.15 ) gives in lemma 15.19.14 the exact range $p<3$ of integrability and the weak $L^3$ endpoint, for every smooth positive density on the resolution. The bounded energy identity already used in theorem 9.11.43 proves theorem 15.19.17 , using smooth strict positivity only away from the exceptional curves. The arguments for the metric completion and the distance in lemma 15.19.21 , proposition 15.19.22 are those of [ v1, Lemma 5.2, pp. 23–24, and Proposition 5.1, pp. 24–26 , GM26 ] . Compact collars in the regular part separate the points added in the completion, and the first and last visits of a path to the finitely many contracting regions give a distance error controlled by these regions; uniform convergence of the metrics on each compact subset of the regular part suffices. The hypotheses on the diameters of punctured neighborhoods in the limit and on the intrinsic diameters for the approximating metrics are stated explicitly; the conifold estimates and the asymptotics of cones needed to verify them are separate geometric inputs. For curves, [ v1, Lemma 4.1, p. 17 , GM26 ] bounds the diameter of $\mathbb P^1$ by a multiple of $A^{1/3}$, where $A$ is the area, under a uniform upper bound for the metric. Averaging over straight coordinate segments and splitting the kernel given by the reciprocal of the distance give the sharper logarithmic estimate of lemma 15.19.24 on every fixed compact Riemann surface. The radial example in example 15.19.25 has the same order, and rescaling it shows that the area alone does not control the diameter. The two radial paths and the connection through the zero section in proposition 15.19.26 give the mechanism of [ v1, Proposition 4.2, pp. 20–21 , GM26 ] , with the uniform bound on the restriction to the curve and the radial bounds stated as explicit hypotheses. Strict singular barriers extend the comparison argument to potentials with minimal singularities. The development starting in section 15.13 follows [ Section 4 , BGL25 ] , where the bounded mass assumption of the earlier sections of that paper is dropped. The equations with minimal singularities, culminating in theorem 15.16.7 , are [ Theorems 4.6–4.7 , BGL25 ] . The solution has finite mass, although the masses in its ordinary singularity type are not assumed to be uniformly bounded.

title: 25.12.2 General measures in semipositive backgrounds
text: The local decomposition of measures used in lemma 5.27.10 is Cegrell's [ Theorem 6.3 , Ceg98 ] , on a bounded hyperconvex domain in dimension at least two; for a non-pluripolar measure its pluripolar part vanishes. The global constructions in lemma 15.24.4 , proposition 15.24.1 patch these local representations together. The bounded-subsolution theorem theorem 15.10.1 , taken from [ Theorem 5.1 , ALS26 ] , solves the exponential equation whose right-hand side has a bounded density with respect to the Monge–Ampère measure of a bounded potential. Truncating the density in such a representation of a general measure brings this theorem into the construction for general measures, and domination then allows passage to the limit. The domination theorem for finite measures, theorem 15.37.6 in section 15.37 , is [ Theorem 3.14 , ALS26 ] : the fixed finite measure prevents collapse, whereas the other members of the envelope class need not have finite mass. The proof of theorem 15.37.10 also allows the measure being compared to be infinite. The singular strict domination principle, theorem 15.2.2 , follows [ Theorem 3.11 , ALS26 ] . The homogeneous range result theorem 15.25.1 is the sufficient direction of Kołodziej and Nguyen's [ Theorem 1.3, p. 2952; proof pp. 2958–2963 , KNHolder18 ] . Their weighted regularization estimate is [ Lemma 2.8, p. 2957 , KNHolder18 ] . The proof here first approximates a Borel density by continuous functions and then chooses smooth references diagonally. Common Hölder bounds give uniform capacity estimates and a weighted modulus for the varying solution measures; bounds above and below for the normalization constants prevent degeneration before the uniform limit is taken. The radial bounded product in lemma 5.27.26 is a direct Bedford–Taylor calculation: the logarithmic derivative of a smooth radial maximum fixes the spherical mass. Summing these local references with geometric weights and controlling a common cutoff gives proposition 15.26.2 . The homogeneous range theorem yields corollary 15.26.3 , with a normalized Hölder solution and an unknown positive coefficient. The bounded-reference theorem yields theorem 15.26.4 for bounded densities against the fixed spherical probability, including singular data on backgrounds with zero lower mass. This is an individual geometric sufficient condition, distinct from solvability for every non-pluripolar measure and from the exact density-threshold question. Passing to the limit in the measures requires that the lower envelopes do not collapse. The continuity theorem for measures dominated by a fixed measure, theorem 15.37.19 , is [ Lemma 4.2 and Theorem 4.1, condition (2) , ALS26 ] ; in this case positive lower mass prevents collapse, and no upper bound on the mass is used. The argument with a common envelope preceding corollary 15.37.24 gives instead the first alternative of [ Lemma 4.2 , ALS26 ] . When the approximants have the ordinary singularity type of the reference, this alternative needs no assumption of positive lower volume. A common barrier in the ordinary singularity type also gives corollary 15.9.4 , the corresponding case of [ Theorem 4.1 , ALS26 ] . The reference need not be an envelope fixed point; the condition in a smaller background suffices. Integrals of bounded potentials against varying mixed measures are handled by the torsion calculation in lemma 5.44.7 , which follows Kołodziej and Nguyen [ Lemma 2.3 , KN22 ] . The resulting equations with general finite non-pluripolar measures, theorem 15.37.4 , are [ Theorem 5.8 and Corollary 5.9 , ALS26 ] . The constructions with a minimal and with a prescribed reference in subsection 15.37.27 , subsection 15.37.30 use the approximations of the density from that proof, and they assume both the condition ( 16.28.67 ) in a smaller background and positive lower mass. The solutions have finite mass, but for arbitrary measures they need not differ boundedly from the reference. For a Hermitian background and the minimal reference, corollary 15.37.32 identifies the scalar in the equation with the density threshold of theorem 15.28.4 , that is, the largest coefficient for which the scaled density admits a subsolution. The question that remains, 24.2.2 in section 24.1 , concerns zero lower mass. The weighted addition theorem theorem 15.11.1 is [ Theorem 5.2 , ALS26 ] ; the proof given here localizes the passage to the equation.

title: 25.12.3 Big backgrounds under mass bounds
text: Li's theory of equations with general measures [ Theorems 6.1–6.2 and Corollary 6.1 , XL26 ] assumes that the manifold has bounded mass and that the Hermitian metric has positive lower mass. It gives theorem 10.31.3 and the constructions with a model reference in subsection 10.31.43 . Under bounded mass, positivity of the lower volume of the model reference implies that the metric has positive lower mass, so expressing the hypothesis through the reference reorganizes this setting without enlarging it. The relative foundations of this theory use the domination, stretching and obstacle estimates discussed in section 25.11 . In ( 10.31.27 ), the required rooftop envelope is constructed before lemma 13.19.4 is applied to the relative projection. Moment and continuity estimates connect these operations on envelopes with existence. The compactness argument with first moments, using ( 10.31.10 ), follows [ Proposition 4.2 , XL26 ] : one chooses a reference potential in the same singularity type whose mass is sufficiently close to the upper volume, which need not be attained. Continuity for a fixed dominating measure is [ Theorem 4.2 , XL26 ] ; there the finite rooftop envelopes use only the envelope class, while the two-sided bounds for the mass prevent collapse and control the tails. The closure theorem for varying references, theorem 10.31.30 , is [ Corollary 4.1 , XL26 ] . Projection to ordered lower models gives a fixed relative class for each tail of the sequence, and an exponential contact estimate prevents collapse. The stability for positive exponents in [ Corollary 6.2 , XL26 ] assumes uniformly bounded $L^ p$ data and the ordinary type of the reference. Theorem 10.31.47 treats instead the relative full-mass class: the models converge for the volume comparison with a common positive lower bound for their lower volumes, and the densities converge in $L^1$ with respect to a fixed finite non-pluripolar measure. Extracting a summable subsequence produces the dominating measure needed for the closure theorem. For a positive exponent, uniqueness gives convergence in capacity of the whole sequence of potentials. For exponent zero, the scalars and the measures converge, every $L^1$ cluster point of the normalized potentials solves the limiting equation, and the corresponding subsequence converges in capacity. In both cases, identifying the right-hand sides in $L^1$ gives convergence of the measures in total variation. For the minimal reference, the equations with general measures in subsection 10.31.21 are [ Theorems 5.2–5.3 , XL26 ] . The estimate for higher moments in subsection 10.31.13 follows the concave-weight argument of [ Proposition 5.1 and Lemma 5.1 , XL26 ] , with the integrability against the fixed singular measure stated explicitly. The smoothing of measures used in the existence proof is collected in lemma 5.44.12 , lemma 5.44.10 . The conclusion of corollary 10.31.56 , that for $L^ p$ data the solutions have the ordinary type of the reference, is [ Corollary 6.1 , XL26 ] . The relative estimate proposition 10.31.54 starts from a solution in the envelope class and uses a uniform moment of order $m>2n+1$. The concave-weight method is related to [ Theorem 5.1 , XL26 ] , which already assumes the ordinary type of the reference and uses the moment exponent $m>n$; that theorem is not used to deduce the ordinary type of an arbitrary solution in the envelope class. Addition of measures requires a common lower bound during truncation. The weighted construction in subsection 10.31.37 is [ Proposition 6.1 , XL26 ] . For unrestricted addition, ( 10.31.50 ) follows [ Theorem 6.3 , XL26 ] ; an additional rooftop envelope gives the common lower bound needed to pass through the cutoff.

title: 25.13 Normalization and adjoint measures
text: The normalization constant can be studied through its adjoint probability measures even when the potential itself is not unique. The differential method for smooth solutions appears in Collins's work [ Collins21 ] ; theorem 11.33.4 replaces differentiation of smooth solutions by mixed products and domination. The continuous-Hessian extension in theorem 11.34.11 uses local bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity and the finite background expansion to linearize the equation along signed potential variations. The supporting-density estimate of corollary 12.9.3 then allows Sobolev duality with lemma 11.24.1 ; the directional derivative is the convex-analytic identity already proved in proposition 11.34.5 . The product formula in proposition 11.34.13 uses curve Green inversion and the smooth Gauduchon multiplier on the other factor. Its two-curve specialization is also covered by theorem 11.45.16 with zero divisor. The non-Dini example uses the same Hopf torsion calculation as ( 23.1.3 ), in complex dimension two. For the mass quotient and the closed examples in section 11.42 , existence and uniqueness of solutions in a prescribed singularity type are due to Darvas, Di Nezza and Lu [ Theorems 1.4(i) and 4.29, pp. 2052 and 2079–2080 , DDNL18mono ] , and the invariance of the mass under bounded changes of the potential is their [ Proposition 2.1, p. 2055 , DDNL18mono ] . Their hypotheses are a compact Kähler manifold, a smooth closed big class, a model reference with small unbounded locus, and positive mass. The factorization with positive residual concerns the ordinary divisorial singularity types themselves; it does not assert an identity of model envelopes for every weighted sum with real coefficients. The dictionary between toric potentials and convex functions used in section 11.43 is that of Berman and Berndtsson [ arXiv v1, Sections 2.1–2.3, especially Proposition 2.3 and Lemma 2.5, pp. 10–13 , BBToric13 ] . The angular coefficient in ( 11.43.4 ) is computed directly, in the book's conventions for the squared logarithm and the operator. The argument with finite envelopes establishes the identity for ordinary models, and a common translated simplex gives both the witness in a smaller background and the volume estimate in terms of the Hausdorff distance. The two families in subsection 11.43.9 , subsection 11.43.14 satisfy these conditions explicitly; since their references have small unbounded locus, the theorem for prescribed singularity types in closed classes cited above applies. The blowup chart and the normal line of the exceptional divisor used to compute the rank and the mass of the residual are taken from [ Chapter VII, equation (12.2) and Proposition 12.4, pp. 356–357 , DemCADG ] . These computations concern fixed modifications and closed backgrounds. The description of the residual in proposition 11.34.18 uses the products of bounded plurisubharmonic functions of Bedford and Taylor [ Section 2 , BT82 ] and the extension of plurisubharmonic functions across pluripolar sets in [ Chapter I, Theorem 5.24 , DemCADG ] . Integration by parts for bounded potentials against a closed positive current is established in [ Theorem 1.14 and Lemma 1.15, pp. 214–217 , BEGZ10 ] ; alternatively, the cutoff in ( 11.34.20 ) can be smoothed explicitly, which makes its estimate a direct Stokes calculation for distributions. In theorem 11.34.21 , the two radial profiles give the coefficients of the divisors before the limit ( 11.34.23 ) of the squares is taken. This distinguishes the relative residual adjoint from the classical adjoints of smooth potentials whose exponential densities concentrate. For the normalization on split products in lemma 15.30.2 , the smooth input is again [ Corollary 1 , TW10 ] , applied to the closed projective factor. The order of the scalars for bounded densities extends the formula to continuous densities on the factor, and the original truncations determine the threshold for every smooth reference volume. The radial flux in lemma 15.30.1 and a separate calculation of non-pluripolar products then give theorem 15.30.3 . The elliptic factor is the threefold of section 12.19 , whose balanced metric has volume $24\pi $ by proposition 12.19.18 ; this gives the fivefold equation with constant $240\pi $. The bounded equation of [ Theorem 0.1 , KN15 ] and closed Stokes extend this result to every integrable density from a closed Kähler factor in theorem 15.30.6 : comparison of the original truncations computes the scalar, and threshold attainment on the factor, together with its non-pluripolar mass bound, makes the lower measure an equality. The root norm formula of proposition 15.32.11 then uses the full Gauduchon test class and identifies a closed subspace of $\mathcal D_ h^0$. The radial family supplies roots outside every higher $L^ r$ class, with explicit logarithmic tails. For arbitrary densities on the product that are merely integrable and have positive threshold, the existence of an exact solution remains the problem of 24.2.2 . The same radial flux gives the criterion for exponential growth in theorem 15.35.9 . Disjoint annuli in projective space and a rapidly convergent smooth baseline adapt the concentration in theorem 15.35.10 to every prescribed sequence of base densities whose scalars collapse. The bounded equations on the products determine the scalars of the components, and for every positive exponent the exponentially weighted pole absorbs their sum. The construction of greatest solutions then gives exact solutions at zero threshold, which are necessarily unbounded, in particular on the elliptic products of dimensions four and five. The explicit barriers there have masses $96\pi $ and $240\pi $, whereas the exact solutions have their own finite positive masses. A general criterion for solvability at zero threshold remains open. That the set of solvable exponents is an upper interval, proposition 15.35.12 , follows by translating a subsolution downward before increasing its exponent. For the collapse of mass at zero threshold in proposition 15.35.13 , normalized exponential damping gives an $L^1$ approximation of the fixed density, and upper semicontinuity of the threshold forces the normalization scalars to tend to zero. This controls the masses of the exact solutions without identifying the limits of the normalized potentials. The criterion for attaining a positive endpoint, proposition 15.35.16 , combines the compactness of normalized potentials with the closure of subsolutions under lower bounds for the density and the existence of greatest solutions. Its common upper barrier comes from the equation of theorem 14.19.3 with the truncated, bounded density, together with singular strict domination. The corrected order in lemma 15.35.15 gives a decreasing family as the exponent decreases to a positive solvable exponent. Monotone convergence in capacity and the closedness theorem for positive exponents identify the limit from the right in proposition 15.35.17 , and maximality of the greatest solutions identifies the limiting potential. Approach from below uses the regularized increasing envelope, giving the exact left limit of proposition 15.35.18 . Integrating the corrected family gives a bounded increasing real function on each compact exponent interval. Its jumps detect the difference between the left limit and the greatest solution, which proves proposition 15.35.19 . For the non-$L^ p$ radial family, lemma 15.36.2 identifies the greatest solutions on the full product through the bounded factor equations and singular strict domination. The proof of theorem 15.36.5 uses their cumulative fluxes to determine the whole normalized limit, including when the density parameter varies. Local uniform convergence outside the fixed pole set and the Hermitian capacity estimate give capacity convergence on both factors and the product. No general full-mass stability theorem is needed for this radial argument. The finite or divergent first moment determines scalar centering in proposition 15.36.8 . The order characterization of separated critical subsolutions in corollary 15.36.11 additionally uses Dinew's closed-class full-mass uniqueness theorem [ arXiv v1, Theorem 1.2, pp. 2 and 5–8 , DinewUniqueness08 ] ; this input is applied only on the projective factor. It neither proves uniqueness of arbitrary nonclosed critical potentials nor supplies a theorem for varying singular references. For the logarithmic product references, proposition 11.45.3 computes the ordinary envelope on the curve and identifies the product envelope by restriction to slices. Divisorial removal transfers the exponential equation and its greatestness to a bounded equation in the positive residual background, as in lemma 11.45.4 . The Green operator on the curve gives uniformly bounded residuals by contraction for small exponents. Its uniformly integrable logarithmic kernel then determines the joint limit and the scalar error in theorem 11.45.9 . The centering uses the critical scalar of each varying datum. The separated order characterization in corollary 11.45.13 follows from closed curve mass and the distributional equation; maximality of the coefficient in the full prescribed class follows instead from greatestness of the positive-exponent solutions. This argument uses the earlier bounded existence and domination theorems and does not impose a mass property on the Hermitian factor. For the product surface in 11.45.14 , the logarithmic model and Green residual are those of proposition 11.45.3 , theorem 11.45.9 . The continuous positive residual allows smooth perturbations of the singular solution, and the supporting inequality on all continuous data makes every supporting probability invariant for the weak linearization. Spherical harmonics reduce uniqueness to the signed-measure resolvent lemma lemma 11.45.15 , whose proof uses the round sphere heat operator. This gives theorem 11.45.16 without an invariant-density regularity assumption. The approximation statement proposition 11.45.18 uses the already proved conformal Gauduchon theorem theorem 11.4.2 for each smooth residual; uniform tensor convergence transfers the operator and then the weighted products. The explicit pole-filling family in example 11.45.19 shows why retaining the divisor is part of this approximation statement. The one-sided divisorial correspondence of lemma 11.41.5 extends the ordinary correspondence of theorem 11.41.1 by the nonclosed divisorial-removal lemma and locality of the extended measures. A uniform submean bound identifies the ordinary envelope type and its explicit smaller-background competitor. The whole one-sided threshold in theorem 11.41.6 then follows from theorem 15.28.4 ; its smooth attainment uses theorem 14.2.1 , rather than a new prescribed-singularity existence theorem. Strictness follows from the elliptic cofactor identity off the divisor and the strong maximum principle. The obstruction in corollary 11.41.7 is consistent with the stronger later smooth-dual rigidity, while example 11.41.8 fixes the Fubini–Study factor to compute the precise restricted coefficient. The inverse realization problem for general densities and annihilating faces remains separate. The curve-measure equations of section 15.31 begin with the normalized logarithmic kernel on the projective line. Its distributional curvature and the degree-one extended measure give proposition 15.31.13 by bounded product expansion and truncation. Under continuity of the potential, local Riesz decomposition gives non-polarity, while rotation smoothing and Dirichlet energy give the canonical Sobolev trace of lemma 15.31.4 . The convex functional in theorem 15.31.8 yields every positive exponent; the bounded Green density and uniform logarithmic tails give continuity, and fixed barriers give uniform selection. The full-product greatestness and coefficient in theorem 15.31.15 use the earlier bounded strict domination and ordered-contact theorems. The latter retains the equality-set term when an unbounded competitor is floored by a bounded solution. The Frostman test includes nonconstant weighted circles. The zero-lower-mass conclusion assumes the factor's vanishing lower mass; the general individual-measure classification is not a consequence of this product construction. The radial residual criterion in section 11.46 uses central mass rather than an ordinary-model envelope identity. The local decreasing-limit property gives the genuine pole, while the radial determinant flux identifies its non-pluripolar probability and inverse. The central density error controls the flux and its first derivative without differentiation of that error, giving theorem 11.46.8 . Flat errors, mass-preserving sharp examples and an open zero annulus follow from the same inverse in proposition 11.46.15 , proposition 11.46.17 , proposition 11.46.20 . The conditional nonclosed product of corollary 11.46.22 uses bounded multilinearity and pullback by a projection, as proved in proposition 5.28.2 , lemma 5.28.4 , followed by the actual non-pluripolar truncation limit. It assumes zero lower mass of the factor and makes no assertion about arbitrary nonsymmetric equations. The singular-obstacle envelopes of section 11.47 use the same sublogarithmic reference as the preceding radial density criterion. Unitary invariance reduces the full envelope to a convex minorant, and supporting tangents control both ends. On the right tail, the weighted slope and second-derivative estimates in ( 11.47.12 ) give uniform projective Hessian bounds even when contact moves to infinity; interpolation with value contraction gives theorem 11.47.11 . The full product formula in proposition 11.47.14 follows from exact slicing of every competitor and the bounded-product expansion before strict-superlevel truncation. It requires no mass property of the Hermitian factor. These results concern this everywhere singular obstacle and the residual in its prescribed ordinary type, while regularity for arbitrary types and compact obstacle sets remains open.

title: 25.14 Perron geometry on Hopf manifolds
text: The closed-base metric inputs in subsection 17.16.15 are Darvas' Kähler completion and CAT$(0)$ theorems [ v3, Theorems 6.1 and 9.2, pp. 20–26 and 30–32 , DarvasCompletion17 ] . Capacity endpoint attainment and preservation of the squared-energy class are [ v3, Theorem 5.2 and Corollary 5.4, pp. 18–20 , DarvasCompletion17 ] . The full-mass model characterization used in proposition 17.16.32 is [ v3, Theorem 4.3, pp. 16–17 , DarvasCompletion17 ] . These theorems are applied on the connected compact Kähler base $\mathbb P^{n-1}$. The source uses $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial $, so potentials are divided by $2\pi $ in ( 17.16.21 ); fiber integration contributes the additional factor $\sqrt{2n}$ to distance. The smooth-endpoint distance formula used in proposition 17.16.22 , proposition 17.16.29 is [ v3, equation (15), p. 8, and Theorem 7.2, p. 28 , DarvasCompletion17 ] . The bounded Dirichlet description is [ v3, Section 2.2, equations (16)–(17), p. 9 , DarvasCompletion17 ] . Section 7, p. 27, gives a bounded-potential counterexample to using the initial-velocity formula outside its regularity hypotheses. The completed action in the book is therefore defined by metric speed. The Hopf conclusions use the elliptic fiber action and the bounded products with smooth corrections already established in the book, followed by canonical finite-level truncation. No bounded-mass property of the Hopf manifold is imposed. Group averaging proves stationarity under all smooth variations, and radial Fourier modes give the negative raw-action directions in theorem 17.16.25 . The explicit diagonal geodesics and singular radial family supply exact distance and energy calculations. Their metric is on basic potentials; its ordinary-model projection is zero throughout the finite-energy domain, so it does not solve the general ordinary-model metric problem.

title: 25.15 Singularity classes and traces
text: The countable-pole construction of theorem 18.13.1 uses the local decreasing-limit and canonical-representative theorems in Demailly's book [ Chapter I, Theorems 5.4 and 5.8, pp. 39–40 , DemCADG ] . Its exponential integrability follows directly from weighted Jensen's inequality and the sublinear logarithmic profiles. The envelope argument of proposition 18.13.4 uses Choquet's lemma and the local upper-envelope theorem [ Chapter I, Lemma 4.23 and Theorem 5.7, pp. 38–40 , DemCADG ] , through the exact nonclosed-background construction of section 5.40 . The bounded unrestricted envelope has the same trivial multiplier ideals as the constructed potential, so it is a competitor for the ideal-equivalence envelope used here. The fixed stronger potential supplies ordinary competitors below every continuous obstacle; the general zero-obstacle implication remains open. A theory of singularities for nonclosed backgrounds must record torsion as well as divisorial information. The quotient of the space of smooth real $(1,1)$-forms by the forms $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$, $f$ smooth, used in section 10.30 , appears in [ Section 1 , BGL25 ] ; fixing the exterior derivative of the form keeps this datum on each modification. Resolution makes additivity of traces accessible to approximation by multiplier ideals. The comparison in theorem 20.3.4 is the argument underlying Cao's additivity theorem [ proof of Theorem 1.4 , Cao15 ] , and it does not require a closed global background. The recovery theorem theorem 13.21.7 combines the arguments with decreasing models and stretching with the local criterion for multiplier ideals. Uniform exponential integrability bounds each local divisorial order of the auxiliary potentials, so the proof does not require a local modification to extend over the compact manifold. The construction on a ruled surface in subsection 16.29.15 , based on Demailly, Peternell and Schneider's [ Example 1.7 , DPS94 ] , exhibits the boundary behavior relevant to this recovery. The transverse recovery of theorem 16.29.22 uses the same positive-volume theorem on $\mathbb P^2$, while the Hopf threefold itself has unbounded upper mass by theorem 23.1.1 . The full ideal envelope is invariant under the elliptic action because its complete competitor family is invariant; a horizontal current test then identifies it with the base envelope. The nonanalytic family uses the summable divisorial criterion of 13.24.8 , whose closed mass and valuative inputs are described above. The general exact-pullback identities in proposition 16.28.59 , proposition 18.4.3 follow from the descent, ideal transform and non-pluripolar product foundations; they do not assert recovery over arbitrary new Hermitian perturbations on a modified manifold. The continuity of model envelopes in closed classes used in theorem 20.3.33 is due to Darvas and Xia [ Proposition 2.1 , DX24 ] ; it is also presented in [ Proposition 3.1.12 , SGPT ] . The argument for Lelong numbers uses small convex corrections from Darvas, Di Nezza and Lu [ Lemma 4.3 , DDNL21 ] . It suffices to apply this continuity on the submanifold, because the restricted approximants have a common curvature bound even when the ambient background is not closed. The projective-base construction of subsection 20.3.41 uses the same positive-mass convergence of decreasing closed models; the October 4, 2026 version of the lecture manuscript gives the statement and proof in [ Proposition 3.1.12, pp. 96–97, with Lemma 2.4.4, pp. 67–71 , SGPT26Oct ] . The ideal-class argument uses its compact Kähler criterion [ Proposition 3.2.1, pp. 122–123 , SGPT26Oct ] ; the cofinality discussion on p. 497 covers prime divisors on arbitrary compact smooth models by finite smooth blowup models. These are closed-base inputs. The finite extraction proof in lemma 20.3.44 uses proper mapping for analytic sets and analytic resolution which preserves the whole nonsingular locus, in the form of Włodarczyk's [ Theorem 2.0.1(1), p. 34 , Wlo09 ] . Its ramification argument uses the local Siu decomposition and Skoda integrability recalled in the foundations. Elliptic symmetry gives the full Hopf envelope and its mass and approximation formulas; the ideal-class argument remains on the projective base. The residual condition in ( 18.27.1 ) implies vanishing of point Lelong numbers by scaling the uniform Lelong bound, and vanishing of polar curvature by the Gauduchon trace and bounded-type invariance. The argument persists on every smooth compact modification. The ideal neutrality of lemma 5.37.5 combines Bergman approximation and the local ideal-addition calculus; the needed Bergman estimate and strong openness are stated in [ v2, Theorem 1.2 and Corollary 2.3 , DemCohomology15 ] . The smoothing step in lemma 18.27.3 is Demailly's [ Main Theorem 1.1 and Section 2 , Dem92 ] , applied to the closed current $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q'$ with smooth representative zero and lower bound $\epsilon h-B$. In the source normalization the potential is $q'/2$. The curvature of a fixed tangent metric is bounded by a large multiple of $h$, and its continuous Lelong approximants converge uniformly to zero. Richberg smoothing is applied to the continuous attenuation intermediates. This operation supplies a smooth positive residual background; the prescribed ordinary type is recovered with an actual small-curvature representative in theorem 18.27.4 . The normal crossing ideal formula in proposition 20.3.8 uses ambient ideals and therefore remains meaningful when the naive residual restriction has poles everywhere on the target. The full ordinary-type optimization in theorem 20.3.66 uses the closed comparison theorem of Boucksom, Eyssidieux, Guedj and Zeriahi [ Theorem 1.16, pp. 217–218 , BEGZ10 ] in both orders, in degrees one and two. Their Definition 1.2, p. 204, applies because every residual potential is locally bounded outside the divisor. Finiteness and closedness of the auxiliary non-pluripolar products are their [ Proposition 1.6 and Theorem 1.8, pp. 206–209 , BEGZ10 ] . Only the dominating Kähler background enters this cohomological comparison; the nonclosed mass is recovered by smooth-background expansion and distributional Stokes. The two ordinary volumes and their divisor and pure-pullback laws are those of [ Definition 3.1 and Proposition 3.3 , BGL25 ] in their bounded-mass setting; here the latter identities are proved through the complete competitor correspondence, and the small-curvature sublogarithmic representatives give the extreme sequences. The ambient ideal orders of proposition 20.3.71 follow from a transverse radial integral. For proposition 20.3.74 , the small-curvature criterion first produces a smooth residual representative; restriction to the last exceptional curve then excludes ordinary-type strictness even over pole centers. The exceptional curvature perturbation constructs a one-sided strict witness inductively. This extends the bounded-center restriction mechanism in example 10.17.9 to the specified finite blowup family. The separate residual volume and cost in 12.35.8 use the all-test dual formula and first variation of this book. The logarithmic degeneration in example 12.35.13 specializes those formulas to the height distribution on the sphere; pairing against a closed base test excludes every strict current at the endpoint.

title: 25.16 Section growth and partial kernels
text: The growth of sections links singular potentials to the algebraic dimension through a projective modification. The form of Moishezon's theorem used in section 19.9 is stated in [ Introduction, p. 1332 , Moi67 ] ; it is used as a classical geometric input. A Kähler modification also gives the bounded mass conclusion of lemma 19.9.12 , by Guedj and Lu's argument pulling back upper volumes [ Lemma 3.6 , GL22 ] . For section rings constructed through the algebraic reduction, see Xiaojun Wu's [ Wu24 ] . The flag construction in section 19.9 uses a fixed compact flag on an auxiliary modification; it makes no assertion about the centers of arbitrary valuations of the field of meromorphic functions. The maximum at maximal mapping rank in proposition 19.9.19 is Qin's [ v1, Proposition B.1, pp. 35–36 , QinCurvatureRank26 ] . The scalar and flag bounds in corollary 19.9.20 use the section-ratio field and period count already established in this book, with the curvature rank measured on its semipositive locus. The fixed-twist and endpoint deductions, Euler polynomial, surface estimate and sharp product follow [ v1, Sections 10.2–10.3 and Example 11.1, pp. 32–34 , QinCurvatureRank26 ] ; they are independent of that paper's all-degree finite-jet estimate, Theorem A. Principalization and its isomorphism off the base ideal are Włodarczyk's [ Theorem 2.0.3, p. 35, and Lemma 4.0.3, p. 42 , Wlo09 ] . The image dimension, proper mapping and Chow inputs are given with proofs in [ Chapter II, Corollary 8.6, Theorem 8.8 and Theorem 8.10, pp. 118–121 , DemCADG ] . Serre duality uses the compact Hermitian setting of [ Chapter VI, Theorem 7.3, p. 310 , DemCADG ] . The analytic Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch formula used in proposition 19.9.23 is [ Theorem (3.4), p. 163 , Ati64 ] ; it applies to compact complex manifolds and requires no Kähler hypothesis. The formulas for derivatives in the weight and the Gevrey bounds in proposition 18.34.5 , theorem 18.34.6 , corollary 18.34.9 follow the mechanism for bounded weights of Marinescu and Xing [ v1, Theorems 1.1–1.2, pp. 2–3, and Section 3, pp. 11–19 , MarinescuXingParameter26 ] , applied to the fixed space of selected sections on a compact manifold. The proof uses the inverse of a compressed Gram matrix and its finite jets, while the degree and the multiplier-ideal space stay fixed. The example example 18.34.12 , concerning control at the boundary, is the explicit example on the disk on p. 3 of that preprint. Marinescu and Xing point to the earlier theory of bounded perturbations of Pasternak-Winiarski; its theorems involving the distance to the boundary require additional weighted openness estimates and are not used in these compact arguments. The estimates for the probability measures in lemma 18.34.16 , proposition 18.34.18 , proposition 18.34.22 follow directly from the reproducing identities in finite dimension. Positivity of the symmetric coupling defined by the squared kernel gives the factor one half in the bound for infinitesimal variations, and integrating the logarithm of the odds of the probability of each Borel set gives a sharper modulus for the global oscillation; the smooth example of rank one, example 18.34.21 , shows that this modulus is optimal as a supremum. Normalizing by the dimension gives a uniform radius of analyticity after rescaling. The calculation on a product in example 18.34.24 expresses the conditional fiber probabilities of section 18.40 as a perturbation of the norm weight of order inverse to the degree. Its nonzero limit of intrinsic measures and its unchanged limit of logarithmic potentials describe different parts of the kernel data. In the fiber-integrability criterion of theorem 18.39.8 , corollary 18.39.9 , example 18.39.10 , a radial calculation on a simplex detects the strict endpoint of integrability and the weighted gain $p\sum _ jb_ j^{-1}$, where $p$ and $b_ j$ are the exponents of the normal and the fiber variables in the anisotropic model of the selecting potential. A global lower bound and a single chart with an upper bound then give a bounded divisorial band, whose loss of sections is controlled by the dimension estimate lemma 18.39.1 . This extends the isotropic theorem on sections vanishing along a divisor, without claiming that the condition is necessary for arbitrary selecting potentials. Theorem 18.39.13 extends this argument to finite families of divisors with simple normal crossings. The calculation of the ideal on the base uses separated normal coordinates, and lemma 18.39.12 controls all the mixed twists arising in the restrictions. In the product model of example 18.39.14 , integrability at points where several poles meet is established directly, by Fubini's theorem in distinct pairs of base and fiber coordinates. The criterion on a modified base, theorem 18.39.16 , combines the same argument with the transformation rule for adjoint ideals, lemma 5.43.22 , and the pushforward identity for non-pluripolar products, proposition 18.35.1 . The projective model with a point pole in example 18.39.17 makes explicit the Jacobian order $q-1$, where $q$ is the dimension of the base, and the positive residual on the blowup. The criterion assumes that the modification and its divisorial data are given; it does not assert that they exist for an arbitrary selecting potential. Corollary 18.39.19 separates the curvature requirements in these proofs: a smooth semipositive residual gives a positive reference current, and a positive top-degree integral gives it the required mass, while the estimates for integrability and restriction need no strict positivity of the curvature. In example 18.39.20 the original base is a blowup. Its contracted lines prevent any choice of gauge from making the residual strictly positive, while Hartogs extension shows that, because of the fixed exceptional divisor, the selected space and the reference space coincide. The calculation of coefficients in proposition 18.39.22 combines this Hartogs identification with the anisotropic local threshold; the remaining conditions are ordinary jet conditions at points of projective space. Exact counts of homogeneous monomials then identify the range of the references in which the mass is positive, the drop in degree at the boundary of this range, and the tensor power at which a more singular selecting potential removes every section. The model with two points in example 18.39.25 keeps positive top-degree volume while the residual has degree zero on the curve joining the two centers. Its nonzero defect, of degree $q-1$, is computed by lemma 18.39.24 , which constructs simultaneous jets from affine linear factors and finite Taylor division and requires the sum of the jet orders to be at most the projective degree plus one. Thus a sharp loss of sections and the obstruction to a smooth strictly positive residual occur in the same explicit family. The metric on projective space in section 18.43 is the one in Chiang's [ v1, Example I.15, pp. 9–10 , ChiangKernel26 ] . The proof of proposition 18.43.3 computes the global norms of monomials directly, in the convention $|e|_ h^2=\mathrm e^{-\phi }$ for a local frame $e$ with weight $\phi $, and for a given integration volume; it uses neither the general spectral localization theorem nor the chain of expansions by Newton polyhedra of that preprint. The transition for growing jets on a compact curve, theorem 18.42.1 , is the result obtained by comparison with a disk in the preceding section on curves, and its full extension to all sublinear orders, at the boundary of the region where the curvature vanishes, is theorem 18.42.15 . The correction on shrinking scales in lemma 18.42.13 uses the $L^2$ estimate with pointwise inverse curvature of [ Theorem 5.2 and its singular-metric extension, pp. 34–35 , DemAM11 ] , whose Hilbert-space estimate comes from the preceding Theorem 5.1 and its proof on pp. 33–34. Applying the estimate to $L^ m\otimes K_ C^{-1}$, where $L$ is the line bundle on the compact curve $C$ and $K_ C$ is the canonical bundle of $C$, takes the Ricci curvature into account, and a bounded function varying on the scale $R$ of the flat region restores strictly positive curvature inside it. The particular free boundary in lemma 18.42.10 is constructed by solving an equation for Fourier coefficients in fixed Hölder spaces of finite order and applying the implicit function theorem in Banach spaces. The argument with Gaussian annuli then gives theorem 18.42.15 , theorem 18.42.27 directly, including slowly growing orders, uniformity in the angle, sharpness on compact curves and the limitation of finite Taylor corrections. On the explicit compact product in section 18.44 , global orthogonal monomials turn ordinary jet conditions of total order into a selection by a half-space. The transition for one curve factor gives the marginal Gaussian laws used in theorem 18.44.2 , and the calculation of moments at a fixed positive radius, together with the exact trace, gives convergence in total variation. The sharp radial correction in proposition 18.44.8 follows from the positive first remainder assumed there. Theorem 18.44.11 then uses the integrability calculation at an isolated pole and constancy along compact connected fibers to transfer norms and kernels exactly; the normalization on the base and the matching of volumes are part of its statement. The selection by an interior Newton polytope in section 18.45 is set up with an integral affine offset, a polytope in the interior, a strictly convex invariant logarithmic weight and a positive invariant sampling probability on the whole compact manifold. Angular orthogonality gives exact norms, lattice approximation gives the lower bound for the envelope, and uniform concentration gives the shell measure in the relative dimension. The local argument with Hessian minors distinguishes this measure from mixed non-pluripolar curvature in lower dimension. The construction does not identify an arbitrary multiplier-ideal envelope. The critical product of multiplier ideals in section 18.46 is computed directly from the integrability formula for smooth centers and the identity for an atom in the plane. Exhausting the curvature mass fiber by fiber identifies its multiplier-ideal envelope. Exact norms given by beta integrals, together with concentration, give two kernel limits depending on parity, whereas dividing by the exact dimension gives a single limit of probability measures. The calculation shows that a fixed growth exponent does not imply convergence of the leading coefficient in the count of sections, even when the growth dimension is positive. For the selection by multiplier ideals at the base points of a pencil in section 18.47 , the lower bound for Lelong numbers implied by inclusions of multiplier ideals at all weights, together with a radial convex maximum, identifies the full classes of competitors for both the multiplier-ideal and the ordinary envelopes, and restriction to the curves of degree two in the pencil controls the competitors that are not invariant. Exact norms of truncated Gaussians keep track of the three bands of finite degree, whose count gives the limiting intrinsic mass three. The bounds at the poles also give convergence in every finite $L^ p$ and uniform convergence of the exponentials, while excluding a uniform additive error on the whole manifold. The compact sampling box and the obstacle are part of the statement.

title: 25.17 Gauduchon variational volume
text: The Gauduchon variational volume extracts a homogeneous concave quantity from an elliptic normalization problem. The method goes back to Collins's construction [ Theorem 2.13 , Collins21 ] ; section 12.1 develops the adjoint formula and its dependence on the chosen probability measure. For a Kähler class represented by a closed form $\theta $, this construction meets the Hessian geometry of the Kähler cone: the metric of section 12.4 is $1/n$ times the Hessian of $-\log \int _ X\theta ^ n$ used by Magnússon [ Section 1 , Magnusson12 ] . Completeness and boundary points of positive volume at finite distance are studied in [ Proposition 4.4 and Lemma 4.5 , Magnusson12 ] ; section 12.6 gives the argument by homogeneity in the present normalization. The cones of invariant nonclosed forms in subsection 12.6.4 are computed directly. Stokes' theorem on the compact quotient shows that invariant $(n-1,n-1)$-forms are closed, and the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality for matrices then determines the quotient and its normalized minimizer. The resolvent argument of lemma 12.6.9 and the normalized chord in a prescribed linear subspace give the completeness statement. The Iwasawa example comes with an explicit compact quotient and a proof, by averaging coefficients, that this quotient is not Kähler. The initial construction uses the normalized invariant probability measure. In dimension three, proposition 12.6.22 , corollary 12.6.25 follow from the formula for the variation of mass proved in the book and from the polynomial continuity of bounded products. On the Iwasawa quotient, theorem 12.6.26 extends the determinant formula to probability measures invariant along the central fibers, by means of a closed equation on the base for the Schur complement. The exact vertical Dirichlet defect characterizes all maximizing smooth densities, and the completion estimates for this larger family concern the means of the coefficients of the minimizing forms. For the warped cones in subsection 12.6.31 , a closed equation on the base and an explicit balanced cofactor give the full quotient. The pullback of the affine Hessian metric becomes flat, and the variance of the trace at the endpoints gives the three alternatives: a strip, a half-plane or the whole plane. Smooth existence for the equation on the closed base is theorem 14.2.1 , and integration fixes its scalar; the warped background on the product may be nonclosed. That the finite faces are not big is tested against closed top-degree forms on the base, so the conclusion applies to singular current representatives as well. In the computations on projective space and on periodic tori, the density and the cone are given explicitly throughout. The cones of currents in proposition 12.6.43 are determined by localized closed test forms and Stokes' theorem for distributions. At the finite faces of the warped cone, proposition 12.6.44 applies theorem 14.19.2 , the existence theorem for continuous solutions with $L^ p$ densities, on the closed base; it fixes the scalar by invariance of the mass under bounded perturbations and expands the pulled-back products. The obstruction to global $C^{1,1}$ solutions is the general bound of currents by determinants in proposition 5.28.6 , derived from the identity for coefficients in proposition 5.28.5 . The convergence of the whole sequence in proposition 12.6.47 combines bounds for the reciprocal densities with the compactness for a fixed background in theorem 14.19.21 . Since the base is closed, the uniqueness theorem for invariant mass, 14.25.2 , identifies every cluster point of the potentials. For any bounded competitor at the endpoint pulled back from the base, the density forced away from the extreme set already exhausts the total mass of the closed class, so positivity excludes residual mass on that set before uniqueness is applied. The alternatives for the trace in proposition 12.6.49 , proposition 12.6.51 follow from the explicit balanced cofactor and from integrals of reciprocal squares over tubes, while the mass on the closed base controls the remaining cofactor term. When the trace diverges, its normalization concentrates on the extreme components where the ratio is minimal; if there is a single extreme point, the whole sequence converges to a fiber current. Both the smooth numerator and the denominator then tend to zero, while their quotient remains equal to one. In section 12.12 , bigness of the closed nef core with positive top self-intersection follows from Demailly and Păun's criterion [ Theorem 0.5 , DP04 ] , as recalled in [ SGPT ] ; no such criterion for arbitrary nonclosed nef backgrounds is used. On the warped paths of section 12.13 , the same balanced cofactor as in subsection 12.6.31 computes the cost for every minimizing test. The finite improper identity follows from the first variation and the actual nef limit, while the five rates of proposition 12.13.4 come from the first and second inverse moments of the fiber coefficient. The exclusion of every closed nef positive-volume core in proposition 12.13.6 uses the smooth-test obstruction to bigness and Demailly–Păun's [ arXiv v2, Theorem 2.12, pp. 12–13 , DP04 ] , together with the global potential consequence of the Kähler $\partial \bar\partial $-lemma. The constant closed case gives exactly the expression in Tosatti's Morse inequality [ v2, Theorem 1.1, p. 1 , Tosatti26 ] ; this comparison does not assign a closed cohomology class to a nonconstant warped coefficient. In the radial model on a projective manifold in section 12.14 , a global bounded potential compensates the coefficient along the fibers and gives the lower bound against every smooth Gauduchon test, and explicit balanced metrics give matching values after perturbation. The test against closed top-degree forms on the base in theorem 12.14.6 excludes every quasi-plurisubharmonic potential whose curvature current is strictly positive. This disproves the conjecture that positive volume implies bigness without further restrictions; its versions for closed forms and for surfaces remain separate questions. The limits of test forms in subsection 12.14.9 are computed from these explicit balanced metrics by Stokes' theorem for closed forms and radial integration. In dimension three the powers normalized by the trace concentrate on the degenerate fiber at a logarithmic rate, whereas in higher dimension their threshold quotient stays positive. Localized closed forms on the base, with a small Kähler correction, give a different balanced family approaching the fiber in every dimension of the model. The initial metric of the Chern–Ricci flow in 12.34.8 is chosen so that, up to a smooth global change of gauge, the radial background is the limiting form at the maximal time, and the maximal-time theorem determines this lifetime. In the normalization $\operatorname {Ric}=-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \omega ^ n$, time one corresponds to time $1/(2\pi )$ for the Chern–Ricci form $-2\pi \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \omega ^ n$ used in this book. A test against a closed form on the base excludes every positive representative at later times, and the support and the vertical rank of all annihilators at the endpoint follow directly from the semipositive representative and the formula for the trace matrix. The averaged trace is a special case of the general identity for the flow proved before. In the criteria of 12.10.22 , invariance of the mass of bounded potentials and the support of the measure on the contact set prevent the stretched obstacle envelopes from collapsing, and the sublinear condition provides competitors. The uniform bound for Lelong numbers in lemma 5.38.8 then gives vanishing Lelong numbers by scaling. The argument with smooth roots of rank two extends the scalar first-order equation across the analytic set, and the support theorem for currents carried by analytic sets, recalled in section 5.38 , removes its residual current. The calculations on Hopf manifolds and quadrics give examples in which the dual problem is attained. The general implications involving moments and entropy remain separate questions. In the example with a point pole, proposition 12.10.33 , radial integration shows directly that the potential has full mass, and the equality case of the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality for matrices, combined with the local strong maximum principle, excludes every smooth semipositive maximizing test form. The argument does not need to identify the potential with the greatest threshold envelope. The thresholds for entropy and weighted integrability in corollary 12.10.35 follow directly from the computed radial density. They concern the density of this single equation, whereas the question of uniform moment or entropy conditions concerns the determinant-weighted probability measures of a maximizing sequence when the supremum is attained by a smooth semipositive test. The bound for the determinant at the endpoint, theorem 12.9.2 , is derived within the book from the criterion for mass invariance and the quotient by the lower mass; related criteria for the mass are [ Propositions 3.2 and 3.3(iv) , GL22 ] . The concentrating family in section 12.18 distinguishes the unique smooth maximizer for one density from maximizing sequences whose higher moments diverge. The coordinate formula ( 12.18.7 ) identifies the intrinsic determinant measure on singular and degenerate positive currents. The proof of theorem 12.18.8 applies Tosatti and Weinkove's [ arXiv v2, Corollary 1, p. 1 , TW10 ] separately to each smooth positive root. The source uses $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial \varphi $; the potential is multiplied by $2\pi $ here, and theorem 11.1.7 fixes the volume coefficient. The last paragraph of that source, p. 8, refers the existence argument to Cherrier and Demailly or the authors' earlier paper. No estimates uniform in the varying right-hand sides are used. The closed and nonclosed torus families in theorem 12.18.13 , theorem 12.18.15 preserve the complete determinant data and positive mass extrema while ellipticity degenerates. For the nonclosed family, the lower-power identities are verified on the two-coordinate block, retaining its fixed nonzero torsion. In theorem 12.18.17 , the Poisson kernel gives uniformly convergent continuous potentials and exact maximizers for varying roots. The limiting current has rank-deficient absolutely continuous and singular coefficient parts, so its determinant measure vanishes although the bounded potential has positive Monge–Ampère mass. These calculations concern scalar perturbations and current limits; they supply no flow existence or convergence theorem. The identity ( 12.17.3 ) of lemma 12.17.2 , for bounded potentials in a background $g$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g^2)=0$, uses the calculus of bounded products and of weighted decreasing limits in proposition 5.28.2 , lemma 5.27.2 , whose classical local foundations are [ Section 2, Theorems 2.1 and 2.4, pp. 4–9 , BT82 ] . That the sign $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g\leq 0$ gives positive lower mass is part of the criteria in terms of the sign of the torsion of Angella, Guedj and Lu [ Theorem 3.2, pp. 4641–4642 , AGL23 ] . The curvature calculation in theorem 12.17.7 identifies this sign on principal elliptic threefolds, and the two quotient constructions give explicit mass constants in the present convention for the operator. The conclusion for the determinant of the full current then follows from the endpoint theorem proved in the book and a change of background. The estimate for local families in theorem 12.9.7 controls the solution form and its Gauduchon factor by two contractions. The elliptic input is the parametrix and Fredholm argument on compact manifolds in Taylor [ Chapter 7, Sections 4 and 10, especially (10.4)–(10.6) , Taylor7 ] , together with the mapping properties on Hölder spaces in [ Chapter 13, (8.7), (8.17) and (8.22) , Taylor13 ] . Invariance of the index is [ Section 7, Proposition 7.4 , TaylorFA ] , and smooth regularity for nonlinear elliptic equations is also formulated in [ Proposition , TaylorReg ] . The estimates for the equation and for the normalized factor give explicit constants for the densities without assuming positive lower mass; instead, the data are restricted to smooth functions in a small $C^{2,\alpha }$ neighborhood. The factor bound in proposition 12.9.15 starts from the conformal theorem of Gauduchon [ Théorème 2 and its proof, pp. 132–133 , GauduchonStandard85 ] . Its general statement has no restriction on the first Betti number; the even-Betti assumption belongs to the surface theorem at the beginning of that article. The smooth maximum principle is recalled and applied in [ pp. 131–132 , GauduchonStandard85 ] . The quantitative estimate here writes the cofactor equation in real divergence form and proves its Harnack bound by power iteration and a dyadic mean-oscillation argument. Since $d(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)=d\omega $, the vector coefficient is controlled by the fixed torsion. This supplies the exact-adjoint bounds of theorem 12.9.18 without derivative bounds on the varying solution form.
