Gauduchon uses $d^ c=\mathrm i(\bar\partial -\partial )$ and $L=-\operatorname {tr}(dd^ c)$; the positive factor equation is unchanged by this scaling and sign conversion. The classical analytic input in section 12.22 is Hironaka's elimination of indeterminacies: every modification is dominated by a composition of blowups with smooth centers. The argument by principalization and domination is explained by Abramovich, Karu, Matsuki and Włodarczyk [ Sections 1.2.3–1.2.4, pp. 538–539, and Section 5.4, p. 564 , AKMW02 ] , where the analytic case is treated explicitly. The curvature of the exceptional divisors then gives the uniform bound for the pairings used here; no factorization into a sequence of blowdowns is needed for this estimate. For the fixed projective cones in section 12.25 , every Gauduchon test is compared with a closed form of constant rank through an explicit logarithm of an exceptional divisor, which gives the exact loss of rank when the prescribed effective divisors are removed. For a general modification whose source is Kähler, proposition 12.25.11 obtains in addition two-sided bounds by powers from the intersection polynomial for closed backgrounds in section 12.20 . Fixed coefficient functions that vanish, cones of residuals without restrictions, and sources that are not Kähler lie outside this construction. The theorem that the line bundle of a smooth anticanonical curve of self-intersection zero is unitary flat near the curve, theorem 12.27.3 , is due to Chen, Filip, Sun, Tosatti and Zhang [ Theorem 1.1, with the standing degree-zero hypothesis in Section 1.1 , CFSTZ26 ] . Its proof uses their identification of the holomorphic fibers in Proposition 4.1, the elliptic inverse independent of the holonomy in Lemma 5.2, and the weighted horizontal inverse and contraction of Propositions 5.4–5.5. The cutoff in proposition 12.27.5 is the construction at the end of their proof in Section 6. The variational bounds in rank one follow from proposition 12.26.1 , and the examples obtained by blowing up nine points on a plane cubic, together with their torsion criterion, follow by restriction to the cubic. Only this local theorem and its direct consequences are used, not the global classification of surfaces in that paper. The pencil in the case of finite holonomy and the rigidity in the non-torsion case, proposition 12.28.2 , theorem 12.28.3 , give the case of a smooth reduced divisor of Koike's [ Lemma 3.5 , Koike26 ] . The Levi-flat level sets of the flat norm have a smooth suspension model, so the density of their leaves and the maximum modulus argument are proved directly. The hypothesis is that the line bundle of the divisor is unitary flat near the smooth compact divisor; the global criteria for semipositivity and the dichotomy between fibrations and the Hartogs phenomenon in Koike's paper are not used. Together with the theorem on anticanonical neighborhoods, these local results explain the non-Stein and Hartogs properties of the nine-point examples with non-torsion normal bundle. The quotient construction in proposition 12.29.3 follows the mechanism of invariant fibers of Denisi and Höring [ v1, Lemma 2.10, p. 6, Proposition 4.2, p. 12 and pp. 14–18, and Theorem 5.1, p. 19 , DH26 ] . Their action has $\kappa =2\pi \mathrm{i}\rho $, where $\kappa $ is the parameter of proposition 12.29.3 and $\rho $ is theirs, and their function $\mu _ Q$ equals $1+2\sigma $, with $\sigma $ the function defined before that proposition. The Laurent argument in lemma 12.29.1 proves directly the obstruction for punctured line bundles used in their Example 2.1, while example 12.29.2 computes the degree of an explicit factor of automorphy by its invariant metric. The statement about the quotient includes the two exceptional parameters, which are treated with compact elliptic curves. The computation of classes in theorem 12.30.4 gives their Proposition 4.2 and Lemmas 4.5 and 4.7–4.8, with explicit generators and conventions for projectivization. The flat unitary character in lemma 12.30.2 treats line bundles of every positive degree $d$ directly; the coefficient of the quotient is then $\kappa =2\pi \mathrm{i}d\rho $. This gives their non-Stein conclusion for split elliptic ruled surfaces without the reduction to a finite cover in their Lemma 5.2. For the split elliptic ruled surface $M$, the algebra $\bigoplus _{r\geq 0}H^0(M,\operatorname {Sym}^ rT_ M)$ in theorem 12.31.4 has the bigness and nonfinite generation stated in [ v1, Theorem 1.4, p. 2, with proof on pp. 9–10 , DH26 ] . The decomposition by polynomial weights in lemma 12.31.1 gives the exact dimensions and the tautological volume in theorem 12.31.3 , and its map to leading coefficients gives a direct proof of nonfinite generation through a quotient by an ideal of square zero. For canonical extensions, [ v1, Remark 3.8, pp. 10–11 , DH26 ] also states bigness and nonfinite generation, leaving the proof to the reader. The homogeneous quadric in lemma 12.32.1 and the decomposition of coefficients under the unipotent action give the description as a polynomial algebra in theorem 12.32.2 . The exact dimensions, the tautological volume and nonfinite generation in corollary 12.32.3 follow for every extension class that is nonzero on the fibers of the ruling, including all Kähler canonical extensions on the split surface. The case of an extension class vanishing on the fibers of the ruling, proposition 12.33.2 , follows directly from the ordinary cotangent quadric and the same decomposition of coefficients. Its section algebra is the same as in the case of nonzero restriction, while proposition 12.33.3 identifies the universal cover of the corresponding torsor, which is not Stein, as the product of $\mathbb C^2$ with the total space of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-2)$. The question whether a weak Monge–Ampère power admits a scalar conformal factor is raised by Lu [ Chapter 3, Section 5 , LuHDR22 ] . The representation by finite currents in theorem 12.8.2 gives a supporting probability measure without defining that weak power or its scalar factor.

title: 25.18 Closed classes and singular loci
text: For closed classes on a Hermitian manifold, almost positive representatives keep the cohomology class separate from the auxiliary metric. The convention in section 10.11 follows Boucksom's thesis [ Section 2.1.2 , BouThesis02 ] ; it does not assign a Bott–Chern class to a nonclosed Hermitian form. The smooth and analytic regularizations of 5.36.3 , used for proposition 10.12.2 , have the lower bounds of [ Theorem 2.1 , Bou04Zariski ] ; see also [ Theorems 1.2.9–1.2.10 , BouThesis02 ] . Smooth regularization loses positivity by a multiple of a continuous approximation of the Lelong numbers, whereas analytic regularization has a curvature error tending uniformly to zero and does not increase Lelong numbers. The minimal multiplicities of definition 10.12.1 are defined through these almost positive approximating families, as in [ Definition 2.1.5 , BouThesis02 ] . They must be distinguished from the Lelong numbers of a single current with minimal singularities: in the example of a nef class on a ruled surface in [ Section 1.2.3 , BouThesis02 ] , a current with minimal singularities has nonzero Lelong numbers. The non-Kähler locus of definition 10.13.1 is defined in [ Definition 2.1.19 , BouThesis02 ] , and the proof of theorem 10.13.2 by finite intersections and regularized maxima is the argument of [ Theorem 2.1.20 , BouThesis02 ] . The equivalence between the existence of a Kähler current and the existence of a Kähler modification, used in section 10.10 , is the classical criterion recalled in [ Theorem 1.2.11 , BouThesis02 ] ; it is used as an external geometric input. The equality of the non-Kähler locus and the null locus of a nef and big class is the transcendental Nakamaye theorem of Collins and Tosatti [ CT15Loci ] , which also holds on compact manifolds in Fujiki's class $\mathcal C$; section 10.10 recalls this theorem from the literature. Restricted volumes give a numerical test for these loci. The numerical restricted volume ( 10.14.1 ) follows Collins and Tosatti [ Section 2 , CT22Restricted ] ; the requirement that the analytic singularities have a smooth remainder is part of that definition. The existence of Kähler models for every subvariety uses Fujiki's theorem that class $\mathcal C$ is closed under passing to closed subspaces [ Lemma 4.6(2) , Fujiki78 ] , followed by Varouchas's theorem on Kähler modifications in the form stated and explained by Barlet [ Theorem 10, pp. 31–32 , Barlet00 ] . A common Kähler refinement is obtained by embedded resolution of the graph in a Kähler product, using Bierstone and Milman [ Theorem 1.6 and Remark 1.7(2) , BM97 ] . These are classical geometric inputs. The descent of potentials is proved in proposition 5.43.18 , so the proof of mass invariance does not repeat it. In proposition 10.16.5 , positive non-pluripolar mass implies bigness by [ Proposition 1.22 , BEGZ10 ] . The definition of the positive product, its agreement with the cup product for nef classes, and the fact that it is attained by currents with minimal singularities are in [ Definition 1.17, arXiv pp. 17–18, and Proposition 1.20, arXiv p. 20 , BEGZ10 ] . The normalized diagonal current ( 10.16.7 ) uses the mass-concentration theorem of Demailly and Păun [ Proposition 2.6 , DP04 ] and makes explicit the coefficient in the construction of [ Theorem 2.12 , DP04 ] . These results on Kähler manifolds are used as classical inputs. The identity for the mass with a bounded residual in lemma 10.17.3 , by contrast, follows directly from the book's formula for bounded masses, by comparison of polynomials. The comparison with the numerical restricted volume for nef classes is [ Lemma 2.6 , CT22Restricted ] , and the final equality in ( 10.16.11 ) uses the theorem [ Theorem 1.1 , CT15Loci ] recalled above. The rigidity criterion for nef boundary classes on tori, theorem 10.26.1 , develops the flat model of Fu and Ouyang [ v1, Section 3, pp. 5–6 , FuOuyang26 ] . Testing against Fourier modes proves the vanishing along the kernel directly, and the metric argument uses a finite covering by dense leaves and a character of the circle. The collapse in this theorem is along a fixed positive perturbation $\theta +t\kappa $, where $\kappa $ is a translation-invariant Kähler form. The calculation with mixed forms in example 10.26.3 shows that the clause in their Lemma 3.1 and Proposition 3.2 allowing arbitrary approaching classes cannot be used in that generality; their Theorem 4.4, which concerns positive perturbations, and the distinction made in their Remark 6.4, p. 18, concern a different setting. Their general theorems on collapse, fibrations and lattice dynamics for K3 surfaces are not used in this argument on tori. The nonrigid class with an irrational ray in proposition 10.27.2 is the explicit Kummer construction of [ v1, Section 7.1, pp. 18–19, proof of Theorem 1.4(a) , FuOuyang26 ] . The resolution of the quotient and its Kähler metric are described in local charts, and the difference of two representatives is given an explicit periodic global $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-primitive. Periods over translated real two-dimensional subtori detect the irrational ray without extending cohomology classes across the punctures. Fu and Ouyang's conclusions about diameters of Ricci-flat metrics, spectra and limit spaces require additional inputs and are not used in this construction. The family obtained from four points and its central metric in section 10.28 are Qin's construction [ v1, Theorem A, p. 1, and Section 3, Lemmas 3.1–3.3, pp. 3–4 , QinMetricExtension26 ] . Qin's proof of the nonextension theorem on p. 5 uses global $L^2$ extension for adjoint bundles. Theorem 10.28.4 instead uses the conics of degree zero of lemma 10.28.3 : Fubini's theorem, averages over disks and Harnack's inequality force the central weights to be harmonic away from the node, and the remaining curvature has logarithmic coefficient one, whereas the metric constructed here has coefficient one half. This shows that the metric has no semipositive extension whose central restriction is at most as singular as the metric itself, without using global adjoint extension and without asserting that this metric has minimal singularities. Varying the conic gives the exact set of restrictions in theorem 10.28.9 : the divisor metric of the negative line multiplied by the pullback of an arbitrary semipositive metric on the base of the pencil. The converse is constructed from the two homogeneous sections of the pencil, and corollary 10.28.10 concerns the least singular metrics among these restrictions. Inoue surfaces were introduced by Inoue [ Inoue74 ] , and their higher-dimensional analogues by Oeljeklaus and Toma [ OT05 ] , who proved that the action of $\mathcal O_ K\rtimes U$ used in section 10.29 is free, properly discontinuous and cocompact, and that the resulting manifolds are not Kähler. Ornea and Verbitsky showed that Oeljeklaus–Toma manifolds with $t=1$ contain no positive-dimensional complex subvarieties, using a semipositive closed form with dense null leaves [ OV11OT ] . The decomposition of Inoue surfaces into three-dimensional tori filled by dense leaves, and a Liouville argument along the leaves for bounded harmonic functions, appear in the work of Fang, Tosatti, Weinkove and Zheng on the Chern–Ricci flow [ Section 2, Lemma 2.1 , FTWZ16 ] , where the Tricerri metric and the identity $\mathrm{Ric}(\omega _ T)=-\alpha $ are also recorded; their form $\alpha =\mathrm i\, \mathrm dw\wedge \mathrm d\overline w/(4y^2)$ equals $2\pi \theta $ in the normalization of section 10.29 , and their $\omega _ T=4\alpha +\beta $ is the Tricerri metric used there. The description of all $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions in theorem 10.29.4 , the mass computations of proposition 10.29.10 and the absence of plurisigned metrics in proposition 10.29.14 are proved directly here. Angella, Guedj and Lu proved that, on a compact threefold, a Hermitian metric with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \geq 0$ gives finite upper mass and one with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \leq 0$ gives positive lower mass; in particular a pluriclosed metric gives both [ Theorem B , AGL23 ] . The general question of finiteness and positivity of these masses is [ Problem 1.8 , AGL23 ] . Angella, Dubickas, Otiman and Stelzig showed that an Oeljeklaus–Toma manifold admits a pluriclosed metric only if $s=t$ [ Corollary 3 , ADOS24 ] ; proposition 10.29.14 shows that for type $(s,1)$ with $s\geq 2$ there is not even a metric whose $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ has a sign.

title: 25.19 Closed classes and metric completeness
text: The examples theorem 10.24.1 , theorem 10.24.7 , theorem 10.24.16 test the completeness question raised by Di Nezza, Guedj and Lu [ v1, Theorem 3.4 and Question 3.5, pp. 14–15 , DNGL26 ] . The first uses a big class that is not nef and an ordinary solution with minimal singularities. The second has a semipositive nef and big background, a solution of full mass and finite energy with vanishing Lelong numbers, and the prescribed nonintegrable pole with smooth strictly positive coefficient; its cusp is complete, but a disjoint null curve lies at finite normal distance. The third, theorem 10.24.16 , satisfies exactly the identities of [ v1, Section 3.1, pp. 12–14 , DNGL26 ] for the initial potential, the resolution, the discrepancy, the class and the prescribed volume. Its class is not nef and has a divisorial reference with minimal singularities, while the solution adds a cusp with vanishing Lelong numbers along a disjoint curve. These examples disprove the two separate completeness assertions for the elliptic equations; whether nefness and compatibility can hold simultaneously, and whether the evolving maximal flow itself is complete, remain open. The torus examples for normal lengths in section 10.25 have instead logarithmically weakened poles whose coefficients tend to zero at the divisor. The energy argument in section 10.24 uses the classical finite-energy class of [ Section 2 , BEGZ10 ] , relative to a reference with minimal singularities; finiteness of the mixed masses and of the relative energy comes from [ Proposition 1.6 and Section 2.2 , BEGZ10 ] . Uniqueness follows from the comparison principle for full mass [ Corollary 2.3 , BEGZ10 ] : the unweighted reference measure is infinite, but the two Monge–Ampère measures being compared are finite. In subsection 10.24.6 , the potential with minimal singularities is $V_\theta =0$, and exact radial identities show that the volume form is smooth and positive across both divisors. The bounded truncations have masses $1-p(T_ k)^2$ for the square and $1-p(T_ k)$ for the mixed product on the transition shell, where $p$ is the slope of the radial profile and $T_ k$ the radius at which the truncation at level $k$ begins; their contributions to the energy tend to zero. The products are computed by smooth convex approximation and the continuity along decreasing sequences proved by Bedford and Taylor [ Theorem 2.1, pp. 4–7 , BT82 ] . This direct computation of the energy agrees with the criterion by canonical approximation of [ Propositions 2.10–2.11, arXiv pp. 26–27 , BEGZ10 ] . Here vanishing Lelong numbers do not imply ordinary minimal singularities. In subsection 10.24.13 , radial barriers and the inversion of a Volterra operator construct the cusp along the curve for a fixed smooth volume form, and explicit charts on the blowup give a smooth positive residual volume and a Kähler residual at the initial time. The reference with minimal singularities is obtained from the extension across isolated points in lemma 5.24.8 . The canonical truncations at level $k$ have cutoff energy $O(k\mathrm{e}^{-k/2})$, so the continuity of bounded products and the criteria for relative energy cited above apply. The remaining smooth pulled-back metric puts the exceptional curve at finite distance. This is an auxiliary solution of an elliptic equation; it is not identified with the evolving smoothing metric. Hölder regularity imposes a further restriction on the metric. If a positive residual current has a Hölder continuous potential and is smooth and strictly positive outside a proper analytic set, theorem 5.39.1 shows that every point of that set lies at finite distance in the metric completion; on a compact manifold, removing a nonempty analytic set therefore gives an incomplete metric. Continuity alone allows complete ends: for the prescribed radial densities of theorem 10.22.7 , boundedness of the minimal remainder and finiteness of the normal length have different logarithmic thresholds. The resulting complete examples with bounded potentials solve equations with prescribed densities; they do not have the compatibility with the flow discussed above. The mechanism of Dang [ v2, Proposition 5.2, pp. 16–17 , Dang26 ] , which bounds distances through a Dini condition on the square root of the modulus of continuity of the potential, is the subject of theorem 5.39.6 . The trace calculation given here keeps the smooth background through the additive term in ( 5.39.5 ) and needs no doubling condition. It gives logarithmic rates and uniform limits of pseudometrics along subsequences in corollary 5.39.7 , corollary 5.39.8 ; a common positive lower bound for the metrics is needed to exclude collapse.

title: 25.20 Locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: In locally conformally Kähler geometry, the Lee form constrains both the rigidity of metrics and the volume forms that can be prescribed. The conjecture on pseudoeffectivity of the Lee class, 23.2.12 , is formulated in terms of Gauduchon degrees by Ornea and Verbitsky [ arXiv version, Conjecture 4.14 and Remark 4.16 , OV25Balanced ] ; its consequence for balanced metrics is proposition 23.2.11 . Their theorem on the volume forms of Vaisman metrics [ arXiv version, Theorem 4.1 and Lemmas 4.2–4.4 , OV24Vaisman ] requires invariance under both the Lee and the anti-Lee vector fields. The proof of theorem 23.2.29 uses theorem 14.2.1 : uniqueness gives a basic potential, transverse integration by Stokes' theorem fixes the scalar, and the Lee form of the new metric is parallel because it is closed and its dual vector field is Killing. The uniqueness argument keeps the scale of the candidate metric in ( 23.2.34 ) as an unknown until integration determines it. The least-eigenvalue criterion 23.2.15 is proved by applying smooth Stokes to the volume polynomial of 23.2.14 . Nonvanishing of the ordinary Bott–Chern class already follows from the conformal Gauduchon argument and the Lee degree ( 23.2.8 ). The Hopf calculations in 23.2.16 , 23.2.17 distinguish constancy of the least eigenvalue from constancy of the whole spectrum, and distinguish first pointwise degeneration from collapse of total volume. These are explicit compact metrics in every dimension at least two. The criterion gives a smooth semipositive representative under its spectral hypothesis; pseudoeffectivity without that hypothesis remains the conjecture above. The classification of radial metrics in 23.2.35 follows from explicit identities for the Hopf forms and a periodic scalar equation. Its positive periodic solutions are strictly ordered by the constant of integration, and their Lee periods fill the negative half-line. The positive twisted potential is constructed in the gauge given by the Lee form of the metric itself. Nonconstant radial volume forms force the metric to be non-Vaisman, and uniqueness of the metric is asserted only within the radial family considered there. The proof of theorem 23.2.47 keeps the divergence terms in the Chern–Ricci-flat specialization of the argument of Barbaro and Otiman [ v2, Section 4, equations (2)–(4), pp. 12–13 , BO25LCK ] . Their Theorem A gives the Gauduchon rigidity conclusion; retaining the scalar-curvature term in the integrated Bianchi identity gives the divergence identity and the equivalence with holomorphicity of the Lee field. The quotient and the two metrics in example 23.2.53 are computed directly: the holomorphic volume trivializes the canonical bundle, the flat gauge has nonzero Lee divergence, and compact pluriharmonic rigidity prevents a simultaneous conformal gauge. The conjecture for manifolds, 23.2.54 , is stated in [ Introduction , BO25LCK ] . The Kodaira example admits a Vaisman metric on its given complex structure, so its conformal obstruction does not refute that conjecture. The dual description of the Lee–Gauduchon cone and its bimeromorphic invariance in subsection 23.2.55 are due to Ornea and Verbitsky [ Theorems 3.11 and 4.5 , OV25LeeGauduchon ] . The distinction between vanishing of the Lee–Gauduchon class and the strongly Gauduchon condition in subsection 23.2.67 follows [ Remarks 5.6–5.8 , OV25LeeGauduchon ] , and the criterion for the existence of strongly Gauduchon metrics used there is due to Popovici [ Proposition 1.2 , Pop13SG ] .

title: 25.21 Regularity and singular spaces
text: Regularity in a big class is first a local question on the locus where strict barriers are smooth. For a closed class on a compact Kähler manifold, existence and uniqueness for ( 10.20.2 ) are due to Boucksom, Eyssidieux, Guedj and Zeriahi [ Theorem A, equivalently Theorem 3.1 , BEGZ10 ] , and the bounds ( 10.20.3 ) in terms of minimal singularities are [ Theorem B, quantitatively Theorem 4.1 , BEGZ10 ] . The same uniqueness theorem for full mass identifies the solutions in closed classes in section 15.22 , section 15.23 , section 10.22 , section 10.23 . Smoothness on the ample locus in the nef case is [ Theorem C , BEGZ10 ] ; theorem 10.20.1 gives this smoothness in every closed big class, for a smooth positive volume form. For a big background that need not be closed, the local Hölder theorem theorem 15.17.1 is Dang's [ v1, Theorem A and Theorem 3.1 , Dang26 ] . It gives the local input for the argument on the ample locus, while allowing the global potential to be unbounded and the lower curvature bound to be nonclosed. Formulating the equation with a positive scalar and only on the regular locus is equivalent, since the complementary analytic set carries neither smooth volume nor non-pluripolar mass. The proof of local regularity also needs a quantitative stability estimate. The estimate with a strict barrier in section 15.15 is [ v1, Theorem 3.3 and Remark 3.4 , Dang26 ] in the case of minimal singularities, with the comparison potential normalized explicitly; the construction with auxiliary subsolutions in section 15.4 first treats a semipositive big background. The interior regularity theorem theorem 15.18.1 combines this Hölder control with the assumption that the density is smooth and positive on the whole regular locus of one fixed strict analytic barrier. This domain is part of the hypothesis: smoothness of the density on a smaller open set does not give the same conclusion by restriction. The compact Pogorelov example example 10.21.10 has a smooth positive density on an inner chart, but its density loses regularity along the divisor in the gluing region, so it does not satisfy this hypothesis. Local smoothing uses the theorem of Guan and Li on the Dirichlet problem [ Theorem 1.1, p. 1186 , GL10 ] . In ( 15.21.3 ) the background is zero and, in local coordinates $z$, the metric is $(\mathrm i/2)\partial \bar\partial |z|^2$; for a smooth positive density $G$, a large quadratic correction gives a strict subsolution. The same theorem constructs the approximants in subsection 15.18.7 and starts the passage to continuous boundary values and to zero density in section 15.7 ; in dimension one it is replaced by the Dirichlet problem for the Poisson equation. Once ( 15.18.6 ) is uniformly elliptic, the Evans–Krylov theorem for variable coefficients [ Definition 3.2, Theorem 3.4, and the paragraph following it , TWWY15 ] , followed by difference quotients and Schauder estimates, gives smoothness. The local identification in section 15.21 uses Bedford and Taylor's uniqueness theorem for the bounded Dirichlet problem [ Corollary 4.4, p. 17 , BT82 ] . Degeneration of the density also matters for global stability: Kołodziej and Nguyen [ Theorem 4.1 , KN21 ] assume that the density satisfies $f\geq c_0$ for a constant $c_0>0$, in addition to their hypotheses on capacity. The densities giving nonuniqueness in section 14.20 have no such lower bound, even when they are positive almost everywhere. For compact sets in a Hermitian manifold, Ahn [ Theorems 1.1–1.2 , Ahn26 ] proves that Hölder continuity of the extremal function is a pointwise local property. The weighted version assumes that both the unweighted extremal function and the weight are Hölder continuous, and that the set is uniformly dense in capacity; the same density condition enters the equivalence with the local and weakly local Hölder properties. These are the regularity settings referred to in section 24.1 . On singular spaces, regularity on a resolution must be combined with descent. Dang [ v1, Theorem B , Dang26 ] proves continuity results for bounded solutions on resolutions under additional geometric and integrability hypotheses, notably for log terminal singularities; this result does not cover the arbitrary unibranch singularities in the problem posed in section 24.1 . Pan [ Theorems A and A' , Pan25 ] constructs a Gauduchon metric on the regular locus of a compact reduced irreducible Hermitian space of dimension at least two; it is conformal and uniformly comparable to the given metric, and unique up to scale among such metrics. Control of the conformal factors on a resolution is central to the construction. This result motivates the questions about singular traces in section 24.1 . The boundary-weighted quadric surface in 9.11.10 is Seo's [ v1, Example 6.2, pp. 29–30 , SeoToricIdeals26 ] . The paper uses the weight $\mathrm{e}^{-2\varphi }$, so the potential here is $u=2\varphi $. The adapted volume comes from a generator of $\omega _ X^{[4]}(4D)$ and pulls back to a constant times $|s|^{-1}$ times Euclidean volume on the finite quotient cover. Splitting the logarithmic quadrant gives the strict monomial test; angular orthogonality and division of convergent series give the full ideal. This proves the explicit example directly, without using the paper's general Newton-body description. The boundary-weighted ideal and the resolution-ideal relation in proposition 9.11.9 use different volume conventions. The affine toric monomial test in theorem 9.11.20 is the holomorphic-character part of Seo's [ v1, Theorem 6.1, pp. 28–29 , SeoToricIdeals26 ] , here restricted to full-dimensional cones and effective rational boundary. Its convex-cone criterion is [ v1, Lemma 4.4 and Theorem 4.6, pp. 18–19 , SeoToricIdeals26 ] ; the proof here obtains coercivity by a compactness argument and sandwiches the actual logarithmic neighborhoods between translated cones. The subtraction test of corollary 9.11.22 is the integral calculation behind [ v1, Proposition 5.10 and Corollary 6.3, pp. 27 and 30 , SeoToricIdeals26 ] . For this holomorphic-character integrability assertion the exponent can be any positive real number, without assigning a rational boundary to the subtracted weight. The quadric threefold and its whole-germ ideal in proposition 9.11.23 are computed directly from the same criterion and the homogeneous coordinate ring. No general fractional-sheaf generation or ideal-envelope statement is used. In the construction on unibranch curves in subsection 9.11.50 , the Green function, the exact mass of the pole, uniqueness in the full singularity type, descent through disks and the projective cusp are all obtained directly. $L^ p$ data on the normalization, $p>1$, give a continuous residual even when the background coming from a local embedding pulls back to a degenerate form. The example of the cusp also computes the exact threshold for densities on the singular curve. This is a result in dimension one; it neither extends the theorem on log terminal singularities cited above nor gives a general equation on nonclosed singular spaces. The calculation at the endpoint in theorem 9.11.60 is another direct construction from the Green function of the curve and the radial primitive of theorem 10.23.1 . For one logarithmic family it distinguishes three properties: finite mass of the density, a bounded residual in the ordinary singularity type, and equivalence of multiplier ideals at all weights. It does not characterize arbitrary integrable data. The equations with nonclosed backgrounds on products with cuspidal curves in subsection 9.11.63 combine a correction of the reference to a smooth positive form, quantitative Fourier inversion, and a comparison of bounded energies in a background all of whose powers are $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed. The weighted limit lemma 5.27.2 is proved by adding one complex variable $w$ and passing to the maxima with $\log |w|^2$, which reduces it to the ordinary convergence of mixed products along decreasing sequences, including top-degree products in one higher dimension. The corresponding classical input is Bedford and Taylor's [ Theorem 2.4 and its proof, pp. 7–9 , BT82 ] ; their operator is $4\pi $ times ours, so products of degree $r$ scale by $(4\pi )^{-r}$. The resulting family with small data in all variables has Hölder continuous solutions on the ambient space, unique among all bounded competitors. The existence of bounded solutions for arbitrary nonnegative $L^ p$ data on the normalization, $p>1$, follows separately from theorem 10.31.3 . These results complement the construction with Green functions on curves, without giving a general equation on singular spaces or a sharp criterion for densities on the singular space.

title: 25.22 Geometric problems
text: A closed strictly positive current has geometric consequences that a positive nonclosed background need not have, and this distinction governs the passage from the normalization of equations to the geometric criteria below. The characterization of Fujiki's class by Kähler currents used in section 24.4 is Demailly and Păun's [ Theorem 0.7 , DP04 ] , and the transcendental Grauert–Riemenschneider conjecture is [ Conjecture 0.8 , DP04 ] ; in the arXiv version of that paper these are Theorem 0.6 and Conjecture 0.7. For nef classes with positive top self-intersection, the equivalence between bigness and bounded mass cited in section 24.4 is Guedj and Lu's [ Theorem 4.9 , GL22 ] . The characterization of Fujiki's class by bounded mass and positive upper volume of the class is [ Theorem C , BGL25 ] ; that upper volume is different from the Gauduchon functional for a fixed probability measure. The transcendental Morse inequality for closed classes on compact Kähler manifolds, and its consequences for differentiability of the volume and duality of cones, mentioned in section 24.4 , are Tosatti's [ Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2, version 2 , Tosatti26 ] ; they are quoted from the literature, and their proofs are not reproduced. The qualitative criterion under bounded mass is [ Theorem 4.12 , GL22 ] . The non-Hermitian locus in section 24.4 is that of Dang [ Definition 2.12 and Theorem 2.14 , DangNull26 ] , where almost analytic singularities have the precise meaning of [ Definition 2.8 , DangNull26 ] , including a smooth remainder on a suitable log resolution. Dang's qualitative identification of this locus with the null locus, for nef and big backgrounds that may be nonclosed, is [ Theorem 1.1 , DangNull26 ] . Theorem A of the same paper gives a numerical criterion under different hypotheses: bounded mass on the ambient manifold and positive lower volume on its submanifolds of positive dimension. Theorem C of [ DangNull26 ] identifies the singularities of the Chern–Ricci flow at a finite time with the null locus when the limiting lower volume is positive, for arbitrary initial metrics in dimension two and for initial metrics of Guan–Li type in higher dimensions, that is, initial metrics $\omega _0$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega _0=0$ and $\mathrm{d}\omega _0\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\omega _0=0$. Once the limiting background is big, [ Theorem 4.3 , DangNull26 ] gives convergence as currents and smooth local convergence away from its non-Hermitian locus. This conditional parabolic input should be distinguished from the implication from positive volume to bigness without further hypotheses, which fails by theorem 12.34.10 . The theorem on the maximal existence time, theorem 12.34.4 , is Tosatti and Weinkove's [ Theorem 1.2, (1.4), and Section 4, arXiv version , TW15 ] . The proof given here combines the positive affine path and time-weighted estimates for the potential with lemma 14.5.1 and classical parabolic regularity. In the conversion to the book's conventions, potentials are multiplied by $2\pi $ and time is unchanged. The conditions for geometric smoothing in [ Section 3.1 , DNGL26 ] include the further compatibility discussed in section 25.19 . Distance estimates for a twisted flow also depend on its parameters. In Section 5.2 of [ v2, p. 18 , Dang26 ] the twist is fixed to be $\operatorname {Ric}(\omega _ X)$, for the reference metric $\omega _ X$ of that paper, and Theorem 5.7, p. 21, there allows the constants to depend on the endpoint of a finite time interval. The flat flows of example 12.34.14 show why the formulation for arbitrary twists in Theorem C of the introduction of that paper needs further control: a fixed initial density and a fixed lifetime do not bound the diameter independently of the twist, and a single positive twist can give unbounded diameter over an infinite lifetime. The conjecture on balanced and pluriclosed metrics referred to in section 24.4 is stated by Fino and Vezzoni [ Conjecture 1.1 , FV26 ] ; there the balanced and the pluriclosed metric are allowed to be different. That a compact manifold in Fujiki's class admitting a pluriclosed metric is Kähler is Chiose's [ Theorem 0.2 in the author manuscript , Chiose14 ] ; the locator refers to Chiose's manuscript version of that paper. The case of parallel torsion, theorem 24.4.20 , is a theorem of Chen and Zheng [ v1, Theorem 1.2, pp. 2 and 8 , CZParallel26 ] . Their projection by integration of parallel forms and their description of the holonomy are [ v1, Lemmas 3.1–3.2 and Propositions 3.3–3.5, pp. 3–6 , CZParallel26 ] ; lemma 24.4.17 proves both descriptions again in a form that keeps track of positivity and of commutation with the differential. The slice of fixed trace and the maximum of the volume are [ v1, Propositions 4.2 and 4.5, Lemmas 4.3–4.4, pp. 7–8 , CZParallel26 ] . The inverse of the positive cofactor map proves the step of taking roots directly, and lemma 24.4.19 proves, by linear algebra of primitive forms, that a Hermitian form which is both balanced and pluriclosed is closed. The additional obstruction of Zhao and Zheng for non-balanced metrics with Bismut-parallel torsion, used in their Corollary 1.3, is a separate ingredient. The conjectured long-time existence and convergence of the pluriclosed flow on balanced manifolds with $c_1(X)=0$ is [ Conjecture 1.2 , FV26 ] . The discussion in section 24.4 distinguishes a conserved balanced trace from a pointwise bound for the metric. The persistence of pluriclosed metrics under deformations, theorem 24.4.28 , which assumes that the Aeppli number $h_ A^{1,1}$ is constant, is Cavalcanti's [ v5, Theorem 8.11, Section 8.3, pp. 41–42 , CavSKT13 ] . The fourth-order Aeppli Laplacian and the realization of Aeppli classes by harmonic forms used in lemma 24.4.24 are due to Schweitzer [ v1, Section 2.c, pp. 9–10 , SchAeppli07 ] , who constructs the elliptic symbol in Section 2.b, pp. 7–8. The proof given here writes the projection onto $\partial \bar\partial $-closed forms explicitly and obtains its smooth dependence on the parameter from the resolvent and the constancy of the dimension of the kernel. It applies to any finite-dimensional smooth parameter space and keeps the prescribed initial metric. This is also the analytic input stated in [ v1, Theorem 2.1, p. 7 , BarDef26 ] ; Barbaro's construction of deformations of Lie groups there requires a separate argument with transverse cohomology.

title: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
search_title: Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: To solve an equation on a singular complex space, we pass to a resolution and then descend the solution. The pullback background can degenerate along exceptional fibers, and removing a logarithmic pole can leave a residual that does not descend. The examples in this appendix address these two difficulties directly. Except in the local toric calculations of 9.11.10 , 9.11.16 , $X$ denotes a reduced irreducible compact complex space of pure dimension $n\geq 1$ that is unibranch : its germ at every point is irreducible, or equivalently, its normalization is a homeomorphism. We write $X_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $X_{\mathrm{sing}}$ for the regular and singular loci. Every point of $X$ has a neighborhood that embeds as a closed analytic subset of an open set in some $\mathbb C^ N$. Smooth functions and forms on $X$ are defined through such local embeddings: they are locally restrictions of smooth functions and forms on the ambient open sets. A Hermitian form on $X$ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form that is locally the restriction of a smooth strictly positive ambient $(1,1)$-form. Fix a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$. A resolution of $X$ is a proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map $\pi :Y\to X$ from a compact complex manifold $Y$; on $Y$ the pullback $\pi ^*\theta $ is an ordinary smooth form, to which the theory of the main text applies. In the last three sections, $X$ is a specific space of this kind. The basic tool is descent through a resolution. The pullback $\pi ^*\theta $ has no component along the fibers of $\pi $, so the maximum principle on the connected compact fibers shows that every $\pi ^*\theta $-plurisubharmonic function on $Y$ is constant on fibers and descends to $X$. This correspondence preserves envelopes and convergence. Exceptional sets carry no non-pluripolar mass, so the extended Monge–Ampère measure defined through a resolution does not depend on the resolution. On a projective cone, a logarithmic pole at the vertex becomes a divisor on the incidence resolution, and removing it leaves a strictly positive residual background. This gives uniqueness in the prescribed ordinary class, including for certain nonclosed backgrounds. The bounded equation on the cone uses closedness and an energy identity. The full logarithmic potential descends even when its smooth residual varies along the contracted divisor. On a curve whose normalization is a torus, a periodic Green function gives a separate construction. It allows the pulled-back background to vanish at singular points, and it treats every potential in a fixed ordinary type with finitely many logarithmic poles. A projective cusp shows that the residual can be continuous even though the density on the curve is unbounded. On products of a cuspidal curve with elliptic curves, a smooth potential repairs the degenerate background of the normalization, and two torsion identities fix the masses of all bounded potentials. For data close to the reference density, a positive solution gives uniqueness in the whole bounded class by a $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ energy comparison, even though the background is nonclosed. We use three facts about unibranch spaces. Resolutions and common smooth refinements of two resolutions exist, and a proper bimeromorphic map to a unibranch space has connected fibers Theorem 9.10.9 , Theorem 9.10.8 (Hironaka's Chow lemma) , Theorem 9.10.5 (Zariski's main theorem) . The Fornaess–Narasimhan criterion identifies plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ as the upper semicontinuous functions that are subharmonic on holomorphic disks Theorem 9.10.13 (Fornaess–Narasimhan) . The ramified disk lift used below is the argument in the proof of Theorem 9.10.14 (Grauert–Remmert) .

title: 9.11.1 Potentials and disk tests
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Since $X$ may be singular, $\theta $-plurisubharmonicity is defined by testing along holomorphic disks. Let $\Delta \subset \mathbb C$ be the unit disk. For a holomorphic map $f:\Delta \to X$, the pullback $f^*\theta $ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $\Delta $ and therefore has smooth local potentials. Disk tests thus express the background inequality even when $\theta $ has no local potential on $X$. Definition 9.11.2 . 76A75EB639CB An upper semicontinuous function $u:X\to [-\infty ,+\infty )$, not identically $-\infty $ on any nonempty open subset, is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic if it satisfies the following disk condition. For every holomorphic $f:\Delta \to X$, the function $u\circ f+a$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ wherever $a$ is a smooth local potential for $f^*\theta $. The set of these functions is denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Two choices of $a$ differ by a harmonic function, so the condition is independent of that choice. On every disk where $u\circ f\not\equiv -\infty $, it gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ f)+f^*\theta \geq 0$ in the sense of distributions. Lemma 9.11.3 . E7163CA56764 Every member of $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is locally the sum of a plurisubharmonic function on $X$ and a smooth function. If $X$ is smooth, this definition agrees with definition 5.22.1 . Proof. In a local embedding, choose an ambient smooth strictly plurisubharmonic function $r$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r\geq \theta $ on a smaller neighborhood. For a disk $f$ and a local potential $a$ of $f^*\theta $, the function $r\circ f-a$ is subharmonic. Hence $(u+r)\circ f$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. The Fornaess–Narasimhan criterion, together with the assumption that $u$ is not identically $-\infty $ on any open set, shows that $u+r$ is plurisubharmonic. The smooth case now follows from lemma 5.43.2 . $\square$

title: 9.11.4 Descent through a resolution
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Let $\pi :Y\to X$ be a resolution. Near a fiber of $\pi $, the background $\pi ^*\theta $ is dominated by the pullback of a local $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact form, so a local correction makes a $\pi ^*\theta $-plurisubharmonic function plurisubharmonic near the fiber. It is then constant on each compact irreducible component of the fiber, and connectedness of the fiber identifies these constants. Theorem 9.11.5 . F4C06D21AA94 Let $\pi :Y\to X$ be a resolution. Pullback $u\mapsto u\circ \pi $ is an order-preserving bijection \[  \pi ^*:\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\longrightarrow \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*\theta ).  \] It preserves suprema of individual functions, boundedness, and ordinary singularity comparisons. Proof. Pullback preserves the disk inequalities. Every nonempty open subset of $Y$ meets the locus where $\pi $ is biholomorphic, so a pullback is not identically $-\infty $ on any nonempty open set. Injectivity follows from surjectivity of $\pi $. For the converse, take $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*\theta )$. Near a fiber, choose the local correction $r$ on $X$ used above. The function $v+r\circ \pi $ is plurisubharmonic on the inverse image of that neighborhood, since \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v+r\circ \pi )\geq \pi ^*(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r-\theta )\geq 0.  \] Its restriction to each compact irreducible component of the fiber is constant, possibly $-\infty $, by the maximum principle on a resolution of that component. Connectedness of the fiber makes these constants equal: intersecting components have the same value, and the finite intersection graph of the components is connected. Since $r\circ \pi $ is constant on the fiber, so is $v$. Thus $v=u\circ \pi $ for a unique function $u$ on $X$. This function is upper semicontinuous: for each real $c$, the closed set $\{ v\geq c\} $ has closed image under the proper map $\pi $, and that image is $\{ u\geq c\} $. If $u$ were identically $-\infty $ on a nonempty open set, the same would hold for $v$ on its inverse image. Hence $u$ is not identically $-\infty $ on any nonempty open set. It remains to verify the disk condition for $u$ with the background $\theta $ itself. Let $f:\Delta \to X$ be a holomorphic disk with $u\circ f\not\equiv -\infty $. Near a given point of $\Delta $, take a curve in the fiber product $\Delta \times _ XY$ dominating the disk. Its normalization gives, after shrinking, a finite cover $\rho (t)=t^ k$ and a holomorphic lift $f':\Delta \to Y$ with $\pi \circ f'=f\circ \rho $. Choose a smooth local function $a$ on the original disk with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a=f^*\theta $. The function \[  (u\circ f+a)\circ \rho =v\circ f'+a\circ \rho  \] is subharmonic by lemma 5.43.2 . Subharmonicity descends through $\rho $ by the finite-disk argument following that lemma. Thus $u\circ f+a$ is subharmonic near every point, which proves that pullback is a bijection. Since $\pi $ is surjective, pullback preserves suprema, uniform bounds and inequalities up to additive constants; this proves the remaining assertions. $\square$

title: 9.11.6 Envelopes and normalized compactness
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Fix a resolution $\pi :Y\to X$. The envelopes of section 5.40 and definition 5.40.4 are defined on $X$ by the same formulas: for an obstacle $f:X\to [-\infty ,+\infty ]$, $P_\theta (f)$ is the upper semicontinuous regularization of the supremum of all $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\leq f$ pointwise, and $P_\theta [u]$ is defined as in definition 5.40.4 . In the next proposition we assume that the family of these competitors is nonempty and locally uniformly bounded above. The descent bijection identifies the competitors on $X$ and on $Y$; the remaining issue is whether upper semicontinuous regularization commutes with pullback. Proposition 9.11.7 . 622B386B559D For such an obstacle $f:X\to [-\infty ,+\infty ]$, the envelope $P_\theta (f)$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and \[  P_{\pi ^*\theta }(f\circ \pi )=P_\theta (f)\circ \pi .  \] The same identity holds for the ordinary envelope $P_\theta [u]$, for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Proof. The preceding theorem identifies the competitor families. Let $s$ be their pointwise supremum on $X$; its pullback is the pointwise supremum upstairs. The regularization of $s\circ \pi $ on $Y$ is $\pi ^*\theta $-plurisubharmonic and not identically $-\infty $, since there is a competitor below it. By the theorem, it descends to a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function $q$. Since $q\geq s$ and $q$ is upper semicontinuous, $q\geq s^*$. For the reverse inequality, fix $x\in X$ and $y\in \pi ^{-1}(x)$. For each neighborhood $U$ of $x$, the unregularized supremum upstairs is bounded by $\sup _ U s$ on the open neighborhood $\pi ^{-1}(U)$ of $y$. Therefore $q(x)\leq \sup _ U s$, and taking the infimum over $U$ gives $q(x)\leq s^*(x)$. This proves the identity and shows that $P_\theta (f)=s^*$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic. The proof for $P_\theta [u]$ is identical, because pullback preserves the ordinary singularity order together with its constants. $\square$ We give the normalized space $\{ u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):\sup _ Xu=0\} $ the $L^1$ topology of the pullbacks to $Y$. By theorem 5.25.2 and descent, it is compact. On a fixed resolution, different smooth positive volume forms give equivalent norms. Under a further modification, pullback is continuous by lemma 5.43.19 and bijective by descent, hence a homeomorphism between the normalized compact spaces. Since any two resolutions are dominated by a common one, the topology does not depend on the resolution; the norms on different models are not compared.

title: 9.11.8 Ideal envelopes defined on resolutions
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Multiplier ideals on smooth models give a singularity relation on $X$. Call two potentials $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ resolution-ideal equivalent if $u\circ \pi \sim _{\mathcal I}v\circ \pi $ on one resolution $\pi :Y\to X$ (the ideal type of section 5.33 ), that is, if $\mathcal I(k\, u\circ \pi )=\mathcal I(k\, v\circ \pi )$ for every real $k>0$. By lemma 5.43.24 , applied on a common refinement, this does not depend on the resolution. The ideal projection of theorem 18.4.2 then defines an envelope in this class. Proposition 9.11.9 . C43A6C429C4D For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, there is a unique potential $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}^{\mathrm{res}}$ on $X$ satisfying \[  P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}^{\mathrm{res}}\circ \pi =P_{\pi ^*\theta }[u\circ \pi ]_{\mathcal I}  \] on every resolution $\pi :Y\to X$, where the right-hand side is the multiplier-ideal envelope of definition 18.4.1 on $Y$. It preserves the resolution-ideal class, is idempotent, has supremum zero, and is independent of the resolution. Proof. For a fixed resolution, the right-hand side exists by theorem 18.4.2 and descends by theorem 9.11.5 . Under a further smooth modification, the competitor families of the ideal envelopes correspond by the descent theorem and lemma 5.43.24 , and the regularized suprema commute by the argument of proposition 9.11.7 . Thus two resolutions give the same pullback on a common refinement, and hence the same function on $X$. Idempotence, preservation of the class and the normalization follow from the corresponding assertions on $Y$ and surjectivity of $\pi $. $\square$ An intrinsic restricted ideal trace on a subspace contained in the singular locus would require a regularization compatible with restriction to that subspace; the resolution-ideal envelope provides neither the regularization nor the trace.

The resolution-ideal relation above uses smooth volume forms on smooth models. DA5FE7ECD89D The plurisubharmonic function \[  u=\max \{ \sqrt2\log |z_1|^2,\, 2\log |z_2|^2\}   \] on $X$ does not have analytic singularities at the origin. eq 0$, $z_3$ is a normal coordinate and $z_1=z_3^2/z_2$, so $\mathrm{d}V_ D$ is a smooth positive factor times $|z_3|^{-1}$ times smooth volume. This is locally integrable. It does not change the resolution-ideal equivalence used in proposition 9.11.9 . The next calculation expresses the exponent test for a general full-dimensional affine toric cone.

title: 9.11.16 Adapted monomial tests on affine toric spaces
search_title: Adapted monomial tests on affine toric spaces
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: The quotient calculation expresses integrability as a strict inequality on exponents. On an affine toric space the same inequality comes from the recession of a convex function, while the canonical bundle and boundary supply the translation of the exponent. This also applies to cones with more rays than their dimension. In this subsection let $N$ be a lattice of rank $n\geq 1$, let $M=\operatorname {Hom}(N,\mathbb Z)$, and let $\sigma \subset N_{\mathbb R}$ be a full-dimensional strongly convex rational polyhedral cone. Its dual cone is $\sigma ^\vee =\{ m:\langle m,v\rangle \geq 0\text{ for all }v\in \sigma \} $. The normal affine toric space \[  X_\sigma =\operatorname {Spec}\mathbb C[\sigma ^\vee \cap M]  \] is understood with its analytic structure. Its dense torus $T=\operatorname {Hom}(M,\mathbb C^*)$ has characters $\chi ^ m$, and its unique closed orbit is a vertex $o$. Choose nonzero generators $b_1,\ldots ,b_ s$ of the semigroup $\sigma ^\vee \cap M$; their characters embed $X_\sigma $ as a closed affine subset of $\mathbb C^ s$ and all vanish at $o$. For each ray $\rho $ of $\sigma $, write $v_\rho $ for its primitive lattice generator and $D_\rho $ for the corresponding prime divisor. Fix an effective rational boundary $D=\sum _\rho a_\rho D_\rho $ such that $K_{X_\sigma }+D$ is $\mathbb Q$-Cartier. With $K_{X_\sigma }=-\sum _\rho D_\rho $, this means that there is $w_ D\in M_{\mathbb Q}$ with A72FB1B5D26F 9.11.17 \begin{equation}  \langle w_ D,v_\rho \rangle =1-a_\rho \quad \text{for every }\rho . \end{equation} Take an integer $q>0$ with $qw_ D\in M$. For torus coordinates $t_1,\ldots ,t_ n$ determined by a basis of $M$, the meromorphic tensor \[  B_ D=\chi ^{qw_ D} \left(\frac{\mathrm dt_1}{t_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \frac{\mathrm dt_ n}{t_ n}\right)^{\! \otimes q}  \] generates $\omega _{X_\sigma }^{[q]}(qD)$. Indeed, its order along $D_\rho $ is $-qa_\rho $. The adapted volume $\mathrm dV_ D=|B_ D|^{2/q}$ is independent of this choice for local integrability, as in ( 9.11.11 ). We use the ideal $\mathcal I_ D^{\mathrm{ad}}(u)$ defined by the holomorphic-germ integral in ( 9.11.12 ) on this $X_\sigma $. Let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function invariant under the compact torus of coordinate rotations. The logarithmic map $\operatorname {Log}:T\to N_{\mathbb R}$ satisfies $\langle m,\operatorname {Log}t\rangle =\log |\chi ^ m(t)|$. There is a finite convex function $g$ on $N_{\mathbb R}$ with \[  u(t)=2g(\operatorname {Log}t).  \] To see convexity, pull $u/2$ back by the exponential covering of $T$. It is independent of the imaginary coordinates, so its distributional complex Hessian is the real Hessian of $g$ up to a positive constant. A nontrivial plurisubharmonic function of this form gives a finite convex function. The factor two matches the weight $\mathrm e^{-u}$. For a finite convex function $g$ write \[  (\operatorname {rec}g)(v)= \lim _{t\to \infty }\frac{g(x+tv)-g(x)}t.  \] The convex difference quotients increase to this limit in $\mathbb R\cup \{ +\infty \} $; the limit does not depend on the base point $x$. The latter fact follows by comparing $g(x+tv)$ with convex combinations of $g(t v/(1-\delta ))$ and $g(x/\delta )$, for $0<\delta <1$, and then reversing the translation. Define the Newton set 4B4F6518339A 9.11.18 \begin{equation}  P(u)=\left\{ \ell \in M_{\mathbb R}: \sup _{x\in -\sigma }\bigl (\langle \ell ,x\rangle -g(x)\bigr )<\infty \right\} . \end{equation} Only its interior will enter the integrability test; the set itself need not be closed. Lemma 9.11.19 . 5D5A847F99AC Let $C$ be a closed full-dimensional convex cone in a Euclidean space, let $g$ be finite and convex, and let $\ell $ be a linear form. Then \[  \int _ C\exp \bigl (2\langle \ell ,x\rangle -2g(x)\bigr )\, \mathrm dx<\infty \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \langle \ell ,v\rangle <(\operatorname {rec}g)(v) \quad (v\in C\setminus \{ 0\} ).  \] This condition is also equivalent to $\ell $ being an interior point of $\{ a:\sup _ C(\langle a,x\rangle -g(x))<\infty \} $. The integral has the same finiteness on every translate of $C$. Proof. Set $F=g-\ell $. Suppose its recession is positive on $C\setminus \{ 0\} $. Then $F(x)\geq \gamma |x|-A$ on $C$ for some $\gamma >0$ and $A$. Otherwise there are $x_ j\in C$ with $|x_ j|\to \infty $ and $F(x_ j)/|x_ j|\leq 1/j$. After taking a subsequence, $x_ j/|x_ j|\to v\in C$ with $|v|=1$. For fixed $t>0$, convexity gives \[  F\left(t\frac{x_ j}{|x_ j|}\right) \leq \left(1-\frac t{|x_ j|}\right)F(0) +\frac t{|x_ j|}F(x_ j).  \] Continuity gives $F(tv)\leq F(0)$ for every $t$, contradicting positive recession. A bound on the remaining compact set gives the asserted $A$. Exponential decay proves integrability. The same bound persists when $\ell $ is changed by a sufficiently small linear form, so $\ell $ lies in the stated interior. Conversely, if $(\operatorname {rec}F)(v)\leq 0$ for some nonzero $v\in C$, then $F(tv)\leq F(0)$ for $t\geq 0$. Choose a compact ball $K$ in the interior of $C$. On the half-tube $\{ tv+x/2:t\geq 1,\  x\in K\} $, convexity gives \[  F(tv+x/2)\leq \tfrac 12F(2tv)+\tfrac 12F(x).  \] Thus $\mathrm e^{-2F}$ has a positive lower bound on a set of infinite volume. If instead $\ell $ is in the stated interior, for each nonzero $v\in C$ one may perturb $\ell $ within that interior by a linear form positive on $v$. Dividing its defining upper bound along $tv$ by $t$ gives the strict recession inequality for $\ell $. Finally, translating $C$ replaces $g(x)$ by $g(x+b)$ and multiplies the exponential by a constant; recession is unchanged. $\square$ Theorem 9.11.20 . CD69C52538E4 For $m\in \sigma ^\vee \cap M$, the following are equivalent: \[  \chi ^ m\in \mathcal I_ D^{\mathrm{ad}}(u)_ o, \qquad \chi ^ m\in \Gamma (X_\sigma ,\mathcal I_ D^{\mathrm{ad}}(u)), \qquad m+w_ D\in \operatorname {int}P(u).  \] Equivalently, $\langle m+w_ D,v\rangle <(\operatorname {rec}g)(v)$ for every nonzero $v\in -\sigma $. Proof. On the torus, polar coordinates turn the weighted monomial integral into a positive constant times \[  \int _ Q\exp \bigl (2\langle m+w_ D,x\rangle -2g(x)\bigr )\, \mathrm dx,  \] where $Q$ is the logarithmic image of the domain. The omitted toric divisors have measure zero on the regular locus. A basis of neighborhoods of $o$ is given by $|\chi ^{b_ j}|<\epsilon $ for every $j$, with $0<\epsilon <1$. Their logarithmic domains satisfy 4CC45280AE88 9.11.21 \begin{equation}  -\sigma -b\  \subset  Q_\epsilon =\{ x:\langle b_ j,x\rangle <\log \epsilon \text{ for all }j\}  \  \subset \  -\sigma , \end{equation} for $b\in \operatorname {int}\sigma $ sufficiently far along an interior ray. Indeed, every $\langle b_ j,b\rangle $ is strictly positive, and the $b_ j$ generate the dual cone. The convex-cone lemma gives necessity and sufficiency at $o$, including divergence when a recession inequality is an equality. For a compact subset of $X_\sigma $, the embedding coordinates have absolute value at most some $R>1$. Its logarithmic image is contained in $\{ x:\langle b_ j,x\rangle \leq \log R\} $, which is contained in $b_ R-\sigma $ for a sufficiently large $b_ R\in \operatorname {int}\sigma $. Under the same strict condition the integral over this translated cone is finite. This proves local integrability everywhere. The converse follows by testing at $o$, and the interior formulation follows from the lemma. $\square$ Corollary 9.11.22 . E77092231FA9 Let $\mathfrak a=(\chi ^{a_1},\ldots ,\chi ^{a_ r})$ be a nonzero monomial ideal on $X_\sigma $, with $a_ j\in \sigma ^\vee \cap M$, and let $c>0$ be real. For the measurable weight \[  v=u-c\log \left(\sum _ j|\chi ^{a_ j}|^2\right),  \] a holomorphic character $\chi ^ m$ is locally integrable with weight $\mathrm e^{-v}\mathrm dV_ D$ at $o$, or everywhere on $X_\sigma $, exactly when \[  m+w_ D+ca_ j\in \operatorname {int}P(u) \quad \text{for every }j.  \] Values on the common zero set do not affect these integrals. Proof. For a finite sum and $c>0$, its $c$-th power is comparable to the sum of the $c$-th powers of its terms. Thus the integrand is comparable to \[  \sum _ j |\chi ^ m|^2|\chi ^{a_ j}|^{2c}\mathrm e^{-u}\, \mathrm dV_ D.  \] Each term gives the preceding logarithmic integral with exponent $m+w_ D+ca_ j$. The cone criterion applies to real exponents, so no rationality of $c$ is needed for this integrability assertion. $\square$ Proposition 9.11.23 . 511E6797B7CD Let $X=\{ xw=yz\} \subset \mathbb C^4$, with vertex $o$, let $\mathfrak m_ o=(x,y,z,w)$, and take zero boundary. For $\lambda >0$ put \[  u_\lambda =\lambda \log (|x|^2+|y|^2+|z|^2+|w|^2).  \] The adapted-volume ideal at the vertex is \[  \mathcal I_0^{\mathrm{ad}}(u_\lambda )_ o =\mathfrak m_ o^{\, \max \{ 0,\lfloor \lambda \rfloor -1\} } \mathcal O_{X,o}.  \] In particular, the constant germ is integrable exactly when $\lambda <2$. Proof. On the torus use $x,y,z$ as characters, so $w=yz/x$. The character lattice is $\mathbb Z^3$, with semigroup generators \[  (1,0,0),\quad (0,1,0),\quad (0,0,1),\quad (-1,1,1).  \] The dual cone has primitive rays $(0,1,0)$, $(0,0,1)$, $(1,1,0)$ and $(1,0,1)$. It is full-dimensional with four rays. The residue form $\Omega =\mathrm dx\wedge \mathrm dy\wedge \mathrm dz/x$ generates the canonical sheaf of this hypersurface; it equals $yz$ times the logarithmic torus form. Hence $w_0=(0,1,1)$, which pairs to one with each primitive ray. Write $d(m)=m_1+m_2+m_3$. Each semigroup generator has degree one. The logarithmic function $g$ differs by a bounded term from $\lambda $ times the maximum of the four linear forms given by those generators. Their convex hull is the section of $\sigma ^\vee $ by $d=1$, so \[  P(u_\lambda )=\{ \ell \in \sigma ^\vee :d(\ell )\geq \lambda \} .  \] Since $w_0\in \operatorname {int}\sigma ^\vee $ and $d(w_0)=2$, the character condition is $d(m)+2>\lambda $. The smallest allowed integer degree is $k=\max \{ 0,\lfloor \lambda \rfloor -1\} $. This also gives the ideal for whole holomorphic germs. Lift a germ to a convergent power series in $x,y,z,w$. On a smaller invariant neighborhood, angular Parseval and Tonelli force every nonzero character coefficient to satisfy the same test. All homogeneous terms of degree less than $k$ therefore vanish in the coordinate ring. They are multiples of the homogeneous relation $xw-yz$, and subtracting those finitely many terms leaves a lift of order at least $k$. Thus the germ belongs to $\mathfrak m_ o^ k$. Conversely, every degree-$k$ monomial is integrable by the character test, and bounded holomorphic coefficient germs preserve integrability. This proves the identity and its strict endpoint. $\square$ These ideals use the adapted canonical volume, whereas the resolution-ideal equivalence above uses smooth volumes on the models. Return now to the compact unibranch space and background fixed at the beginning of the appendix.

title: Corollary 9.11.22
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Corollary 9.11.22 . E77092231FA9 Let $\mathfrak a=(\chi ^{a_1},\ldots ,\chi ^{a_ r})$ be a nonzero monomial ideal on $X_\sigma $, with $a_ j\in \sigma ^\vee \cap M$, and let $c>0$ be real. For the measurable weight \[  v=u-c\log \left(\sum _ j|\chi ^{a_ j}|^2\right),  \] a holomorphic character $\chi ^ m$ is locally integrable with weight $\mathrm e^{-v}\mathrm dV_ D$ at $o$, or everywhere on $X_\sigma $, exactly when \[  m+w_ D+ca_ j\in \operatorname {int}P(u) \quad \text{for every }j.  \] Values on the common zero set do not affect these integrals. Proof. For a finite sum and $c>0$, its $c$-th power is comparable to the sum of the $c$-th powers of its terms. Thus the integrand is comparable to \[  \sum _ j |\chi ^ m|^2|\chi ^{a_ j}|^{2c}\mathrm e^{-u}\, \mathrm dV_ D.  \] Each term gives the preceding logarithmic integral with exponent $m+w_ D+ca_ j$. The cone criterion applies to real exponents, so no rationality of $c$ is needed for this integrability assertion. $\square$

title: Proposition 9.11.23
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Proposition 9.11.23 . 511E6797B7CD Let $X=\{ xw=yz\} \subset \mathbb C^4$, with vertex $o$, let $\mathfrak m_ o=(x,y,z,w)$, and take zero boundary. For $\lambda >0$ put \[  u_\lambda =\lambda \log (|x|^2+|y|^2+|z|^2+|w|^2).  \] The adapted-volume ideal at the vertex is \[  \mathcal I_0^{\mathrm{ad}}(u_\lambda )_ o =\mathfrak m_ o^{\, \max \{ 0,\lfloor \lambda \rfloor -1\} } \mathcal O_{X,o}.  \] In particular, the constant germ is integrable exactly when $\lambda <2$. Proof. On the torus use $x,y,z$ as characters, so $w=yz/x$. The character lattice is $\mathbb Z^3$, with semigroup generators \[  (1,0,0),\quad (0,1,0),\quad (0,0,1),\quad (-1,1,1).  \] The dual cone has primitive rays $(0,1,0)$, $(0,0,1)$, $(1,1,0)$ and $(1,0,1)$. It is full-dimensional with four rays. The residue form $\Omega =\mathrm dx\wedge \mathrm dy\wedge \mathrm dz/x$ generates the canonical sheaf of this hypersurface; it equals $yz$ times the logarithmic torus form. Hence $w_0=(0,1,1)$, which pairs to one with each primitive ray. Write $d(m)=m_1+m_2+m_3$. Each semigroup generator has degree one. The logarithmic function $g$ differs by a bounded term from $\lambda $ times the maximum of the four linear forms given by those generators. Their convex hull is the section of $\sigma ^\vee $ by $d=1$, so \[  P(u_\lambda )=\{ \ell \in \sigma ^\vee :d(\ell )\geq \lambda \} .  \] Since $w_0\in \operatorname {int}\sigma ^\vee $ and $d(w_0)=2$, the character condition is $d(m)+2>\lambda $. The smallest allowed integer degree is $k=\max \{ 0,\lfloor \lambda \rfloor -1\} $. This also gives the ideal for whole holomorphic germs. Lift a germ to a convergent power series in $x,y,z,w$. On a smaller invariant neighborhood, angular Parseval and Tonelli force every nonzero character coefficient to satisfy the same test. All homogeneous terms of degree less than $k$ therefore vanish in the coordinate ring. They are multiples of the homogeneous relation $xw-yz$, and subtracting those finitely many terms leaves a lift of order at least $k$. Thus the germ belongs to $\mathfrak m_ o^ k$. Conversely, every degree-$k$ monomial is integrable by the character test, and bounded holomorphic coefficient germs preserve integrability. This proves the identity and its strict endpoint. $\square$

title: 9.11.24 Extended measures and finite damping
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text: Choose a resolution $\pi :Y\to X$. Two resolutions are isomorphic over the complement of a proper analytic subset of $X$, and their extended measures agree there. Since these measures do not charge pluripolar sets, the omitted analytic sets do not affect the comparison, even when the total mass is infinite. For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ define 96D4B9F40B0A 9.11.25 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta }(u) =\pi _*\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{Y,\pi ^*\theta }(u\circ \pi ), \end{equation} where $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{Y,\pi ^*\theta }$ is the extended measure of theorem 13.14.3 on $Y$. Theorem 9.11.26 . D12D6E199E87 The right-hand side of ( 9.11.25 ) is the same for every resolution, including resolutions that modify regular points. It is a positive $\sigma $-finite Borel measure, gives zero mass to $X_{\mathrm{sing}}$ and to locally pluripolar sets, and may have infinite total mass; for bounded $u$ it is finite. Put $r_ n=\max (n-2,0)$. There are finite constants $C$ and, for each $q>r_ n$, $C_ q$, depending only on the fixed background data and, for $C_ q$, on $q$, such that for every nonpositive $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and every $p>0$, \[  \int _ X\mathrm{e}^{pu}\, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta }(u) \leq C(1+p^{-1})^{r_ n},\qquad \int _ X(1-u)^{-q}\, \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta }(u) \leq C_ q.  \] The constants may be obtained on any one fixed resolution. Proof. Given two resolutions, choose a proper analytic subset $S\subset X$ containing $X_{\mathrm{sing}}$ and the images of both exceptional sets. Each map is an isomorphism over $X\setminus S$, and there the two measures are given by the same bounded local products, followed by truncation and exhaustion. On each resolution, the inverse image of $S$ is a proper analytic subset and has zero extended mass by theorem 13.14.3 . Hence both pushforwards give $S$ zero mass. This proves independence, including for resolutions whose exceptional sets lie over regular points. Positivity follows from positivity on $Y$. On $X\setminus S$ either resolution is a Borel isomorphism, so a countable exhaustion of $Y$ by sets of finite measure pushes forward to one on $X$; adjoining the null set $S$ proves $\sigma $-finiteness. A locally pluripolar subset of $X$ pulls back to a pluripolar set off the exceptional locus, and the exceptional locus itself has zero mass. This gives the asserted vanishing. If $u$ is bounded, its pullback is bounded on the compact manifold $Y$, and local bounded-product estimates give finite total mass. For general nonpositive $u$, apply theorem 13.15.23 on $Y$ to the smooth background $\pi ^*\theta $. Pushforward and the identity $u\circ \pi $ identify the weighted integrals exactly, and the constants come from $\pi ^*\theta $ and a Hermitian metric on $Y$. $\square$ We define convergence in capacity on $X$ as convergence in capacity of the pullbacks to a resolution, using a smooth Hermitian metric there. The local capacity comparison of section 5.29 makes the metric immaterial, and lemma 5.43.20 , applied on a common resolution, makes the choice of resolution immaterial. By theorem 13.15.23 and proper pushforward, both damped measures in the theorem depend weakly continuously on nonpositive potentials for this convergence in capacity. For nonpositive potentials $u_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ converging in capacity, the undamped measures $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta }(u_ j)$ converge weakly if, in addition, their total masses are uniformly bounded and their masses on $\{ u_ j<-T\} $ tend to zero uniformly in $j$ as $T\to \infty $. Pullback preserves these mass and sublevel conditions. General equations on singular spaces require estimates for the degeneracy of the pulled-back background and of the density; see 24.11.1 . For the cone geometry below, a radial construction gives solutions in a prescribed logarithmic class and in the bounded class of a closed background.

title: 9.11.27 Equations on projective cones
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces
text:
The residual construction of section 15.22 has a counterpart on a projective cone, which is a singular space. A logarithmic pole at the vertex becomes a divisor on the incidence resolution, and removing it leaves a positive residual background. The radial equation below determines both the solution and its normalization scalar. Uniqueness among bounded residuals holds because the lifted density is smooth and its positive locus is connected and dense, even though the density vanishes on the exceptional section. Let $B\subset \mathbb P^ N$ be a smooth connected, linearly nondegenerate, projectively normal variety of dimension $n-1$, where $N\geq n\geq 2$. Let $X\subset \mathbb P^{N+1}$ be its projective cone, with vertex $p=[0:\cdots :0:1]$, and let $	heta _0=\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}|_ X$ be the restriction of the Fubini–Study form of $\mathbb P^{N+1}$. Write the ambient homogeneous coordinates as $[Z:W]$, with $Z=(Z_0,\ldots ,Z_ N)$. The incidence resolution $\pi :Y	o X$ is a smooth $\mathbb P^1$-bundle $f:Y	o B$; its section $E=\pi ^{-1}(p)$ is contracted, and $\pi $ is an isomorphism off $E$. These cones are reduced, irreducible, compact and normal, hence unibranch, and their vertices are singular. Indeed, the homogeneous coordinate ring of $B$ is normal by projective normality. Adjoining $W$ preserves normality, and so do the degree-zero projective charts. Algebraic normality passes to the associated analytic space by the algebraic–analytic normality theorem. Smoothness and connectedness of $B$ give irreducibility. In the chart $W=1$, the ideal of the affine cone has no linear terms, by linear nondegeneracy. Its tangent space at the origin therefore has dimension $N+1>n$, so $p$ is singular. The incidence construction is the bundle of lines in $\mathcal O_ B\oplus \mathcal O_ B(-1)$ and has the stated contraction and isomorphism properties. Write \[   egin{gathered} \omega _ B=\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}|_ B,\qquad  eta =\pi ^*	heta _0,\qquad \sigma =f^*\omega _ B,\ d=\int _ B\omega _ B^{n-1},\qquad x= rac{\| Z\| ^2}{\| Z\| ^2+|W|^2}. \end{gathered}  \] The same symbol $x$ denotes its pullback to $Y$. Choose $\Psi \in C^\infty (\mathbb P^ N,\mathbb R)$ with $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi >0$ and $k\in C^\infty ([0,1])$ with $k>0$. text:
The logarithmic pole supplies the tangential positivity that $ eta $ lacks along $E$. Fix $0<a<1$ and put $\varphi =a\log x$, with value $-\infty $ at $p$. Set 593FB9025947 9.11.31  egin{equation}   egin{gathered}  eta _ a=(1-a) eta +a\sigma ,\qquad V=d(1-a^ n),\qquad c_ a=V/M,\ P_ a(s)=\left(a^ n+c_ an\int _0^ s k(r)r^{n-1}\, \mathrm{d} right)^{1/n},\ Q_ a'(s)= rac{P_ a(s)-a-(1-a)s}{s(1-s)},\qquad Q_ a(1)=0,\ q_ a=a\psi +(1-a)\ell +Q_ a(s),\qquad A_ a= eta _ a+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_ a. \end{gathered} \end{equation} The singularities of $Q_ a'$ at $s=0$ and $s=1$ are removable. As the proof below shows, the form $ eta _ a$ is strictly positive everywhere, whereas $A_ a$ is semipositive and strictly positive off $E$. Off $E$, we may therefore view $A_ a$ as a positive form on $X\setminus \{ p\} $. Choose a relatively compact coordinate ball $O\subset X\setminus \{ p\} $ and a smooth compactly supported endomorphism $H$ of $T^{1,0}O$ that is self-adjoint and trace-free with respect to $A_ a$. For tangent vectors $v,w$ of type $(1,0)$ at the same point of $O$, define 1F428FF466CA 9.11.32  egin{equation}  A_ H(v, ar w)=A_ a(\exp (H)v, ar w),\qquad \eta _ H=A_ H-A_ a,\qquad 	heta _ H=	heta _0+\eta _ H, \end{equation} where $\eta _ H$ is extended by zero. We call $H$ admissible if 03EEDEF4E91B 9.11.33  egin{equation}  	heta _ H>0,\qquad  eta _{a,H}:= eta _ a+\pi ^*\eta _ H>0. \end{equation} These are explicit open conditions on the prescribed data, and every sufficiently small $H$ satisfies them. Theorem 9.11.34 . 3DAEEE3C82F5 Let $H$ be admissible, and let \[  \mathcal C_{a,H}=\{ w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ H):\  \varphi -C\leq w\leq \varphi +C	ext{ for some }C<\infty \}   \] be the ordinary class of $\varphi $. There is a unique pair $(c,u)$, with $c>0$ and $u\in \mathcal C_{a,H}$ normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$, such that \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,	heta _ H}(u)=c\mu .  \] It is given by $c=c_ a$ and \[  u\circ \pi =\varphi \circ \pi +q_ a-K,\qquad K=\sup _ Y(\varphi \circ \pi +q_ a).  \] Every member of the class has finite extended mass. The solution has mass $V$ and is the same for every admissible $H$. For $H=0$, every member of the class has mass $V$. The solution is continuous with values in $[-\infty ,+\infty )$, is smooth off $p$, and tends uniformly to $-\infty $ at $p$. Its smooth residual $q_ a-K$ on $Y$ satisfies \[  (q_ a-K)|_ E=a\psi +Q_ a(0)-K.  \] If $\psi $ is nonconstant, this residual is not the pullback of any function on $X$. There are arbitrarily small admissible $H$ for which $	heta _ H$ is not closed. text: Without a logarithmic pole, the residual background is $\beta $, which degenerates along $E$. The radial construction still gives a bounded solution, and closedness of $\beta $ gives an energy argument for its uniqueness. Put EFA25DCE0A09 9.11.42 \begin{equation}  \begin{gathered} c_ b=\frac dM=\frac1{nI},\qquad R(s)=\left(c_ bn\int _0^1 k(sr)r^{n-1}\, \mathrm{d} r\right)^{1/n},\\ Q'(s)=\frac{R(s)-1}{1-s},\qquad Q(1)=0. \end{gathered} \end{equation} Here $R$ is smooth and positive, $R(1)=1$, and $Q$ is smooth at both endpoints. Theorem 9.11.43 . 4CE6B71B5B25 For the same cone and prescribed measure, there is a unique pair $(c,u)$, with $c>0$ and $u$ a bounded $\theta _0$-plurisubharmonic function normalized by $\sup _ Xu=0$, such that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta _0}(u)=c\mu $. The scalar is $c_ b$. The smooth function $\ell +Q(s)$ on $Y$ is constant on $E$ and descends to a continuous function on $X$; its normalization with supremum zero is $u$. Every bounded $\theta _0$-plurisubharmonic function has mass $d$. Formula ( 9.11.35 ), with $\theta _0$ in place of $\theta _ H$, holds on every resolution and common refinement. If $\Psi =0$ and $k$ is nonconstant, or if $\psi $ is nonconstant, the solution is nonconstant. Proof. Set $P(s)=sR(s)$ with the data in ( 9.11.42 ). Since $R(1)=1$, $Q$ is smooth at $s=1$, and its derivative is also smooth at zero. Put $U=\ell +Q(s)$. It is smooth on $Y$ and equals $Q(0)$ on $E$. On $0<x<1$, a local potential for $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U$ is $F(\rho _\psi )$, where $F(r)=h(r)+Q(h'(r))$. Differentiation gives $F'=P(s)$ and $F''=c_ bk(s)s^ n(1-s)/P(s)^{n-1}$. At infinity the horizontal coefficient is one and the transverse coefficient is positive. Thus $A$ is semipositive on $Y$ and strictly positive on $Y\setminus E$. By theorem 9.11.5 , $U=u_0\circ \pi $ for some $u_0\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _0)$. The proper surjection $\pi $ is a quotient map, so continuity of $U$ makes $u_0$ continuous. Subtracting $K_ b=\sup _ Xu_0$ gives the required solution. Let $w$ be a bounded $\theta _0$-plurisubharmonic function. Its pullback $g=w\circ \pi $ is bounded and $\beta $-plurisubharmonic. Its bounded Monge–Ampère measure gives analytic sets zero mass and pushes forward to $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,\theta _0}(w)$. Integrating the bounded expansion and using that $\beta $ is closed gives $\int _ Y(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g)^ n=\int _ Y\beta ^ n=d$; this forces the scalar of any solution to be $c_ b=d/M$. The resolution identity follows from theorem 9.11.26 . Now suppose that $w$ solves the equation, and put $q=U-K_ b$, $D=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ and $v=g-q$. The bounded integration-by-parts calculus of section 5.27 gives \[  0=\int _ Yv(D^ n-A^ n)=-\sum _{j=0}^{n-1}\int _ Y\mathrm{d}v\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}v\wedge D^ j\wedge A^{n-1-j}.  \] Each integral in the sum is nonnegative, so all of them vanish; in particular, so does the one with the smooth factor $A^{n-1}$. In the weak-gradient interpretation, strict positivity of $A$ on each relatively compact chart of $Y\setminus E$ forces $\mathrm{d} v=0$ there. Since $Y\setminus E$ is connected, $v$ is constant almost everywhere on it. The divisor $E$ has volume zero, so lemma 5.24.3 gives equality everywhere on $Y$. Surjectivity of $\pi $ and the normalization give $w=u$ on $X$. If $\Psi =0$ and the solution is constant, then $U=Q(x)$ is constant, so $Q'=0$ and $R=1$. Differentiating ( 9.11.44 ) then gives $c_ bk=1$, so $k$ is constant. If $\psi $ is nonconstant, the restriction of $U$ to the infinity section is $\psi $, so the solution is nonconstant for every $k$. $\square$ Example 9.11.46 . 659B6A5D3749 Without the assumption $\Psi =0$, a nonconstant $k$ does not force a nonconstant solution. The normalized solution is zero, although $k$ is nonconstant.
