text: Let $X=\{ Z_0Z_1=Z_2^2\} \subset \mathbb P^3$. Its base conic is the quadratic Veronese image of $\mathbb P^1$, so $n=d=2$. Its homogeneous coordinate ring $\mathbb C[\xi ^2,\xi \eta ,\eta ^2]$ is the invariant ring of the sign involution acting on the normal polynomial ring $\mathbb C[\xi ,\eta ]$, and is therefore normal; thus the base is projectively normal. In the chart \[  \pi (z,t)=(t,tz^2,tz),\qquad S=1+|z|^2+|z|^4,\qquad L=1+|t|^2S,  \] one has $\beta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log L$. Differentiation gives \[  \det ((\log L)_{j\bar k})=\frac{|t|^2(SS_{z\bar z}-|S_ z|^2)}{L^3}=\frac{|t|^2(1+4|z|^2+|z|^4)}{L^3}.  \] Writing $\lambda _4$ for Euclidean volume, we obtain 6E82FAF4001B 9.11.48 \begin{equation}  \frac{\beta ^2}{2}=\frac{|t|^2(1+4|z|^2+|z|^4)}{\pi ^2(1+|t|^2(1+|z|^2+|z|^4))^3}\, \mathrm{d}\lambda _4. \end{equation} The transverse vanishing order on $E=\{ t=0\} $ is exactly two. For $\Psi =0$ and $k=1/2$, one has $I=1/4$ and $M=1$, so $\mu _0=\theta _0^2/2$, extended by zero at $p$, is a probability measure. The logarithmic scalar and the solution mass are $c_ a=2(1-a^2)$ for every admissible deformation, including the nonclosed ones. This exact normalization follows from the preservation of the determinant. For $\Psi =0$ and $k(s)=1+s$, one has $I=5/6$, $M=10/3$ and $c_ b=3/5$. Put $R(x)=\sqrt{(3+2x)/5}$ and $r_0=\sqrt{3/5}$. text:
On a curve the pulled-back background can be degenerate, but its total mass still determines the equation. A periodic Green function on the normalization compensates for the degeneracy. The normalization also gives direct control of descent, of the atoms at the poles and of continuity. Let $X$ be a connected compact reduced unibranch curve whose normalization is a torus: \[  \pi :E=\mathbb C/\Lambda \longrightarrow X,  \] a finite bijective holomorphic map, where $\Lambda \subset \mathbb C$ is a lattice. It is biholomorphic outside a finite set. Let $h$ be a Hermitian form on $X$ in the sense of the beginning of this appendix. In the flat coordinate $z=x+\mathrm iy$ on $E$, set \[  dA=dx\, dy,\qquad V=\int _ EdA,\qquad  eta _0=dA/V,\qquad  eta =\pi ^*h=b eta _0.  \] Here $b$ is smooth and nonnegative, positive over $X_{m reg}$, and may vanish at the other points. Put $H=\int _ E eta >0$. Every two-form on a curve is closed, and this is essential for the following construction. Lemma 9.11.51 . 99DF4FD89931 There is a real periodic distribution $G$ with mean zero, smooth off zero, such that E623581B83B2 9.11.52  egin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G=\delta _0- eta _0,\qquad G(z)=\log |z|^2+	ext{a smooth function near }0. \end{equation} For $r\in L^ p(E, eta _0)$, $p>1$, its convolution satisfies \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}} igl (G*(r eta _0) igr ) =\left(r-\int _ Er eta _0ight) eta _0.  \] The convolution is bounded and continuous, and it is smooth if $r$ is smooth. Proof. With the normalization of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ fixed in the Conventions, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=(\Delta v)/(4\pi )\, dA$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |z|^2=\delta _0$, as in lemma 5.37.18 . Cutting off this logarithm in a coordinate disk, with a cutoff equal to one near zero, gives a function $L$ on $E$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}L=\delta _0+q eta _0$, where $q$ is smooth and $\int _ Eq eta _0=-1$ by Stokes' theorem. Let $e_\xi $ be the characters of the torus, with $-\Delta e_\xi =\lambda _\xi e_\xi $. The nonconstant characters have $\lambda _\xi >0$, growing quadratically on the dual lattice. Define the correction $S$, of mean zero, by its Fourier coefficients \[  S_\xi = rac{4\pi }{V} rac{(q+1)_\xi }{\lambda _\xi } \quad (\xi 
e 0),\qquad S_0=0,  \] where $(q+1)_\xi $ is the Fourier coefficient of $q+1$. Integration by parts shows that these coefficients decay faster than any power of $\lambda _\xi $. Hence the series and all its derivatives converge uniformly, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S=-(q+1) eta _0$. Conjugate symmetry of the coefficients makes $S$ real. Subtracting the mean of $L+S$ from $L+S$ proves ( 9.11.52 ). In particular, $G$ belongs to $L^ r$ for every finite $r$. The convolution uses the group law and the Haar probability $ eta _0$. Write $K=G*(r eta _0)$. Testing against smooth functions and using Fubini's theorem proves its distributional equation. Smooth input gives smooth output by the same Fourier argument. For $p'=p/(p-1)$, Hölder's inequality gives \[   egin{aligned}  \| K\| _\infty & \leq \| G\| _{p'}\| r\| _ p,\  |K(z+s)-K(z)| & \leq \| r\| _ p\| G(\cdot +s)-G\| _{p'}. \end{aligned}  \] Approximating $G$ by smooth functions shows that translation is continuous in $L^{p'}$, and hence that $K$ is continuous. $\square$ Choose finitely many distinct points $q_1,\ldots ,q_ k\in E$ and weights $a_ j>0$, possibly none, with \[   egin{aligned}  A& =\sum _ j a_ j<H,&  M& =H-A,\  \Phi & =G*((H-b) eta _0),&  \Psi & =\Phi +\sum _ j a_ jG(\cdot -q_ j). \end{aligned}  \] The function $\Phi $ is smooth, and 0567315FF18B 9.11.53  egin{equation}   eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi =M eta _0+\sum _ j a_ j\delta _{q_ j}. \end{equation} Thus $\Psi $ is a $ eta $-plurisubharmonic function, not identically $-\infty $, whose logarithmic poles are exactly the points $q_ j$, with coefficients $a_ j$ measured on the normalization. The ordinary type of $\psi $ consists of the potentials $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ with \[  w\leq \psi +C,\qquad \psi \leq w+C  \] for a finite constant $C$, the inequalities being understood for extended real values. Theorem 9.11.54 . 2489A49CB212 Let $0\leq f\in L^ p(E, eta _0)$ for some finite $p>1$, with $F=\int _ Ef eta _0>0$, and set $
u =\pi _*(f eta _0)$. Every potential in the ordinary type of $\psi $ has extended non-pluripolar mass $M$. In this type there is a unique normalized solution of \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u)=c
u , \qquad \sup _ Xu=0, \qquad c= rac{H-A}{F}>0.  \] Every member of the type that solves $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(w)=c'
u $ for some constant $c'>0$, with no regularity assumed, has $c'=c$ and differs from the normalized solution by a constant. The solution is continuous with real values off its finite pole set, and continuous at the poles as a map into $\mathbb R\cup \{ -\infty \} $ with the order topology. Its residual relative to $\psi $ extends to a continuous real function on $X$. If there are no poles, the solution itself is continuous with real values everywhere. The type and the equation do not depend on the choice of a resolution or of a common refinement. The measure $
u $ is non-pluripolar. Proof. The supremum $S=\sup _ EU$ is finite, and we put $u=(U-S)\circ \pi ^{-1}$. Every holomorphic disk $g:\Delta 	o X$ lifts holomorphically to $\widetilde g=\pi ^{-1}\circ g$. Indeed, for a nonconstant disk the inverse image of the finite singular set is discrete, and off this set the lift is holomorphic. Since $\pi ^{-1}$ is a homeomorphism, $\widetilde g$ is continuous on the whole disk. Near an omitted point its image therefore stays in a bounded coordinate neighborhood in $E$, and the removable singularity theorem in one variable extends it holomorphically. A constant disk lifts to a constant map, and a nonconstant disk cannot have image in a finite set. Choose a smooth local primitive $\eta $ of $ eta $ near the lifted image, that is, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\eta = eta $. Then $\eta \circ \widetilde g$ is a primitive of $g^*h$, and \[  u\circ g+\eta \circ \widetilde g=(U-S+\eta )\circ \widetilde g  \] is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. That the composition is subharmonic follows from decreasing smooth local regularizations and the holomorphic chain rule for the Laplacian. This follows from the planar atom identity of lemma 5.37.18 . Explicitly, choose a smooth local primitive $\eta $ of $ eta $ near $q_ j$, and let $m(r)$ be the circular mean of $W+\eta $ around $q_ j$. If $	au =T_ W(\{ q_ j\} )$, integration gives $m(r)/\log r^2	o 	au $, while the bounded logarithmic remainder gives the limit $a_ j$. Hence the non-pluripolar product of $W$, defined in dimension one by truncation, is \[  \langle  eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}Wangle =\mathbf1_{E\setminus Q}T_ W.  \] Indeed, on each relatively compact set avoiding $Q$, a sufficiently low truncation equals $W$, and the indicator removes the poles. Its mass is $H-A=M$ for every member of the type. For ( 9.11.55 ), removing the atoms leaves $cf eta _0$. The definition ( 9.11.25 ) gives the asserted equation on $X$. A locally pluripolar set pulls back to a set on which some quasi-subharmonic function, not identically $-\infty $, equals $-\infty $; such sets have zero flat area. Hence $
u $ is non-pluripolar. Suppose that $w$ solves the equation with a constant $c'>0$. Comparing total masses gives $c'F=M$, so $c'=c$. Since $\pi $ is a Borel homeomorphism and the atoms are fixed, $T_ W=T_ U$. Thus $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(W-U)=0$, where $W-U$ is an integrable function. Every nonconstant Fourier coefficient of $W-U$ vanishes, so the difference is constant almost everywhere. Subharmonic functions are determined by their averages over shrinking disks, so the values of $W$ and $U$ differ by the same constant everywhere, and the same holds on $X$. This includes members of the type with no regularity assumed. Finally, a resolution $ho :Y	o X$ factors through $E$ by the disk-lifting argument. The resulting proper holomorphic map $Y	o E$ has generic degree one. For smooth compact curves, the multiplicities in a fiber sum to the degree, so every fiber is a single point of multiplicity one, and the map is biholomorphic. The same holds for every common refinement, which proves the independence assertion directly. $\square$ The integrability hypothesis on $f$ refers to flat area on $E$. On $X_{m reg}$, the density of $
u $ with respect to $h$ is $(f/b)\circ \pi ^{-1}$; both measures give the finite singular set zero mass. No positive lower bound for $b$ and no bound for the density on $X$ is required.

text:
The following example has a normalization of genus one and a singularity that is not normal. Its background and its equation can both be computed explicitly. Example 9.11.57 . 77EE41C1372C There is a projective unibranch curve with one ordinary cusp, normalized by $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z)$, for which the restricted Fubini–Study background has mass $H=6$. For the reference with one pole of weight one at the preimage of the cusp, every potential of its ordinary type has mass five. With \[  f(z)=1+	frac 12\cos (2\pi \operatorname {Re}z),\qquad 
u =\pi _*(f eta _0),  \] the normalized equation has $c=5$. Its residual is continuous on the curve, although the density on the regular locus with respect to the background is unbounded at the cusp. That density belongs to $L^ r(X,h)$ exactly for $1\leq r<2$. Proof. For the square lattice define \[  x(z)=z^{-2}+\sum _{\substack {\lambda \in \mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z\ \lambda 
e 0}}  igl ((z-\lambda )^{-2}-\lambda ^{-2} igr ), \qquad y=x'.  \] The summands are $O(|\lambda |^{-3})$ on compact sets away from the lattice, so the series converges normally. Pairing opposite lattice points shows that $x$ is even. The differentiated series is absolutely and normally convergent, and reindexing shows that $y$ is periodic. Thus $x(z+\omega )-x(z)$ is constant for $\omega =1,\mathrm i$; evaluating at $-\omega /2$ and using evenness shows that this constant is zero. Both functions are meromorphic on $E$, with their only poles at zero and expansions \[  x=z^{-2}+a_2z^2+a_4z^4+\cdots , \qquad y=-2z^{-3}+2a_2z+4a_4z^3+\cdots .  \] Cancelling the Laurent expansions leaves an elliptic function with no poles and zero constant term, which vanishes by the maximum principle. This gives E7FF7E63C71E 9.11.58  egin{equation}  y^2=4x^3-g_2x-g_3, \qquad g_2=20a_2,\quad g_3=28a_4. \end{equation} The argument principle on a translated fundamental parallelogram shows that $x-c$ has two zeros, counted with multiplicity, for every finite $c$. Its fibers are therefore of the form $\{ z,-z\} $. If $y(z)=0$, the local multiplicity is at least two. Distinct points $z,-z$ would then give at least four zeros, so $z=-z$ on $E$, the multiplicity is exactly two, and $x''(z)
e 0$. Since $y$ is odd, the map $(x,y)$ is injective and immersive away from zero: use $dx$ where $y
e 0$, and $dy=x''dz$ otherwise. Define \[  \pi (z)=[1:x:y:x^2:x^3],\qquad \pi (0)=[0:0:0:0:1].  \] In the last affine chart its holomorphic coordinates are \[  [s^3:s^2:t:s:1],\qquad s=1/x=z^2+O(z^6),\qquad t=y/x^3=-2z^3+O(z^7).  \] Equation ( 9.11.58 ) becomes \[  t^2=s^3(4-g_2s^2-g_3s^3).  \] Dividing $t$ by an analytic square root of the nonvanishing factor gives the ordinary cusp $t'^2=s^3$. Choose the local parameter $\zeta $ so that $s=\zeta ^2$ and $t'=\zeta ^3$. The local ring of the cusp is $\mathbb C\{ \zeta ^2,\zeta ^3\} $, with normalization $\mathbb C\{ \zeta \} $. To see this directly, note that division by $t'^2-s^3$ writes every germ as $A(s)+t'B(s)$, and the even and odd parts identify the image ring. Its fraction field contains $\zeta $, which is integral since $\zeta ^2=s$, and the larger ring is a finite module generated by $1$ and $\zeta $. An integral meromorphic germ cannot have negative order: in a monic equation, its highest power would have strictly smallest order. Hence $\mathbb C\{ \zeta \} $ is the full integral closure. The image is the reduced projective locus \[   egin{aligned}  Z_1^2& =Z_0Z_3,&  Z_1Z_3& =Z_0Z_4,\  Z_3^2& =Z_1Z_4,&  Z_2^2& =4Z_0Z_4-g_2Z_0Z_1-g_3Z_0^2. \end{aligned}  \] On $Z_0
e 0$ these equations describe the graph of the affine cubic, and since the fibers of $x$ have degree two, both square-root values of $y$ occur. On $Z_0=0$ they force $Z_1=Z_3=Z_2=0$, leaving only $\pi (0)$. In the last chart they give exactly the cusp displayed above. The finite local module at the cusp and the biholomorphic charts elsewhere show that $\pi $ is finite. Hence $\pi $ is the bijective normalization of a connected curve that is smooth away from this one cusp. For the restricted Fubini–Study form, $ eta =b eta _0$ is positive away from zero and \[  C_1|z|^2\leq b(z)\leq C_2|z|^2  \] near zero. The hypothesis $p>1$ in theorem 9.11.54 guarantees that the Green correction is bounded and continuous. For merely integrable densities, the solution can leave the ordinary type. u _\gamma =\pi _*(f_\gamma  eta _0).  \] The local integral of $f_\gamma $ is finite exactly for $\gamma >1$. For every such $\gamma $, this density lies outside $L^ p(E, eta _0)$ for every $p>1$. Since $f_\gamma  eta _0$ is absolutely continuous on $E$, the measure $
u _\gamma $ is non-pluripolar by the pullback argument in the proof of theorem 9.11.54 . Theorem 9.11.60 . E80960D59FB4 For this family, the equation $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{X,h}(u)=c
u _\gamma $ with some constant $c>0$ has a solution in the ordinary type of $\psi $ if and only if $\gamma >2$. u _\gamma  \] with non-pluripolar mass $M$, whose pullback to $E$ has the same multiplier ideals as $\Psi $ at every positive weight. text:
On a cuspidal curve, the pullback of a Hermitian form to the normalization degenerates at the preimage of the cusp, but adding a smooth potential turns it into a positive form. On the products below we perturb the background by a nonclosed form all of whose powers are $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed. This fixes the mass of every bounded potential and gives an energy comparison, although the background is not closed. A perturbative solution near a constant-coefficient form then provides a positive solution against which every bounded solution can be compared. Fix $n\geq 2$. For $j=1,\ldots ,n$, let $E_ j=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z)$ with coordinate $z_ j$, and put $\kappa _ j= rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j$. Replace a neighborhood of a point $p\in E_1$ by the cusp with normalization $z\mapsto (z^2,z^3)$; equivalently, the holomorphic functions at the marked point are the functions on $E_1$ whose first derivative vanishes there. Denote the resulting compact curve by $C$ and its cusp by $q$. Put \[  X=C	imes E_2	imes \cdots 	imes E_ n,\qquad Y=E_1	imes \cdots 	imes E_ n.  \] The normalization $\pi :Y	o X$ is finite and bijective, hence a homeomorphism, and has generic degree one. The space $X$ is reduced, irreducible and unibranch, and its singular locus is $\{ q\} 	imes E_2	imes \cdots 	imes E_ n$. Choose a Hermitian form $h_ C$ on $C$ which near $q$ is the restriction of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(|x|^2+|y|^2)$, where $(x,y)=(z^2,z^3)$ are the coordinates of the cusp. Its pullback is $\eta =ho \kappa _1$, where $ho $ is smooth, positive off $p$, and B5525E6496F5 9.11.64  egin{equation}  ho =4|z|^2+9|z|^4\quad \hbox{near }p. \end{equation} Write $\lambda >0$ for the average of $ho $ on $E_1$, and set \[  h_0=h_ C+\sum _{j=2}^ n\kappa _ j,\quad H_0=\pi ^*h_0=\eta +\sum _{j=2}^ n\kappa _ j,\quad K_0=\lambda \kappa _1+\sum _{j=2}^ n\kappa _ j,\quad \Omega =K_0^ n.  \] Forms on the factors are pulled back to the products without change of notation. Proposition 9.11.65 . At a point where $\partial A=0$, $\partial  ar\partial A
e 0$ and $\partial B
e 0$, \[  \partial \alpha =-\partial A\wedge \partial  ar\partial B +\partial  ar\partial A\wedge \partial B
e 0.  \] Thus $\mathrm d\alpha 
e 0$. The form $\alpha $ vanishes near the singular locus. Its operator norm relative to $H_0$ is bounded on its support, and its norm relative to $K_0$ is bounded everywhere. Choose $|\varepsilon |$ so small that both norms, multiplied by $|\varepsilon |$, are less than $1/2$. This proves positivity of $h$ in the ambient sense, semipositivity of $H$, and the inequality $K_0+\varepsilon \pi ^*\alpha \geq 	frac 12K_0$. title: Corollary 9.11.72
section: 9.11 Potentials and equations on unibranch spaces

The torus $Y$ is Kähler, so it has bounded mass by lemma 19.9.12 . Since $k>0$, zero is an ordinary model for $k$: $P_ k[0]=0$. title: 1.1.2 Scope, attribution and conventions
text: Classical potential theory is developed through spherical means, harmonic measures, Green functions, capacities, sweeping, and Martin boundary representations. We work in real dimension $d\ge 2$, with ordinary Laplacian $\Delta $, unnormalized sphere area $s_{d-1}$, and unit ball volume $v_ d=s_{d-1}/d$. Put $\Phi (x)=|x|^{2-d}$ for $d\ge 3$ and $\Phi (x)=\log (1/|x|)$ for $d=2$. Then $-\Delta \Phi =c_ d\delta _0$, where $c_2=2\pi $ and $c_ d=(d-2)s_{d-1}$ for $d\ge 3$. Unless explicitly normalized otherwise, Green functions use this convention. Thus $G_{\rm Helms}=c_ dG_{\rm Foundations}$ and $C_{\rm Helms}=C_{\rm Foundations}/c_ d$. Superharmonic functions are lower semicontinuous, super-mean-valued and nontrivial on each component; positive means nonnegative unless strict positivity is stated. A potential is a nonnegative superharmonic function whose greatest harmonic minorant is zero. Measures are positive Radon measures unless signedness is specified. On noncompact spaces weak measure convergence in the source means vague convergence against $C_ c$. The prerequisites are multivariable calculus, Lebesgue integration, measure decomposition, and compact-metric measure representation. The harmonic and subharmonic results used below are established in the preceding Pome sections.

title: 3.3.1 Differentiating compact parameter integrals
text: Lemma 3.3.2 . 77E9E0297059 Let $U\subset \mathbb R^ m$ be open, let $C$ be compact, and let $\mu $ be a finite signed Borel measure on $C$. Suppose $u$ and all the partial derivatives $\partial _{x_ j}u$ are jointly continuous on $U\times C$. Then $F(x)=\int _ Cu(x,y)\, d\mu (y)$ is of class $C^1$ on $U$, and \[  \partial _ jF(x)=\int _ C\partial _{x_ j}u(x,y)\, d\mu (y).  \] Proof. Choose a closed ball $K\subset U$ whose interior contains $x$. All the functions in the hypotheses are bounded and uniformly continuous on $K\times C$. For sufficiently small $h\neq 0$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \[  \frac{u(x+he_ j,y)-u(x,y)}h =\int _0^1\partial _{x_ j}u(x+she_ j,y)\, ds.  \] This converges to $\partial _{x_ j}u(x,y)$ uniformly in $y\in C$. Integrating the uniform error against the finite measure $|\mu |$ proves the differentiation formula. The same uniform continuity, now applied to $\partial _{x_ j}u$, proves continuity of the derivative integral as $x$ varies inside $K$. Joint continuity of $u$ also makes $F$ finite and continuous. The ball $K$ can be chosen about every point of $U$, proving the assertion. $\square$ Continuity of the $x$ derivatives alone is insufficient. For example, an $x$-independent measurable function $u(x,y)=g(y)$ can fail to be integrable on $C$ even though all those derivatives are zero. The compact-parameter Poisson kernels used below satisfy the corrected hypotheses.

title: 3.3.6 Measures on a compact metric boundary
search_title: Measures on a compact metric boundary
text: In this section we use the Riesz representation theorem for continuous linear functionals on $C(X)$, with $X$ compact metric: a bounded real functional is integration against a unique finite signed regular Borel measure, and its operator norm is the measure's total variation. This is an explicit measure-theory prerequisite, not an unproved potential-theoretic input. Theorem 3.3.7 (Compact-metric measure selection) . 2C91786CB405 Let $X$ be a compact metric space, and let $(\mu _ j)$ be finite signed Borel measures with $\sup _ j\| \mu _ j\| \leq M<\infty $. There is a subsequence and a finite signed Borel measure $\mu $, with $\| \mu \| \leq M$, such that \[  \int _ X f\, d\mu _{j_ k}\longrightarrow \int _ X f\, d\mu \qquad (f\in C(X)).  \] If all the $\mu _ j$ are positive, then $\mu $ is positive. Proof. If $X$ is empty or $M=0$, every measure is zero and the assertion is immediate. First construct a countable dense subset of $C(X)$. For each positive integer $n$, choose a finite $1/n$-net $x_{n,1},\ldots ,x_{n,N_ n}$, and put \[  p_{n,i}(x)=\frac{(2/n-\operatorname {dist}(x,x_{n,i}))^+}{\sum _{l=1}^{N_ n}(2/n-\operatorname {dist}(x,x_{n,l}))^+}.  \] The denominator is everywhere positive. These continuous functions form a partition of unity, and $p_{n,i}(x)>0$ implies $\operatorname {dist}(x,x_{n,i})<2/n$. For $f\in C(X)$, choose rational $q_{n,i}$ within $1/n$ of $f(x_{n,i})$. Then $\sum _ iq_{n,i}p_{n,i}$ converges uniformly to $f$ by uniform continuity. All rational combinations for all $n$ form a countable dense family. Enumerate that family as $(g_ l)$. For every $l$, the sequence $\int g_ l\, d\mu _ j$ is bounded by $M\| g_ l\| _\infty $. Successive subsequences and diagonal extraction yield a subsequence along which all these integrals converge. If $f\in C(X)$ and $g_ l$ is uniformly close to $f$, then \[  \left|\int f\, d\mu _{j_ k}-\int f\, d\mu _{j_{k'}}\right| \leq 2M\| f-g_ l\| _\infty + \left|\int g_ l\, d\mu _{j_ k}-\int g_ l\, d\mu _{j_{k'}}\right|.  \] Hence the integrals of every $f$ are Cauchy. Their limit $L(f)$ is a real linear functional with $|L(f)|\leq M\| f\| _\infty $. Riesz representation gives the required $\mu $ with $\| \mu \| \leq M$. If the original measures are positive, $L(f)\geq 0$ for $f\geq 0$; the positivity part of Riesz representation makes $\mu $ positive. $\square$ This form also applies to compactified boundaries, which need not be subsets of a fixed Euclidean space.

title: 3.2.11 Bounded boundary data
text: Theorem 3.2.12 (Half-space Poisson integral) . 9ADD2DF19642 Let $f:\mathbb R^{d-1}\to \mathbb R$ be bounded and Lebesgue measurable, and let $c\in \mathbb R$. Then \[  u(x',t)=ct+\int _{\mathbb R^{d-1}}P_ H((x',t),z)f(z)\, dz  \] is harmonic on $H$, and $|u(x',t)-ct|\leq \| f\| _\infty $. If $f$ is continuous at $z_0$, then $u(x',t)\to f(z_0)$ as $(x',t)\to (z_0,0)$ within $H$, with no restriction on the approach. Moreover $u(0,t)/t\to c$ as $t\to \infty $. Proof. We first verify the normalization AB2849CD8791 3.2.13 \begin{equation}  \int _{\mathbb R^{d-1}}P_ H((x',t),z)\, dz=1. \end{equation} Translation and the substitution $z=x'+tw$ reduce the integral to $\frac{2}{s_{d-1}}\int _{\mathbb R^{d-1}}(1+|w|^2)^{-d/2}\, dw$. The map \[  F(w)=\frac{(w,1)}{\sqrt{1+|w|^2}}  \] parametrizes the upper hemisphere. With $m=d-1$, its metric matrix is $DF^{\mathsf T}DF=(1+|w|^2)^{-1}I-(1+|w|^2)^{-2}ww^{\mathsf T}$. Its eigenvalues are $(1+|w|^2)^{-1}$ in the $m-1$ perpendicular directions and $(1+|w|^2)^{-2}$ in the direction of $w$. The square root of its determinant is $(1+|w|^2)^{-d/2}$. At $w=0$ this formula holds by continuity. The surface area formula and reflection in the equatorial plane show that the last integral is $s_{d-1}/2$, proving ( 3.2.13 ). This also treats $d=2$, when $m=1$ and there are no perpendicular directions. The weighted measure $|f(z)|\, dz$ satisfies ( 3.2.8 ), by the same integral at $(0,1)$. Applying the differentiation estimates in the proof of Theorem 3.2.6 to the positive and negative parts of $f$ proves harmonicity. The positivity and normalization of $P_ H$ give the stated bound. Fix $\varepsilon >0$. At a continuity point $z_0$, choose $\delta >0$ so that $|f(z)-f(z_0)|<\varepsilon $ for $|z-z_0|<\delta $. The contribution of this set to $|\int P_ H(x,z)(f(z)-f(z_0))\, dz|$ is at most $\varepsilon $. If $|x'-z_0|<\delta /2$ and $|z-z_0|\geq \delta $, then $|z-x'|\geq \delta /2$. Writing $s_{d-2}$ for the area of the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^{d-1}$ (in particular $s_0=2$), polar integration gives \[  \int _{|z-z_0|\geq \delta }P_ H(x,z)\, dz \leq \frac{2t}{s_{d-1}}s_{d-2}\int _{\delta /2}^{\infty }r^{-2}\, dr =\frac{4s_{d-2}}{s_{d-1}}\frac{t}{\delta }.  \] Thus \[  |u(x',t)-f(z_0)|\leq |c|t+\varepsilon + \frac{8s_{d-2}}{s_{d-1}}\| f\| _\infty \frac{t}{\delta }  \] near $(z_0,0)$. Letting $(x',t)\to (z_0,0)$ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ proves the boundary limit. Finally $|u(0,t)/t-c|\leq \| f\| _\infty /t\to 0$. $\square$ For continuous bounded boundary data, varying $c$ gives distinct harmonic solutions with the same finite boundary values. This states nonuniqueness without a growth condition; it does not classify all such solutions.

title: 3.3.8 Radial boundary limits from symmetric densities
search_title: Radial boundary limits from symmetric densities
text: Theorem 3.3.9 . CAE5D89698DF Let $B=B(0,R)\subset \mathbb R^ d$, $d\ge 2$, and let $\sigma $ be surface measure on $S=\partial B$. Let $\mu $ be a finite signed measure on $S$. For $\zeta \in S$ put $C_ s=\{ y\in S:|y-\zeta |\le s\} $. If $\mu (C_ s)/\sigma (C_ s)\to a\in \mathbb R$ as $s\downarrow 0$, then $P_ B\mu (t\zeta )\to a$ as $t\uparrow 1$. Proof. Subtract $a\sigma $, whose Poisson integral is the constant $a$. Thus $F(s)=\mu (C_ s)=o(A(s))$, where $A(s)=\sigma (C_ s)$. In particular $\mu (\{ \zeta \} )=0$. Fix $0<\delta <2R$ so that $|F(s)|\le \varepsilon A(s)$ for $0<s\le \delta $. The ball Poisson kernel at $t\zeta $ is a function of $s=|y-\zeta |$: \[  k_ t(s)=\frac{R^2(1-t^2)}{s_{d-1}R\, [R^2(1-t)^2+ts^2]^{d/2}}.  \] Here $s_{d-1}$ is the area of the unit sphere. This function is decreasing and smooth for $s\ge 0$, $0<t<1$. Integration of $k_ t(s)=k_ t(\delta )+\int _ s^\delta (-k_ t'(v))\, dv$ against the pushforward of $\mu |_{C_\delta }$, using finite signed Fubini, gives \[  \int _{C_\delta }k_ t(|y-\zeta |)\, d\mu =k_ t(\delta )F(\delta )+\int _0^\delta (-k_ t'(s))F(s)\, ds.  \] For each fixed $t$ all integrands are bounded and $\mu $ is finite, so this identity also holds when $F$ has jumps. Its absolute value is at most $\varepsilon \int _{C_\delta }k_ t\, d\sigma \le \varepsilon $, by positivity and normalization of the Poisson kernel. On $S\setminus C_\delta $, $\sup k_ t\to 0$, so the remaining integral tends to zero, bounded by $|\mu |(S)\sup _{s\ge \delta }k_ t(s)$. Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. $\square$

title: 3.3.10 Fine coverings and differentiation on a sphere

text:
Lemma 3.3.11 . 3FB36EAD186A Let $X$ be a compact metric space and $A\subset X$. Let $\mathcal F$ be a family of closed sets of positive diameter such that every $x\in A$ belongs to members of arbitrarily small diameter. There is a finite or countably infinite disjoint sequence $F_ j\in \mathcal F$ such that, in the finite case, $A\subset  igcup _ jF_ j$, and, in the infinite case, for every $j$, \[  A\subset  igcup _{i\le j}F_ i\  \cup  igcup _{i>j}N(F_ i,3\operatorname {diam}F_ i).  \] Here $N(F,r)=\{ x:d(x,F)<r\} $. If a finite complete measure $m$ satisfies $0<m(F)$ and $m(N(F,3\operatorname {diam}F))\le C m(F)$ for all eligible members, the sequence covers $A$ except for an $m$-null set. Proof. If $A=\varnothing $, choose the empty sequence. Otherwise choose any $F_1$. After $F_1,\ldots ,F_ j$, stop if they cover $A$. If they do not, a point outside their closed union belongs to sufficiently small members $F$ with $N(F,\operatorname {diam}F)$ disjoint from that union. Let $e_ j>0$ be the supremum of their diameters, and choose such an $F_{j+1}$ with diameter $>2e_ j/3$. All chosen sets are disjoint. Fix $x\in A\setminus  igcup _{i\le j}F_ i$ and choose a member $F$ containing $x$ whose diameter is so small that its diameter-neighborhood avoids the first $j$ sets. It must meet a later chosen $F_ k$ in that neighborhood. Otherwise it remains eligible forever, so all subsequent chosen diameters exceed $2\operatorname {diam}F/3$; choosing a point in each yields an infinite uniformly separated subset of compact $X$, impossible. At the first such $k$, $\operatorname {diam}F_ k>2\operatorname {diam}F/3$. Some point of $F_ k$ is within $\operatorname {diam}F$ of $F$, hence $d(x,F_ k)<2\operatorname {diam}F<3\operatorname {diam}F_ k$. This proves the covering assertion. In the measure case the outer measure of the uncovered set is at most $C\sum _{i>j}m(F_ i)$ for every $j$; the tail tends to zero because the sets are disjoint and $m(X)<\infty $. Completeness makes every subset of the resulting null set measurable. $\square$ Theorem 3.3.12 . 5F363A880A82 Let $S=\partial B(0,R)\subset \mathbb R^ d$, $d\ge 2$, with completed surface measure $\sigma $. A finite signed measure $\mu =f\sigma +\mu _ s$ has, for $\sigma $-almost every $\zeta $, the derivative \[  \lim _{\substack {\zeta \in K\ \operatorname {diam}K	o 0}}  rac{\mu (K)}{\sigma (K)}=f(\zeta ).  \] The sets $K$ are closed spherical caps of positive diameter less than a hemisphere. Moreover almost every $\zeta $ is a Lebesgue point: \[   rac1{\sigma (K)}\int _ K|f(y)-f(\zeta )|\, d\sigma (y)\longrightarrow 0 \quad (\zeta \in K,\  \operatorname {diam}K	o 0).  \] Proof. Small spherical caps satisfy uniform estimates $c r^{d-1}\le \sigma (K)\le C r^{d-1}$, $r=\operatorname {diam}K$, and $\sigma (N_ S(K,3r))\le C'\sigma (K)$. To verify them, cover $S$ by finitely many graph charts over tangent hyperplanes on which the graph map and its inverse have bounded derivatives and the surface Jacobian is bounded above and below by positive constants. title: Lemma 3.3.11
text: Lemma 3.3.11 . 3FB36EAD186A Let $X$ be a compact metric space and $A\subset X$. Let $\mathcal F$ be a family of closed sets of positive diameter such that every $x\in A$ belongs to members of arbitrarily small diameter. There is a finite or countably infinite disjoint sequence $F_ j\in \mathcal F$ such that, in the finite case, $A\subset \bigcup _ jF_ j$, and, in the infinite case, for every $j$, \[  A\subset \bigcup _{i\le j}F_ i\  \cup \bigcup _{i>j}N(F_ i,3\operatorname {diam}F_ i).  \] Here $N(F,r)=\{ x:d(x,F)<r\} $. If a finite complete measure $m$ satisfies $0<m(F)$ and $m(N(F,3\operatorname {diam}F))\le C m(F)$ for all eligible members, the sequence covers $A$ except for an $m$-null set. Proof. If $A=\varnothing $, choose the empty sequence. Otherwise choose any $F_1$. After $F_1,\ldots ,F_ j$, stop if they cover $A$. If they do not, a point outside their closed union belongs to sufficiently small members $F$ with $N(F,\operatorname {diam}F)$ disjoint from that union. Let $e_ j>0$ be the supremum of their diameters, and choose such an $F_{j+1}$ with diameter $>2e_ j/3$. All chosen sets are disjoint. Fix $x\in A\setminus \bigcup _{i\le j}F_ i$ and choose a member $F$ containing $x$ whose diameter is so small that its diameter-neighborhood avoids the first $j$ sets. It must meet a later chosen $F_ k$ in that neighborhood. Otherwise it remains eligible forever, so all subsequent chosen diameters exceed $2\operatorname {diam}F/3$; choosing a point in each yields an infinite uniformly separated subset of compact $X$, impossible. At the first such $k$, $\operatorname {diam}F_ k>2\operatorname {diam}F/3$. In the measure case the outer measure of the uncovered set is at most $C\sum _{i>j}m(F_ i)$ for every $j$; the tail tends to zero because the sets are disjoint and $m(X)<\infty $. Completeness makes every subset of the resulting null set measurable. $\square$

title: 3.3.15 Harmonic reflection across a sphere
text: Lemma 3.3.16 . B0CFE200676D A nonnegative harmonic function $h$ on a punctured neighborhood of $a$ has the form $c\Phi (\cdot -a)+v$, where $c\ge 0$, $v$ is harmonic across $a$, and $\Phi (z)=\log (1/|z|)$ for $d=2$, $\Phi (z)=|z|^{2-d}$ for $d\ge 3$. Proof. This is a short consequence of the checked local Riesz decomposition. On a sufficiently small ball define $u=h+\Phi (\cdot -a)$ off $a$ and $u(a)=+\infty $. The fundamental function tends to infinity, and $h\ge 0$; thus $u$ is lsc and is superharmonic, using locality off $a$ and the trivial supermean inequality at $a$. It is locally integrable by the checked local integrability theorem. Its positive Riesz measure $-\Delta u$ is supported at $a$, so it equals $b\delta _ a$ with $b\ge 0$. Since $-\Delta \Phi =c_ d\delta _ a$, where $c_2=2\pi $ and $c_ d=(d-2)s_{d-1}$ otherwise, Weyl's lemma gives $u=(b/c_ d)\Phi +v$ almost everywhere. Equality holds everywhere off $a$ by continuity. Hence $h=(b/c_ d-1)\Phi +v$ there, and its nonnegativity near $a$ forces $c=b/c_ d-1\ge 0$. This also proves removability when $h$ is bounded, or when a one-sided bounded harmonic function has a finite limit along one approach to $a$. $\square$ Theorem 3.3.17 . 14F410C2E770 Let $0<r<R$ and let $h$ be continuous on the closed annulus $r\le |x-a|\le R$, harmonic on its interior, and zero on $|x-a|=R$. It has a harmonic extension across that sphere to $r<|x-a|<R+\varepsilon $ for some $\varepsilon >0$. Proof. First, odd reflection across a hyperplane preserves harmonicity for a harmonic function continuous and zero at that plane. The reflected function is continuous; at a center on the plane its spherical means vanish by the reflection symmetry, and away from the plane sufficiently small spheres have the usual harmonic mean property. The checked local mean characterization therefore proves harmonicity across the plane. Translate $a=0$. Add a sufficiently large positive multiple of $\log (R/|x|)$ if $d=2$, or of $|x|^{2-d}-R^{2-d}$ otherwise, so that the result is nonnegative on the inner sphere. The minimum principle makes it nonnegative throughout the annulus. These added functions already extend harmonically across the outer sphere, so it suffices to treat $h\ge 0$. Choose $b$ on the outer sphere and invert about a sphere centered at $b$. The outer sphere minus $b$ becomes a hyperplane, and the inner closed ball becomes a compact ball strictly in one of its half-spaces. The Kelvin transform is harmonic outside that compact ball in the half-space, continuous and zero at its planar boundary. Reflect it oddly. Applying the inverse Kelvin transform gives a harmonic extension on a neighborhood of the original closed annulus, except possibly at $b$. On its exterior side this extension is nonpositive, since the reflected function is nonpositive and the Kelvin multiplier is positive. On the interior side it tends to zero at $b$, so it is bounded above on a punctured neighborhood of $b$. Apply the preceding lemma to a constant minus this extension. Its singular coefficient must vanish because the extension has limit zero along the interior approach. Thus the singularity at $b$ is removable. Compactness of the outer sphere gives one $\varepsilon >0$ valid around the whole sphere. Finally subtract the added radial harmonic function. $\square$

title: 3.5.1 Harmonic lowering and greatest harmonic minorants
search_title: Harmonic lowering and greatest harmonic minorants
text: The following arguments use superharmonic functions in the nontrivial componentwise sense. Harmonic lowering $L_ Bu$ equals the Poisson integral of $u|_{\partial B}$ in $B\Subset \Omega $, and equals $u$ outside $B$. The checked comparison and Poisson boundary lower-limit statements show that $L_ Bu$ is superharmonic and $L_ Bu\le u$: at a boundary point it is lsc, and its sphere averages are at most those of $u$, with the same center value. In $B$ it is harmonic, and elsewhere locality applies. Lemma 3.5.2 . AC0C4669DCBF Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty family of superharmonic functions on an open set $\Omega $, closed under pairwise minimum and under every harmonic lowering. Its infimum is harmonic or identically $-\infty $ on each component. Proof. On a ball $B\Subset \Omega $ its infimum is also $\inf _{u\in \mathcal F}L_ Bu$, since $L_ Bu\le u$ and $L_ Bu\in \mathcal F$. The lowered harmonic functions form a downward directed family: $L_ B(\min (u,v))\le \min (L_ Bu,L_ Bv)$ by positivity of the Poisson kernel. A downward directed family of harmonic functions has harmonic infimum or infimum identically $-\infty $ on a ball. To see this from the checked Harnack convergence theorem, negate and restrict to the cofinal subfamily above one fixed member; its differences from that member are nonnegative harmonic. If bounded at one point, Harnack chains bound them on compact subsets, and harmonic compactness shows their directed supremum harmonic. If unbounded at a point, Harnack chains make the supremum infinity everywhere. Thus the infimum is locally harmonic or locally identically $-\infty $. The regions of these two alternatives are disjoint open sets; connectedness of each component leaves only one alternative. $\square$ Theorem 3.5.3 . 2791D284428C Let $u$ be superharmonic on $\Omega $ and $W\subset \Omega $ open. Choose balls $B_ j\Subset W$ covering $W$, with each chosen ball repeated infinitely often, and set $u_0=u$, $u_ j=L_{B_ j}u_{j-1}$. Then $u_ j$ decreases to $u_\infty $, equal to $u$ outside $W$, and harmonic or identically $-\infty $ on each component of $W$. If $u$ has a harmonic minorant on $W$, the restriction $u_\infty |_ W$ is its unique greatest harmonic minorant, independent of the ball sequence. This operation is additive on superharmonic functions having harmonic minorants. Proof. Lowering makes the sequence decrease and leaves it fixed outside $W$. On each fixed ball, the subsequence of stages just lowered there is harmonic and decreases to the same limit; the checked harmonic monotone convergence theorem makes that limit harmonic or $-\infty $. Connectedness propagates the alternative as in the preceding proof. If $v$ is any harmonic minorant on $W$, positivity of the Poisson kernel proves inductively $v\le u_ j$ there. Thus $v\le u_\infty \le u$, which excludes $-\infty $ and proves maximality and uniqueness. For two functions use the same sequence of balls. Linearity of each lowering gives $(u+v)_ j=u_ j+v_ j$; the limits are finite on $W$ when harmonic minorants exist, so their sum is the corresponding greatest harmonic minorant. No claim is made that the unregularized $u_\infty $ is superharmonic across $\partial W$. $\square$

title: 3.5.4 Minimal Green functions on general open sets
search_title: Minimal Green functions on general open sets
text: Write $\Phi _ a(x)=\Phi (x-a)$, with the normalization of Lemma 3.3.16 . A minimal Green function on an open set $\Omega $ is a nonnegative kernel $G$ such that $G(a,\cdot )=\Phi _ a+h_ a$, $h_ a$ harmonic on $\Omega $, and $G(a,\cdot )\le \Phi _ a+w$ whenever $w$ is superharmonic on $\Omega $ and $\Phi _ a+w\ge 0$. At $a$, both kernels have value infinity; differences of singular kernels below mean the harmonic extension of their difference off the pole. Theorem 3.5.5 . F3C6870EA9A8 For $a\in \Omega $ put $\mathcal B_ a=\{ \Phi _ a+w\ge 0:w\text{ superharmonic on }\Omega \} $. A minimal Green function exists exactly when all these classes are nonempty, and then $G(a,\cdot )=\inf \mathcal B_ a$ and it is unique. Existence holds for every open set if $d\ge 3$, every bounded open set if $d=2$, every open subset of a Greenian open set, and every planar open set which is not dense or is disconnected. The whole plane, and the plane minus a closed discrete set, have no Green function. In $\mathbb R^ d$, $d\ge 3$, the Green function is $\Phi _ a$. Proof. The class $\mathcal B_ a$ is closed under minimum and lowering on balls away from $a$, since $\Phi _ a$ is harmonic there and lowering preserves superharmonicity of $w$. Its infimum $v$ is nonnegative and harmonic away from $a$ by Lemma 3.5.2 . On a ball about $a$, every member dominates the ball Green function: their harmonic singularities cancel and the superharmonic difference has nonnegative boundary lower limits. Hence $v$ also dominates that ball Green function. The local Bôcher lemma gives $v=c\Phi _ a+h$ with $c\ge 0$; the preceding domination forces $c\ge 1$. This expression defines harmonic $h$ across $a$ and on all of $\Omega $. Now $v/c=\Phi _ a+h/c\ge 0$ belongs to $\mathcal B_ a$, so $v\le v/c\le v$. If $c>1$, this would force $v=0$ off $a$, contradicting the ball domination. Thus $c=1$, and $v$ is the required minimal kernel. Uniqueness and necessity follow at once from the definition. For $d\ge 3$, $\Phi _ a\ge 0$ is an admissible member. For a bounded planar set, $\Phi _ a+C\ge 0$ for a sufficiently large constant. Restriction of an existing Green kernel supplies a member on any smaller open set. If a planar open set avoids a closed ball, translate and dilate so that it avoids $\overline{B(0,1)}$. For $a,y$ in it, \[  \log \frac{2|a||y|}{|a-y|} =\Phi _ a(y)+\log |y|+\log (2|a|)\ge 0,  \] since $|1/a-1/y|<2$. The last two terms are harmonic in $y$ there. For a disconnected planar open set, each component avoids a ball in another component and is Greenian. For a pole in one component, extend its harmonic correction by $-\Phi _ a$ on all the others; the resulting admissible member is zero on those other components. This proves existence for the union. A planar Green kernel would have a harmonic correction $h_ a\ge -\Phi _ a=\log |\cdot -a|$, which tends to infinity at infinity. On arbitrarily large circles the minimum principle would then force $h_ a(0)$ to exceed every constant, impossible. A minimal kernel is bounded outside every ball $B\Subset \Omega $ containing its pole. Indeed let $m=\max _{\partial B}G(a,\cdot )>0$, and replace it outside $B$ by $\min (G(a,\cdot ),2m)$. This agrees with $G$ near the sphere, is superharmonic, and after subtracting $\Phi _ a$ is superharmonic across the pole. Minimality bounds $G$ by this replacement. On a plane minus a closed discrete set, this bound and the Bôcher lemma remove every deleted point as a bounded harmonic singularity. The resulting nonnegative kernel has a harmonic correction on the whole plane, contradicting the preceding minimum-principle argument. Finally in dimension at least three on the whole space, $G=\Phi _ a+h_ a\le \Phi _ a$ makes $h_ a\le 0$ entire harmonic, hence constant by Liouville. Its constant must be zero because $G\ge 0$ and $\Phi _ a\to 0$ at infinity. $\square$ Theorem 3.5.6 . 9E37095B7A8A Minimal Green functions are monotone under inclusion of open sets and increase to $G_\Omega $ along an increasing exhaustion of a Greenian $\Omega $. They are symmetric, zero between different components, and strictly positive within one component. They are jointly continuous off the diagonal and tend to infinity jointly at the diagonal. For $\overline{B(b,r)}\subset \Omega $, the spherical average $\int _{\partial B(b,r)}G(z,y)\, d\sigma (y)$ is a finite continuous function of $z\in \Omega $. Proof. Restriction is admissible, proving domain monotonicity. Along an exhaustion the increasing limit is bounded above by $G_\Omega $ off the pole, hence harmonic there. The harmonic corrections $G_ j(a,\cdot )-\Phi _ a$ also increase and are bounded above by $h_ a$; harmonic monotone convergence across the pole makes their limit harmonic on all of $\Omega $. The limit is a nonnegative admissible kernel and is therefore $G_\Omega $ by minimality. Every harmonic minorant $v$ of $G(a,\cdot )$ satisfies $v\le 0$, since $G-v$ is admissible and minimality gives $G\le G-v$. Thus its greatest harmonic minorant is zero. In the simultaneous lowering process of the preceding theorem, applied to $G(a,\cdot )=\Phi _ a+h_ a$, the harmonic correction is invariant, so \[  0=(\Phi _ a)_\infty +h_ a,\qquad G(a,y)=\Phi _ a(y)-(\Phi _ a)_\infty (y).  \] We verify that $q(a,y)=(\Phi _ a)_\infty (y)$ is harmonic in $a$ for each fixed $y$. Choose a locally finite cover of $\Omega $ by relatively compact balls, and enumerate it with repetitions. Such a cover is obtained by covering the compact layers of a nested compact exhaustion by finitely many small balls lying in adjacent exhaustion layers; only finitely many distinct balls meet each compact subset. Its union of boundary spheres $C$ is relatively closed. At a finite lowering stage, integration of $\Phi _ a(z)$ against the successive compact-sphere Poisson kernels is harmonic in $a$ away from those spheres and, until a ball containing $y$ has been used, possibly away from $y$. Differentiation is justified locally by positive distance from the finite union of spheres and bounded derivatives of the fundamental kernel; iterated finite integrals preserve those bounds. Once a ball containing $y$ has been used, there is no remaining point-pole exception. Consequently, on $\Omega \setminus C$ the decreasing stage limits are harmonic or $-\infty $. They are finite because $q(a,y)=-h_ a(y)$ for all $a,y$, as the preceding identity shows; hence they are harmonic there. They are finite by local surface integrability of a superharmonic function on interior spheres. The squeeze gives continuity at the pole on the sphere. Multiply by the constant surface area to pass from means to the stated integrals. $\square$

title: Theorem 3.5.5
text: Theorem 3.5.5 . F3C6870EA9A8 For $a\in \Omega $ put $\mathcal B_ a=\{ \Phi _ a+w\ge 0:w\text{ superharmonic on }\Omega \} $. A minimal Green function exists exactly when all these classes are nonempty, and then $G(a,\cdot )=\inf \mathcal B_ a$ and it is unique. Existence holds for every open set if $d\ge 3$, every bounded open set if $d=2$, every open subset of a Greenian open set, and every planar open set which is not dense or is disconnected. The whole plane, and the plane minus a closed discrete set, have no Green function. In $\mathbb R^ d$, $d\ge 3$, the Green function is $\Phi _ a$. Proof. The class $\mathcal B_ a$ is closed under minimum and lowering on balls away from $a$, since $\Phi _ a$ is harmonic there and lowering preserves superharmonicity of $w$. Its infimum $v$ is nonnegative and harmonic away from $a$ by Lemma 3.5.2 . On a ball about $a$, every member dominates the ball Green function: their harmonic singularities cancel and the superharmonic difference has nonnegative boundary lower limits. Hence $v$ also dominates that ball Green function. The local Bôcher lemma gives $v=c\Phi _ a+h$ with $c\ge 0$; the preceding domination forces $c\ge 1$. This expression defines harmonic $h$ across $a$ and on all of $\Omega $. Now $v/c=\Phi _ a+h/c\ge 0$ belongs to $\mathcal B_ a$, so $v\le v/c\le v$. If $c>1$, this would force $v=0$ off $a$, contradicting the ball domination. Thus $c=1$, and $v$ is the required minimal kernel. Uniqueness and necessity follow at once from the definition. For $d\ge 3$, $\Phi _ a\ge 0$ is an admissible member. For a bounded planar set, $\Phi _ a+C\ge 0$ for a sufficiently large constant. Restriction of an existing Green kernel supplies a member on any smaller open set. If a planar open set avoids a closed ball, translate and dilate so that it avoids $\overline{B(0,1)}$. For $a,y$ in it, \[  \log \frac{2|a||y|}{|a-y|} =\Phi _ a(y)+\log |y|+\log (2|a|)\ge 0,  \] since $|1/a-1/y|<2$. The last two terms are harmonic in $y$ there. For a disconnected planar open set, each component avoids a ball in another component and is Greenian. For a pole in one component, extend its harmonic correction by $-\Phi _ a$ on all the others; the resulting admissible member is zero on those other components. This proves existence for the union. A planar Green kernel would have a harmonic correction $h_ a\ge -\Phi _ a=\log |\cdot -a|$, which tends to infinity at infinity. On arbitrarily large circles the minimum principle would then force $h_ a(0)$ to exceed every constant, impossible. A minimal kernel is bounded outside every ball $B\Subset \Omega $ containing its pole. Indeed let $m=\max _{\partial B}G(a,\cdot )>0$, and replace it outside $B$ by $\min (G(a,\cdot ),2m)$. This agrees with $G$ near the sphere, is superharmonic, and after subtracting $\Phi _ a$ is superharmonic across the pole. Minimality bounds $G$ by this replacement. On a plane minus a closed discrete set, this bound and the Bôcher lemma remove every deleted point as a bounded harmonic singularity. The resulting nonnegative kernel has a harmonic correction on the whole plane, contradicting the preceding minimum-principle argument. Finally in dimension at least three on the whole space, $G=\Phi _ a+h_ a\le \Phi _ a$ makes $h_ a\le 0$ entire harmonic, hence constant by Liouville. Its constant must be zero because $G\ge 0$ and $\Phi _ a\to 0$ at infinity. $\square$

title: 3.5.7 Potentials and global Riesz decomposition
text:
Throughout this section $G_\Omega $ is the unnormalized minimal Green kernel, $-\Delta G_\Omega (\cdot ,y)=c_ d\delta _ y$. Measures are positive Radon measures; they need not have finite total mass. A potential means $p=G_\Omega \mu $ which is not identically infinity on any component. Theorem 3.5.8 . 977ECF0867E0 The integral $G_\Omega \mu $ is lsc and supermean, hence superharmonic on every component where it is nontrivial. Every finite measure has a potential. For any potential, \[  -\Delta (G_\Omega \mu )=c_ d\mu  \] in distributions. Its greatest harmonic minorant is zero. It is harmonic on an open set exactly when that set has $\mu $-measure zero. Two potentials whose difference is harmonic almost everywhere on an open set have equal measures there. If $S\subset \Omega $ is open, $\mu $ is supported in $S$ and $G_\Omega \mu $ is a potential, then $G_\Omega \mu =G_ S\mu +h$ on $S$ with $h\ge 0$ harmonic. Reciprocity $\int G\mu \, d
u =\int G
u \, d\mu $ holds in $[0,\infty ]$. Proof. Fatou's lemma applied to the nonnegative continuous extended kernel gives lsc; Tonelli and the supermean inequality for each pole give supermeans. If $\mu $ is finite and gives zero mass to a closed interior ball containing $x$, the bound for $G(x,\cdot )$ outside that ball makes its potential finite at $x$, hence superharmonic on that component. Split a finite measure into its part on a small interior ball and its complement. Each part misses some interior ball in the component, so both have superharmonic potentials and their sum is superharmonic. Apply this separately to every component, using that $G$ vanishes between components. A potential $p$ is locally integrable by superharmonic local integrability. For $\varphi \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$, \[  \iint G(x,y)|\Delta \varphi (x)|\, dx\, d\mu (y) =\int p(x)|\Delta \varphi (x)|\, dx<\infty .  \] Thus signed Fubini is legitimate, and the fundamental-solution identity plus harmonicity of the correction gives $\int p\Delta \varphi =-c_ d\int \varphi \, d\mu $. In particular a harmonic potential has zero measure; more generally subtracting the distributional identities proves equality of measures wherever the difference is harmonic. If $\mu (U)=0$, Weyl's lemma gives a harmonic representative on $U$; canonical representative uniqueness identifies it pointwise with $p$. For the greatest minorant use the same sequence of harmonic lowerings for $p$ and for every kernel $G(\cdot ,y)$. Induction and nonnegative Tonelli show $p_ j(x)=\int G_ j(x,y)\, d\mu (y)$. For each $y$, $G_ j(x,y)\downarrow 0$, because the greatest harmonic minorant of the minimal Green kernel is zero. In each connected component choose $x_0$ with $p(x_0)<\infty $. Dominated convergence gives $p_\infty (x_0)=0$; its nonnegative harmonic minorant is therefore zero on that component by the minimum principle. This is a componentwise argument, even when $\Omega $ is disconnected. On $S$, domain monotonicity gives $0\le G_ S\mu \le p$. Both potentials are locally integrable; their distributional difference is harmonic and nonnegative almost everywhere, hence a nonnegative harmonic $h$. Equality $p=G_ S\mu +h$ holds everywhere by uniqueness of superharmonic representatives. Finally symmetry of $G$ and nonnegative Tonelli give reciprocity, including infinite values. None of these arguments separates divergent fundamental and harmonic-correction integrals. $\square$ Theorem 3.5.9 . 9453A8C660CC Let $u$ be superharmonic on a Greenian open set $\Omega $. Its unique Riesz measure is $
u =-\Delta u/c_ d$. For each open $W\Subset \Omega $, \[  u=G_ W(
u |_ W)+h_ W\quad \hbox{on }W,  \] where $h_ W$ is the greatest harmonic minorant there. If $u\ge 0$ on $\Omega $, the same formula holds globally with $W=\Omega $ and a nonnegative harmonic $h$. Thus a nonnegative superharmonic function is a Green potential exactly when its greatest harmonic minorant is zero. Proof. The checked distributional characterization gives the positive Radon measure $
u $. We first suppose $u$ is bounded below by a constant $m$ on its Greenian domain $D$ (either $D=W\Subset \Omega $, or $D=\Omega $ and $m=0$). For a compact $K\subset D$ put $p_ K=G_ D(
u |_ K)$, a potential of a finite measure. The locally integrable difference $u-p_ K$ has nonpositive Laplacian, so it has a superharmonic representative $w_ K$, and $u=w_ K+p_ K$ everywhere by canonical representative uniqueness. The function $p_ K$ is bounded outside some compact neighborhood $K'\Subset D$. Here is the required uniformity: cover $K$ by finitely many small balls whose closures lie in $D$. On each, Harnack chains bound $G_ D(x,y)$ for $y$ in its smaller concentric ball by a fixed multiple of $G_ D(x,y_ i)$, whenever $x$ lies outside the union of the larger balls. Each fixed-pole kernel is bounded away from its pole; integrating the resulting finite uniform bound against $
u |_ K$ proves the assertion. Choose $K'$ containing these larger closed balls. On $D\setminus K'$, $w_ K=u-p_ K\ge m-M$; on $K'$ it is bounded below by lsc and compactness. Hence $w_ K$ has a constant harmonic minorant on all of $D$. The greatest-minorant operation is additive, and $p_ K$ has greatest minorant zero. Thus $H_ Du=H_ Dw_ K\ge m$ because $u\ge m$. Consequently $w_ K\ge m$ and $p_ K\le u-m$. Exhaust $D$ by increasing compact $K_ j$. Monotone convergence gives $p=G_ D(
u |_ D)\le u-m$. This is finite almost everywhere, hence a potential. Its Riesz measure is $
u |_ D$, so $u-p$ is harmonic in distributions and has a harmonic representative $h$. Canonical uniqueness gives $u=p+h$ everywhere, and additivity of greatest minorants makes $h=H_ Du$. When $m=0$, $h\ge 0$. Applying this construction to every relatively compact $W$ proves the local assertion without assuming $u$ bounded below on the entire $\Omega $. Uniqueness of $
u $ follows from its distributional identity, and the last characterization follows from the zero-minorant property of potentials. $\square$

title: 3.5.10 Continuity of potentials and bounded densities
search_title: Continuity of potentials and bounded densities
text: Theorem 3.5.11 . 64E880580F0E Let $\mu $ have compact support $K\Subset \Omega $. If $(G_\Omega \mu )|_ K$ is continuous at $a\in K$, then $G_\Omega \mu $ is continuous at $a$, in the extended sense. If $G_\Omega \mu $ is finite on $K$, then for every $\varepsilon >0$ there is a compact $C\subset K$ with $\mu (K\setminus C)<\varepsilon $ for which $G_\Omega (\mu |_ C)$ is finite and continuous throughout $\Omega $. Proof. Near $K$ the Green potential differs from its fundamental potential by a harmonic function. Both potentials are locally integrable and have the same distributional Laplacian, so Weyl's lemma gives a harmonic difference. Adding that harmonic function preserves superharmonicity; canonical representatives then identify the equality everywhere, including infinite values. No joint continuity of a cancelled diagonal kernel is assumed. It suffices to prove the first assertion for $U\mu (x)=\int \Phi (x-y)d\mu (y)$. If $U\mu (a)=\infty $, lsc suffices. Otherwise choose a small ball $B$ about $a$ and split $\mu =\mu '+\mu ''$, with $\mu '=\mu |_ B$, so that the local singular integral $U\mu '(a)<\eta $. In the planar case take all relevant distances less than one so this local kernel is nonnegative. The remainder $U\mu ''$ is harmonic near $a$. If $z_ x\in K$ is a nearest point to $x$, then $z_ x\to a$ as $x\to a$, and $|z_ x-y|\le 2|x-y|$ for $y\in K$. For $d\ge 3$ this gives $U\mu '(x)\le 2^{d-2}U\mu '(z_ x)$. For $d=2$ it gives $U\mu '(x)\le U\mu '(z_ x)+(\log 2)\mu '(B)$. The restriction of $U\mu '$ to $K$ is continuous at $a$, being the difference of the assumed continuous restriction of $U\mu $ and the harmonic remainder. Thus the limsup of the local contribution is at most $2^{d-2}\eta $, or $\eta +(\log 2)\mu (B)$ in dimension two. In that case $\mu (\{ a\} )=0$ by finiteness of the potential, so $\mu (B)\to 0$ as the radius shrinks. The harmonic remainder is continuous; letting $\eta \to 0$ proves continuity. For the second assertion, Lusin's theorem gives compact $C\subset K$ with lost mass less than $\varepsilon $ and $G\mu |_ C$ finite continuous. On $C$, $G(\mu |_ C)=G\mu -G(\mu |_{K\setminus C})$ is upper semicontinuous, since the second term is lsc; it is also lsc. It is therefore continuous on $C$, and the first assertion gives continuity at every point of $C$. Off $C$ it is harmonic. This proves global finite continuity. $\square$ Theorem 3.5.12 . 9CF388990FE4 If $f\in L^1(\Omega )\cap L^\infty (\Omega )$, then $G_\Omega f$ is finite continuous on $\Omega $. For a ball and compactly supported measure its potential tends to zero at every boundary point. More generally suppose $\Omega $ is connected, has finite volume for $d\ge 3$, and is bounded for $d=2$. If $G_\Omega (x,y_0)\to 0$ as $x\to a\in \partial \Omega $ for one $y_0\in \Omega $, then $G_\Omega f(x)\to 0$ for every bounded measurable $f$. Proof. Separate the positive and negative parts of $f$. They are finite measures, so have superharmonic potentials. On an interior ball, the contribution from its complement is harmonic; the local contribution differs from a fundamental potential by a harmonic function. Its singular integral over a ball of radius $r$ is uniformly at most $\| f\| _\infty s_{d-1}r^2/2$ for $d\ge 3$, and $2\pi \| f\| _\infty \int _0^ r s\log (1/s)ds$ in the plane, after adding a harmless local constant. These bounds tend to zero. To justify that a ball centered elsewhere has no larger integral of the radial decreasing positive kernel, use its layer-cake representation: intersection with every centered superlevel ball has volume at most the smaller of the two ball volumes. The nonsingular part is continuous by dominated convergence, proving the first assertion and finiteness. For the boundary assertions, Harnack chains in the pole variable make $G(x,\cdot )\to 0$ uniformly on any fixed compact subset when it tends to zero at one pole. The explicit ball kernel supplies this condition at every ball boundary point, so compactly supported potentials tend to zero. Exhaust $\Omega $ by compact $K_ j$. In dimension at least three, $G(x,y)\le |x-y|^{2-d}$, and the layer-cake estimate just proved yields \[  \sup _ x\int _{\Omega \setminus K_ j}G(x,y)|f(y)|dy \le \tfrac 12s_{d-1}\| f\| _\infty (|\Omega \setminus K_ j|/v_ d)^{2/d}\longrightarrow 0.  \] For a bounded planar domain choose $D>\operatorname {diam}\Omega $; $G(x,y)\le \log (D/|x-y|)$ by minimality, and the same estimate is the integral of this radial kernel over a disk of the tail's area, tending to zero. Thus the compact-support integrals approximate $Gf$ uniformly in $x$, and their boundary limits are zero. $\square$

title: 3.5.13 The generalized Laplacian

If $u$ is continuous and $\widetilde\Delta u=0$ on an open set, then $u$ is harmonic there. Proof. Near a fixed $x$, the contribution of the measure outside a small closed ball is harmonic, and the local Green potential differs from its fundamental potential by a harmonic function. Harmonic functions contribute zero to the generalized Laplacian. The sphere average of $\Phi (\cdot -y)$ at center $x$ is $\Phi (r)$ when $|x-y|\le r$ and $\Phi (x-y)$ otherwise. For the second case this is the harmonic mean property. For the first, rotation invariance gives a radial harmonic function of $y$ inside the sphere, smooth there by differentiation, hence constant, with its value at the center equal to $\Phi (r)$. Here is uniform control at the sphere: its surface measure in any ball of radius $s$ centered on or near it is at most $Cs^{d-1}$, by finitely many bounded graph charts. Layer-cake integration therefore bounds its fundamental singular integral on such a cap by $Cs$ for $d\ge 3$, and by $Cs(1+|\log s|)$ for $d=2$. These bounds tend to zero uniformly in the pole. The remaining kernel is uniformly continuous, proving continuity across the sphere. Consequently \[  \frac{2d}{r^2}(M_ rGf(x)-Gf(x)) =\frac{2d}{r^2}\int _{|y-x|<r}[\Phi (r)-\Phi (x-y)]f(y)dy.  \] The bracket is nonpositive. Its absolute integral is $\pi r^2/2$ for $d=2$, since $2\pi \int _0^ r s\log (r/s)ds=\pi r^2/2$; for $d\ge 3$ it is $s_{d-1}r^2(1/2-1/d)$. Thus the expression for constant $f(x)$ is exactly $-c_ df(x)$, while the error is at most $c_ d\sup _{|y-x|<r}|f(y)-f(x)|$, tending to zero. For the converse fix a ball $B\Subset \Omega $, let $H$ be the continuous Poisson solution with boundary values $u$, and let $w=G_ B1$, continuous, zero at the boundary, with $\widetilde\Delta w=-c_ d$ by the first part. For $t>0$, both $u-H+tw$ and $H-u+tw$ have strictly negative generalized Laplacian. Hence at every point they satisfy the strict local supermean inequality for all sufficiently small radii. The elementary minimum principle for continuous locally supermean functions, proved by the open-and-closed minimum set argument, implies they are nonnegative on $B$ because their boundary values are zero. title: 4.3.1 Global polar functions and exact compact pole sets
search_title: Global polar functions and exact compact pole sets
text: Theorem 4.3.2 . 253540032CE5 Every polar subset $A\subset \mathbb R^ d$, $d\ge 2$, is contained in the infinite locus of an entire superharmonic function. If $a\notin A$, that function can be chosen finite at $a$. For $d\ge 3$ it can be chosen as a Newtonian potential of a finite positive measure. If $K\Subset \Omega $ is compact and polar in a Greenian open set, there is a finite compactly supported measure $\mu $ on $\Omega $ with $G_\Omega \mu =\infty $ on $K$ and $G_\Omega \mu <\infty $ everywhere else in $\Omega $. Proof. We use the checked Foundations polar globalization : every bounded polar set has a finite compactly supported fundamental measure whose potential is infinite on that set. For the prescribed point put $A_ j=A\cap \{ 1/j\le |x-a|\le j\} $. Apply that result and restrict the resulting measure to $\{ |y-a|>1/(2j)\} $. The removed part has a bounded kernel at each point of $A_ j$, so the restricted fundamental potential $p_ j$ is still infinite on $A_ j$ and finite at $a$. In dimension at least three choose $b_ j>0$ so that $\sum b_ j(\mu _ j(\mathbb R^ d)+p_ j(a))<\infty $. Then $\mu =\sum b_ j\mu _ j$ is finite and its positive Newtonian potential is finite at $a$ and infinite on $A=\bigcup A_ j$, by Tonelli. In dimension two set $q_ j=p_ j-m_ j$, where $m_ j$ is the finite infimum of $p_ j$ on $\overline{B(a,j)}$. Such an infimum is finite by lsc and local integrability. Choose $b_ j>0$ with $\sum b_ jq_ j(a)<\infty $. For each fixed integer $k$, the tail $\sum _{j\ge k}b_ jq_ j$ is a monotone sum of nonnegative superharmonic functions on $B(a,k)$, finite at $a$; it is superharmonic there. Adding the finite initial sum gives an entire superharmonic function, finite at $a$ and infinite on $A$. Without a prescribed point, first choose $a$ outside the polar (hence null) set. For the last assertion first treat $K$ contained in an interior ball $B$. Its normalized ball capacity is zero by the checked polar zero capacity . Choose decreasing compact neighborhoods $K_ j\Subset B$ with intersection $K$; their capacitary potentials $v_ j$ lie in $[0,1]$, equal one near $K$, and decrease to zero off $K$. Indeed the limit is bounded harmonic off $K$, extends harmonically across $K$ by polar removability, and is dominated by the zero-minorant potential $v_1$, so is zero. On every compact subset of $B\setminus K$ this convergence is uniform by Dini. Pass to a subsequence such that both $\operatorname {cap}_ B(K_ j)<2^{-j}$ and $v_ j<2^{-j}$ on the first $j$ members of a compact exhaustion of $B\setminus K$ (and put every support in one fixed compact subset of $B$). This is possible by decreasing capacity continuity and the preceding uniform convergence. Write $v_ j=G_ B\mu _ j$, scaling the normalized Riesz measures by $1/c_ d$ for our kernel. Then $\sum \mu _ j(B)<\infty $. The potential of $\mu =\sum \mu _ j$ is $\sum v_ j$, infinite on $K$ and finite off $K$ in $B$. Its fundamental potential differs by a harmonic function on $B$; thus it has exactly the same finiteness set there. Off the common compact support it is finite automatically. The same distributional/harmonic-correction argument transfers it to $G_\Omega \mu $ without changing its poles. The sum is finite, compactly supported in $\Omega $, infinite on $K$ and finite at every point outside $K$. $\square$

title: 4.3.3 Boundary minimum principles with polar exceptions
search_title: Boundary minimum principles with polar exceptions
text: Theorem 4.3.4 . 09FD5942CD4F Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ d$ be Greenian and let $u$ be superharmonic and bounded below on $\Omega $. Suppose $\liminf _{\Omega \ni x\to z}u(x)\ge \alpha $ for every boundary point outside a polar set $Z$. Then $u\ge \alpha $ if $d=2$, or if $\Omega $ is bounded. For an unbounded domain in dimension at least three the same conclusion holds provided $\liminf _{x\in \Omega ,|x|\to \infty }u(x)\ge \alpha $. Proof. For a bounded $\Omega $, a global polar function infinite on $Z$ can be made nonnegative on $\overline\Omega $ by adding a constant. Call it $v$. Then $u+\varepsilon v$ has boundary lower limits at least $\alpha $ at all points, including $Z$, since $u$ is bounded below. The bounded-domain minimum principle gives $u+\varepsilon v\ge \alpha $. Average over a small interior ball; its average of $v$ is finite. Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and then the radius decrease to zero to obtain $u\ge \alpha $ everywhere. The case with a condition at infinity follows by truncating with large balls, using $u\ge \alpha -\eta $ outside such a ball, and then letting $\eta \downarrow 0$. We need one planar fact: the boundary of a nonempty Greenian open set is not polar. If $\Omega $ is not dense and its boundary were polar, take an entire superharmonic polar function $v$ infinite there and replace it by infinity on one component of $\Omega $. The result is lsc, locally supermean (the boundary values are infinity), finite somewhere in the open complement, and hence superharmonic on the plane. It cannot be infinity on a nonempty open set, a contradiction. If $\Omega $ is dense, its complement equals its boundary. A fixed-pole Green function is bounded away from its pole, so polar removability extends it harmonically across the complement outside a small pole ball. Its harmonic correction then extends to the whole plane, and the resulting nonnegative fundamental-plus-harmonic function contradicts the whole-plane nonexistence proved earlier. Thus the planar fact holds. For unbounded planar $\Omega $, choose $z_0\in \partial \Omega \setminus Z$. For any $\eta >0$ choose $r>0$ with $u\ge \alpha -\eta $ on $\Omega \cap \overline{B(z_0,r)}$. On $D=\Omega \setminus \overline{B(z_0,r)}$ the function $v(x)=\log (|x-z_0|/r)$ is nonnegative harmonic and tends to infinity at infinity. Since $u$ is bounded below, $u+\varepsilon v$ satisfies the required boundary inequality $\alpha -\eta $ on a sufficiently large outer sphere and on the inner sphere, and on the original boundary outside $Z$. The bounded-domain result gives $u+\varepsilon v\ge \alpha -\eta $ on every large truncation of $D$. Let the truncation grow, then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, then $\eta \downarrow 0$. Together with the inner ball inequality this proves the assertion on $\Omega $. $\square$

Repeated use gives the finite excess inequality \[  C^*( igcup _{i\le m}E_ i)-C^*( igcup _{i\le m}F_ i) \le \sum _{i\le m}(C^*(E_ i)-C^*(F_ i)),\quad F_ i\subset E_ i,  \] when the right side is finite; if a term is infinite use the equivalent inequality with sums on opposite sides. title: Theorem 4.3.6
text: Theorem 4.3.6 . C651523E22C3 For any $E$, $0\le \widehat R_ Eu\le R_ Eu\le u$, and the regularized reduction is superharmonic. It equals $u$ on the interior of $E$, is harmonic and equal to $R_ Eu$ outside $\overline E$, and differs from $R_ Eu$ only on a polar subset of $\partial E$. Reductions preserve order in $E,u$, positive scaling, and subadditivity in $u$. If $K\Subset \Omega $ is compact, then $\widehat R_ Ku$ is a Green potential, without assuming $u$ bounded on $K$. Proof. The family of majorants is nonempty (it contains $u$), closed under minimum and locally bounded below. The checked Foundations subharmonic envelope and polar limit discrepancy , applied after sign reversal, give superharmonic regularization and a polar discrepancy set. On $E$ the unregularized infimum equals $u$, and locality gives equality of the regularization on the interior. Outside $\overline E$, the family is saturated under ball lowering, so its infimum is harmonic by Lemma 3.5.2 ; it is nonnegative, excluding $-\infty $. Order and scaling follow from the defining families. Sums of majorants majorize the sum; the unregularized inequality passes to regularizations almost everywhere by the polar discrepancy assertion, and then everywhere by ball-average representatives. For bounded $u$ on $K$, in each component meeting $K$ choose a pole $a$. A multiple of $G(a,\cdot )$ majorizes $u$ on that component's compact intersection with $K$, since its positive lsc kernel has a positive minimum there. On all other components use $u$. This competitor shows $\widehat R_ Ku\le C G(a,\cdot )$ on the chosen component, so it has zero greatest harmonic minorant there. Components disjoint from $K$ have zero reduction. title: 3.5.15 A global extension finite outside a prescribed ball
search_title: A global extension finite outside a prescribed ball
text: Lemma 3.5.16 . 7C49056207BE If $u$ is superharmonic on $B(a,R)$ and $0<r<R$, there is an entire superharmonic function equal to $u$ on $B(a,r)$ and finite outside $\overline{B(a,r)}$. Proof. Shrink $R$ while keeping $r<R$, and subtract a lower bound so $u\ge 0$ on a neighborhood of the new closed ball. Reduce $u$ onto $K=\overline{B(a,r)}$ relative to $B(a,R)$. The regularized reduction $p$ equals $u$ inside $K$, is a potential with measure supported in $K$, and is harmonic outside $K$. Its measure is finite by compact support, so $p\to 0$ on the outer sphere. Harmonic reflection extends it to a slightly larger annulus; denote the extension again by $p$. Let $F(x)=\alpha (\Phi (x-a)-\Phi (Re_1))$. It is radial harmonic outside $a$ and zero on the outer sphere. The normal derivative of $\Phi $ is strictly negative there. Since $p$ is smooth on a compact collar of that sphere and zero on it, a sufficiently large $\alpha >0$ makes $F\ge p$ on the inner half of a thinner collar and $F\le p$ on its outer half: divide the radial differences by $|x-a|-R$ and use uniform continuity of the radial derivatives. Define $u^*=p$ inside the sphere and $u^*=F$ outside. In the collar it is the minimum of two harmonic functions, hence superharmonic, so locality proves it is entire superharmonic. It is finite outside $K$. Finally restore the subtracted constant. $\square$
